The Play

May 1988

May 3

So this boy just walks in smelling of Lip Smacker, Matterhorn cigarettes, and sex sweat. He doesn’t tell me his name and I don’t ask for it. Not that I gave him mine, but he didn’t ask for that either. Fine. Be one of them people. Don’t catch anybody’s name until proof that they have a name worth catching, but two can play that game. So, at the beginning his name was Yo. My sister said to me last week, “Eddy, your superpower is that you always read people right, from one sentence, one word, even over the phone.” Which is what she said to me last week when she handed me the phone in the middle of a call with Robbie Lindo because between telling her who she is prettier than and why she needs to check out his bedroom because he have him own video player she couldn’t tell if he was too cool or just some asshole trying to pull down her panties.

As for this hombre, he is more concerned with flinging himself into the armchair onstage, a prop for the play I suppose, throwing his right leg over the red velvet arm and spreading as wide as possible. Brown Levi’s 501 jeans, hard to find even in America. But his smell: Lip Smacker or candle wax maybe, although his lips look like he licks them too much. Matterhorn cigarettes because that is one of three that I know, and only because it was a menthol, meaning that it could have been any fucking cigarette. And fuck sweat, yes mos def. With this sort of homo gay is what he does, not who he is, and he was gay only an hour ago.

He’s first here other than the stage manager, who introduces himself as the stage manager. No Christian names for this bunch, but they sound like they know each other, which is likely in battyboy circles. Stage manager’s lips smile but the rest of his face couldn’t care less. On the brown jean boy’s shoulders is a Stüssy or Gap T-shirt. Somebody’s daddy can afford flights to Miami. Loose because this brother is no friend of fat. Vegetarianism, meaning “greens without the Rasta,” took off like a kite at the university but I’ve never seen this one on campus.

I wouldn’t call it an afro, but there must be a name for high, loose, curly hair that you neither cut nor style. Skin darker than me, darker than the stage manager, but lighter than chocolate. Toffee? There’s another name for that which don’t sound like it come from a four-year-old. Caramel? Now I’m starting to sound like a poem from primary school with snow in it. He is pissing me off. Mostly by being sort of cute. I mean, dimples, but screw him because he is giving this fuck-the-absurdity-of-it-all smile, which I see on every boy who graduated five years ago but still roams campus. Every time he looks at me he raises his left eyebrow. Big eyes, the kind that make you think a brother is friendly. No, not friendly, interested. No, not interested, curious. A neat beard wrapped around his chin, and a mustache over the thick lips that he keeps on licking reminds me that I am eighteen and only recently grew shit to shave. Wild hair but tame beard, who knows what that means. I try to stop myself from doing what I always do, which is to match him to somebody on TV. Okay, Michael Warren from Hill Street Blues. Shit, there I go again.

Sometimes I wish that what I wrote sounded like Prince lyrics. Instead I sound like a high school English lit student with a teacher who when he said he remembers the war, meant World War Two. For real. I wanted to tell him that nobody singing ’bout war no more, busha. Bob Marley still dead, and Prince is singing about AIDS. Bruce Springsteen has a song called “War,” but it’s not him who sang it first, and I’m only writing about it because Bruce is wearing jeans in that video, and Jeeeeeeesus man, them trousers acting like they been waiting from the day they were just cotton balls to run up the length of his legs to hit-and-run the biggest boss bulge in rock and roll where those two thighs are only too happy to meet, so happy that if he turns around to show his backside, right above the crack will be a patch of sweat in a perfect V.

The rain just spent the whole afternoon beating Kingston into a gray that stays that way even when it gets dark. There is this thing about Jamdown, which I never notice in foreign, that by evening even the city starts to smell and sound like country. Crickets and dewy grass and car tires rolling over what sounds more like mud than road, and mosquitoes that think they sing like birds, and won’t leave you alone. And just this, I don’t know, sadness. I love it.

There is no window in this room, so all I know about the evening is coming from sound. As if you need to see sky to know when night is falling. Darkness is a mood in Jamaica. I never told anybody this but from I was eight, I could feel the day change in my body, like when afternoon turns to evening turns to night. The flyer on the supermarket bulletin board said 5:30. It’s 5:52 and the only people here are the boy in brown jeans, the stage manager, and me.

This room was somebody’s living room once. Or some great hall where white people and Syrians used to dance. That would make sense, since not far away is the haunted house where the prime minister used to live, and nearby all those mansions belonging to people who now own hotels but used to keep shops downtown before poor customers made them rich. Now it’s just an empty space with shiny wood floors, meaning somebody was still taking care of it. There’s a white platform in the middle of the room. The stage maybe, with the brown jeans boy sitting on the set? Right boot on the chair, left boot rubbing against the Persian rug. Maybe this was going to be one of those stark, minimalist plays I read this semester. And here I was hoping it would be a pantomime about sweet ol’ Jamaica. That’s sarcasm.

To the far wall behind us somebody left up some art, the sorta abstract-expressionist-but-check-out-the-titties kinda art in just about every uptown hallway.

“Them just leave a Christopher González hanging like that,” someone new says walking into the room.

“A who?” I ask.

“The painting. The painting you was looking at. It’s a González,” he says. Tall, tailored, and more interested in the painting than us.

“Worth money?” I ask.

“Depend on what you mean by money.”

“Can’t buy this house with it but you could buy a houseboy,” says brown jeans.

“Brown,” the man says in a way that makes you think a sigh is coming.

“Titus.”

Names finally. Homos must be the only men who will send a fist all the way up your bottom and a tongue past your tonsils before they tell you what their parents call them. Not even here an hour and I am tired of people already.

Then the man says he is surprised everybody was late, even though (1) we were early, (2) it was raining, and (3) he was late, too.

I am thinking I should leave, but then the stage manager ushers in everybody at once. I wonder if they were watching the house, which usually looks abandoned, waiting to see who went in, wondering if somebody was watching them as they watch to see who was disturbing this dead address on a busy street.

Brown, the brown jeans boy, didn’t get up from his seat, but started humming ba-da da-da ba-da da-da ba-da da-da DAH dah for like six or seven times before I recognized “Sleng Teng.” Sure, brethren offer up more shit to annoy the fuck out of everybody.

“Well, well, thank you all for coming here,” Titus says, adding, “In this rain,” like an afterthought. I can’t read his face. It wasn’t happy, but it wasn’t sad either. Sorta like Mama Jo when you tell her that there are four more pills left on the tray.

The stage manager appears at my back, and I try to act like he didn’t fucking startle me. Titus goes over to him and swear to God, this man honestly thinks he is whispering, even though we hear every word.

“This is it, this is all?” Titus says.

“Marshall’s one, Marshall’s two, everybody I know who hosting a party in this month, every man in my church dance ministry and flower circle.”

“What about the Closet? The Interim Closet? Andante? What about Fanny Hill?”

“It’s 1988, Havelock.”

“Don’t be fresh.”

“Three bars, every private party I know of, Church battymen, and two uptown supermarket bathroom. If there is anywhere else, it don’t open yet.”

“Oh. I see,” Havelock says.

“You the one who didn’t want to put flyers up at School of Drama. Or any actual theater.”

“Lawks, enough.”

“I saw the flyer at JR Wong Supermarket,” I say.

“You must can read gay code,” says somebody I don’t see.

“No need code. ‘Drama audition’ already weed out normal man,” says another voice as thin as the man who says it.

“I thought this was an audition?” says a new guy at the back. Brown. Tall. Half-Chinese-looking. Wide grin. Wow.

“Audition implies that Titus here have a choice. Way it looking, we might be it, Titus,” Brown says.

“Brethren, is Jamaica you deh or you forget?” a tall, thick man says as he steps up on the stage. Stout-stout, as Mama Jo would say. Maybe late forties or early fifties, wearing a navy blue suit that said he was coming from a job that paid more money than any of us will make. Still fresh haircut and a trimmer beard than Brown. Head shaped like Hottentot Venus’s backside if I’m being honest.

“Everybody in this fucking country run on Jamaica time,” he adds.

Including you and everybody but two, I’m thinking.

“If you all want to keep waiting, suit yourself. But nobody else coming,” Brown says. “Yow, watch this. Thanks for coming. You’re all hired!”

“Jordan Brown, just fucking shut it, nuh? Just shut it,” Titus snaps back. I was beginning to like him.

He joins the other two onstage and tells us to gather around, which makes everybody move just one step. He did that clearing throat thing that people with British accents do and introduces himself as Havelock Titus. And yes, he is the director, and yes, this is the audition for the play, well, it was supposed to be. Well, is. Well…let him just get on with it then.

I thought he was going to do that tedious thing where we all have to give our names and say something clever or corny about ourselves, but he asks only for names. The big guy in the suit is Omar. The chubby-cute stage manager is Clive. The half-Chinese wow calls himself Matt Chin (I know, I didn’t believe it either) and sits on the side of the stage. Not in a suit, but his tie is loose, like he was coming from a hard day at a desk job. “Orrin,” says the one I’m already designating the top queen, not because he is matchstick thin, or buckles his belt at the waist, or that his skin is smoother than the lotion he uses, or that he blows out his hair with the hair dryer on blast every day, but mostly because he says, “All the people who talk to me call me Orrin Turner.” I think the last guy’s name is Rainford, but he is so quiet that it feel like I made the name up. Honestly it could be, because I just couldn’t move past how pretty Matt Chin is.

“Short for Matthew?” I whisper to him.

“Just Matt,” he says. I spend the rest of the evening watching him listen.

I can’t say when everybody gathered around, or when Havelock pointed to Clive, who handed out scripts, or when Havelock said this is not the full script but that he would have more if…when we come back same time Thursday, just early, please. I would have said, “That means you, too,” but I was trying to find a color for Matt Chin’s bottom lip: not brown, not pink, plum maybe, thick too and pillow soft, I bet. Light brown skin, Chinese eyes (whatever that means), black hair exactly as it means, cheekbones as high as Grace Jones’s, thin mustache, stubble. Wow.

I have the script in my hand but look over at his.

“Yours saying something different?” he asks and grins, and right there I remember that unlike everybody else, my blush shows.

“So how come a white boy hear about this little shindig?” Omar asks.

White boy. He means me.

“My daddy’s black,” I say.

“Him know?” Omar asks and walks off.

I knew that I could have said something so smart that it would singe the hair off his balls. I also knew that this comment would come to me twenty-four hours after I needed it. Fine, my hair is closer to Don Johnson than Philip Michael Thomas. And I like to wear brown because my eyes take on whatever color shirt I’m wearing and “pussy-eye” was not about to follow me to college. And my daddy would call himself brown or mixed or a fucking mestizo before he call himself black. But I heard that in America even one millionth black is still black, so that’s what I call him.

Omar goes over to speak to Havelock; here I am hoping he isn’t telling him to call me the white one. More people who know each other, it seems. Omar spreads his arms, breaks into a grin, and spins to look right around the room. Havelock nods, looks at his copy of the script, and takes out a pen. Maybe they all know each other in some sort of way. Maybe they are all theater people, which would make me the odd one out. Now I was happy that we didn’t begin with us telling each other our reasons for responding to the casting call flyer. Maybe I would have told them that doing a gay play in Jamdown was the kind of thrill that would come closest to what wiping your backside with a US thousand-dollar bill must feel like. Now, if only there would be nudity—artistically done, of course. I mean if we’re going to stage a battyboy revolution, then we can’t half-ass it.

As for me. I was still looking over at Matt’s script when I saw the name of the play:

Fortune and Men’s Eyes, a play by John Herbert.

Matt looks at me, I look at Havelock who is ready for me with this now I goin’ have to school the plebians look. I want to say Check this out you old bitch, as I know the title comes from a Shakespeare sonnet, having put up with him in A levels. But I want to hear how he talks down to people.

“Canadian play from 1967. Caused a little fracas when it opened. Anyway it’s set in a prison,” Havelock says.

“Like Caged Heat?” Matt asks.

“What? No.”

“Penitentiary? Penitentiary II? Penitentiary III?”

“What are you talking about?”

“Him fucking with you,” I say.

“You think so? Today’s discerning cocksucker prefers La Cage aux Folles or Grease 2,” interrupts Jordan.

“Maybe you’re not that discerning a cocksucker,” says Matt, who looks away too soon to see how hard that punch landed. But I see it.

Not goin’ lie, but there were some deer trapped in headlights in this room, and one was me. Matt holds out his hands for Havelock’s copy, then scans the jet-black cover, the title in white and red and the author’s name in leaf green, while two sad white men behind bars stare at the reader from a high contrast photo.

“Cover is like Genet’s The Blacks,” I say. I want Matt to look but get Jordan.

“Anyway, this is an adaptation,” Havelock says.

“Into what, pantomime?” Jordan asks.

“No.”

“Sad. As much fun as always, Titus.”

I grab the book. The back says “a bitter play about degradation and brutality in a Canadian reformatory.” The cast of characters includes a queen named Queenie, a ragamuffin punk named Rocky, and another prisoner named Mona. “So this is a gay play?” I ask.

“No…it’s not…Why the two of you don’t shut up and let me talk.”

Easily flustered, this queen. He then tells everybody else that the play has all these layers about the individual and society, the nature of violence, the inevitability of corruption and the fall of man. “It’s like Lord of the Flies with big people.”

“But with man-on-man fucking,” Jordan says.

“Anyway, this is the kind of play that blows open the whole fragile myth of Jamaican male sexuality and homophobia,” Havelock says. “Because prison is the ultimate male institution and yet masculine sexualities that could never happen outside in the normal world flourish in there all the time. Does prison make the gay, does gay make the prison, or do homosexuals just have a criminal nature because our very existence is a crime? But the love that dares not speak its name speaks loudly behind bars.”

“Look at you, Titus, dropping Oscar Wilde like ah no nothing. Scared o’ yuh,” Jordan says.

“Bosie,” I say.

“What?”

“Bosie. The one who called it the love that dare not speak its name. It’s there in his poem ‘Two Loves.’ ”

“I know where it is,” Jordan snaps, but I don’t look in his direction for what would definitely be a frown, but to Havelock for what I knew would be a smile. Not even one evening done and all the bitchiness was beating itself out like dust from a rug. A reason for me to stay after all.

“You ever go prison, Havelock?” Matt asks.

“He’s definitely been some places dark,” Jordan says.

“Will you shut your fucking shit. Just this one time” comes from Havelock.

“So this is some Kid Ralph kinda thing?” Orrin asks.

“Who is that, please?” Havelock sighs out. He’s already so tired of us.

“Come now, Havelock Titus, even me know ’bout the one Kid Ralph,” Matt says. “In prison in the 1950s for assault. As soon as they let him out, he commit some crime guaranteed to get him locked back in. Usually rape. Word is there is a man in penitentiary who he keeps going back to. They even staged a wedding in the cell.”

“And people say Jamaica don’t have no love story,” Jordan says.

“Anyway,” Havelock cuts back in. “The love that dares not speak its name shouts all sort o’ ways in prison. Even a Jamaican prison. Yes, there will be violence. Yes, there will be tenderness. Yes, there will be rape. Sal Mineo, the actor in Rebel Without a—”

“Rape? Man and man really goin’ fuck in this?” Orrin asks.

“Those are two different things, sir,” says Jordan.

“You know what the man asking,” says Matt.

“Gay men doing a gay play. Which part of this is shocking to you? Pantomime auditions are in October if that’s the excitement level you looking for. But I was figuring that if you came through that door you’re expecting to do something that has never been done before, or am I wrong, gentlemen?”

May 4

Me mother must did hit her head. Just now—no lie, just now she comes into my room to tell me she is exactly like Clair Huxtable. Not even a good morning.

“Really, Mummy, which part?” I ask. “The part that speak Flemish or the part that look like you’re the mother of the Osmonds, not the Jacksons?” Mummy knows neither, which is why it was funny.

“I am a working woman who holds her family together, you don’t know how it’s hard,” she says and honestly anybody can take one look at Daddy and know how hard it is. But right there I shudder a little because more and more it’s starting to look like she’s picked me as the one to tell serious shit to. I mean to raas man I’m not the oldest. Also not a daughter that she could talk girl stuff to. Or woman stuff. Or whatever stuff that I would never in a million years be able to talk about.

“You better not let any of your Key Club friends hear you say that,” I say. “Especially the black American ones.”

She frowns at the exact second I knew she would, because God would spread legs and plop out another son before a black American woman joins Key Club. And by join I mean one of Mummy’s friends would have to invite her, but didn’t you hear? In Jamaica it’s not about race but class. Meaning that it would be because her people don’t know their people. Yes, I realize the irony about race coming from a boy who could pass for white. A boy who once watched another boy he really wanted to French-kiss get turned away from Mingles nightclub because of what he was wearing. One minute later they let me in, even though I was also wearing T-shirt and jeans. I told him to look at it as punishment for pretending that we weren’t arriving together, but he didn’t find that funny.

Maybe I was being too hard on Mummy, after all she is not British. I’m sure the Belgians are responsible for all sorts of serious fuckery, but not British fuckery. Most of what Americans talk about when they talk about racism goes right above her head. You know I don’t hate a living soul, darling Edmond, alors, look at my husband! I don’t shoot back what her husband thinks.

The thing is, I know what she meant by her being just like Huxtamom. It’s not that she thinks she’s like a black TV character. It’s that Clair is just like her, a modern woman. She’s said that exact phrase to me at least seven times now: “You know, Edmond, I want you to know that I am a modern woman.” And she always says it in a way that expects me to say something back. I don’t know what. For example, last week I was leaving the house kinda late, because the new boy at badminton practice told me that he wasn’t new, that this was his second time at the court, and he come back to check if I was practicing today or just chilling (because a badminton court is where all the cha-cha boys go to chill) because his preacher said you can never make too many friends. Code for anything you want it to mean. Anyway, I was heading out to Devon House, neutral but uptown territory. Mummy asked me where I was going and I said out. “What do you mean by this out?” she asked and I said, “Outsiiiide, Mummy!” She nodded, and then when I was just out the door, she said, “You know I am a modern woman.” I wanted to say to her, Mummy, if you ever want me to say Y, you have to first say X, but that would fly over both our heads.

American families talk all the time on TV. To everybody. I watch Family Ties, mostly because Michael J. Fox sits cute. And stands cute. And laughs cute. And wisecracks cute. And the way he grabs and shakes his belt when he says he’s got eighteen years under it makes me forget what he says next. But he tells his parents everything and sometimes they tell him everything, and I don’t know anybody in real life who does that, certainly none of my friends or their parents. Anyway, what would the point be? Jamaican families just don’t run that way, as if I know fuck about Jamaican families beyond the ten houses outside my window. I don’t even know the difference between King Street and Duke Street. But I know enough about my mummy to understand that there is no question I have that she can answer. Daddy even less.

At least I’m on summer holidays so I have a reason to be bored. The first summer where I’m not going back to high school. How is that supposed to feel? High school was fuckery for a lot of reasons, none of which I want to write about. Okay, some that I want to write about. Right now, I’m remembering all the cool boys who used to like hating me. Sometimes they would hate liking me especially when I walk into class with the Audio Two album or tell them that Rob Base is saying “can’t stand sess,” not “sex,” which means I must be cool. But cool people can’t be…It’s the weirdest thing seeing some ragamuffin youth wanting to drop some shit on me, either a bitch lick or a wicked diss, but hesitate because nobody in Jamaica was raised to say or do anything bad to somebody lighter than him. But hear this: It’s about class, not race. Which means they take me on because I live up Heights, not because I look like 90 percent of TV.

The last day of school as soon as the bell went off, I jumped up and ran out of the classroom, then through the gate. I mean I take foot so fast and so far that I hit Crossroads before realizing that my bag and books were still in class. No, I never went back.

Mummy pops back in to tell me Dionne called. She told her I was busy, then says, “Don’t turn getting your mother to lie into a habit.”

May 5

Everybody shows up at the Lady Musgrave Road house early this time, except for Jordan, who was earlier than everybody. Rehearsal begins.

Dear diary, journal, logbook, whatever the fuck you is, let’s get this out of the way: Matt Chin is the kind of pretty that only gets prettier. That is not how this is supposed to work, especially with boys. The first time you see a pretty boy, half the time you seeing with your dick. The second time lust stops blinding you and you see the crooked nose, the more than four pimples, the flat head, the fuckery personality, the inability to string a sentence, and/or that the bredda really wasn’t that cute. No. This boy took the day off to get hotter. I know what it is. It’s because nothing gave him reason to laugh the last time, and now I’m seeing that he’s one of those men who laughs with all of his face, unlike Clive who do so only with his lips. Chiney eyes, mulatto skin, coolie hair, and negro mouth. Somebody’s going to send me to hell for describing the perfect man like a house slave. I won’t bother to write then that I was at the door grabbing one of the stacked chairs when he comes in and from behind I see the backside that nobody full, half, or quarter Chinese is supposed to have. But (1) I’m already assuming he has a man, and (2) I hate whoever that is. Besides, I am eighteen and he’s definitely older than that. Not because he drove here, but because it looks like he owns the car. I’ve never felt so much like a high school student.

Baggy pants. Fucking baggy pants. He’s sitting across from me in those baggy pants everybody is wearing, which means that even though he spread his legs wide, I can’t see nothing. Fuck. This is the part where I want to talk about how I waited seven years to wear ’70s clothes only to realize we’re no longer in the ’70s. The one guy I know who dress disco is the madman who usually goes to Barbican Square to piss on the traffic police, who then beat the shit out of him, which of course makes him laugh, which of course makes Babylon beat him harder.

“Hear this, Portia. Thank whoever you pray to that you didn’t show up. I still don’t know why anybody was there, including myself. Who is we?”

Silence, this time from me. As much as Miss Ingrid love me, Daddy is the one signing her paycheck.

Yeah yeah yeah, just like God I must have had a sick sense of humor for picking this place. Eddy’s joke was clearer than day; he just didn’t deserve the satisfaction of knowing. Besides, this place didn’t just stink of unfinished business; the smell was ammonia, pissy toilet water, shit, old sweat, and walls after you scream into them. Might as well look at the boy. I would have sworn he got taller, but that might have been because it’s near three months since I see him. Plus it’s a proven fact that boys with cars look taller. A mustache that says I’ve finally grown one. Balls fully drop a month ago, it seems, because he’s carrying himself like a man now, not that he looks like one but that he’s starting to do what men do, like pulling off way too much from the napkin roll for just one forehead to dab, and taking up too much space.

Eddy was one of those handsome boys who didn’t know it. You could tell from the way he hunched his shoulders and looked away once you locked your eyes on him. But he sounded bold even if he didn’t look it. Smart. The word I’m looking for is “smart.” He was the only one in the group who looked like one day he would say something that surprised me. “When that come off?” he asked, pointing at my cast.

“Shit.”

“Them foot yah don’t pass through here since…since…well,” I say.

“Fourth time.”

“Yeah.”

“You don’t know.”

For real I’ve been daring to come back to this place but couldn’t find the right reason. Not true, I have a hundred reasons, a new one for each day. Sometimes I thought that if I just go back and take my own damn time to leave that I regain something they took away, no, I don’t fucking know what. Maybe I regain freedom to leave. To choose. I don’t know. Other times I thought if I went back I would learn something, but I don’t know what that is. Maybe if I knew what it was then I wouldn’t need to learn it. These are the thoughts that start wars in my head whenever my mind lands on this place. Other times I picture going in and the first thing I smell is blood, or flesh, or iron, something that scream violence. Or maybe I would smell me. Or maybe all the screaming became its own thing and never stopped. But I was not smelling or hearing anything. I don’t fucking know why I wanted to come back here, but now that I was here I wanted to both stay and leave. Meanwhile this boy passed through four times already. I was still at the door while Eddy was all the way inside and I wanted to follow him and learn something, but I also didn’t want to follow him because I might learn something.

Yes, this was the house on Lady Musgrave Road and maybe what I was looking for wasn’t reason but nerve. I have a feeling none of this true. That I’m just jam-packing my mind because it wouldn’t make any sense that I have no reason at all. Because a victim going back to the scene of the crime sounds perverted, as if I have some relationship to the place, which I can’t imagine a child saying if his mother used to beat the shit out of him right here.

“You looking for it?” I say.

“Huh?”

“For why you come here four times. You looking for a reason?”

He turned to me, waiting for me to say more but I didn’t.

“You’re still at the door,” he said.

We broke in. There was a padlock on the front door now, which we knocked off with a rock. Between the streetlights and the constant flashing from car headlamps we didn’t need flashlights. But it was my idea to come here and whatever he wanted to say might have nothing to do with this place.

“Part of you really wish you did drop in that night,” I said.

“What else, Professor Xavier?”

“How come you never show?”

“Daddy was in the midst of abusing us, or family was falling apart. Pick whichever version you like.”

“Sorry.”

“Not as much as me.”

“And you feeling fucking guilt—”

“Never said I was feeling guilt.”

“Of course not. You come back here four times for the ambiance.”

“Don’t presume to know anything about me, Jordan Brown.”

“Bitch, cut the shit. You not that deep. Don’t know why you wished you was here anyway, unless you have some level of perversion that can’t even measure. Besides, you would have been the first to run.”

“I know you not calling me no coward.”

“Some people fight. Some people flee.”

“Yeah, man, ah it that brethren. Stay and fight like you? Sure, bad boy. Must be you who break your own damn arm that night.”

And then it happened. I don’t know how since I didn’t will it, wish it, and I sure as fuck didn’t want it, the one tear that freed itself from my left eye and ran down my cheek. Just like a homosexual to turn everything into melodrama. But I knew it was coming. I knew it as soon as I reached the doorway and froze like John Wayne in The Searchers.

“Sorry,” he said and approached me. I wiped my face before he could see it, but then him not seeing it made me feel worse.

“I don’t need your fucking ‘sorry,’ ” I said and walked past him.

Of all the pathetic battymen I could be tonight, weepy queen was not on my list. Not goin’ lie—I thought only my father had this gift, this way of saying just one little thing that would make my whole body crumble before my ears was sure what they heard.

“Jordan—”

“Just shut up, Eddy.”

At least I was inside.

They left the González painting up but they’d knocked down the stage and taken it away. I didn’t realize I was counting on seeing it or that it would have made me feel better. It’s not that it was gone but that somebody tore it down that bothered me. And I knew right then that I was going to find other things to bother me, and maybe coming here was a mistake. Like this window with a splatter of dead red that looks like a shopping graphic that should say “For Sale!” but is dried blood. And all these black streaks on the walls and floors were scuffs from our shoes trying to run and fight. Swirls and curls and streaks mark the floor, not because somebody was trying to be pretty, but that they used a dirty mop with dirty water on the dirty floor. Wiped like they didn’t even try, like they didn’t give a shit about wiping anything clean, like we didn’t even merit erasing. Who in Jamaica would hide beating up a homo? A battyman has a sign on his back that says “Kill us any which way then move on,” a sign we wearing since eleven. This is how it makes me feel. That I am sick and tired of people hating me and me not hating them back.

“You said you have something to tell me,” I said.

“Jesus, that’s blood, right?”

“You come here before and just notice that?”

“I wasn’t looking for blood.”

“Well, turns out if you prick us we do bleed.”

“I wonder if—”

“It’s ours? Whose other fucking blood it goin’ be?”

“Oh. I was going to ask if they leave the bloodstains as a—”

“Sign that they don’t even care to erase us? You really did get your money’s worth out of that high school education, didn’t you?”

“As a warning.”

“To all future battymen who decide to come here for no reason.”

“What was your reason?”

This is one of those moments when Eddy Porteous reminds me he is too fucking smart. I can’t tell if I like it or hate it, only that I walk into a trap when I underestimate it. So I pretend I am looking for something. Fuck if I know what it is, but I’ll know it when I find it. Corners and crevices start to pop out. Under chairs, behind the painting of Jesus with the exposed heart, mops, rakes, and brooms. Piles of dirt and chipped paint. In a side room, underwear, too much underwear, the white briefs now dried blood brown. One of them mine. A loose shoe, a hill of clothes, bottle tops, torn tissue, dust bunnies, and clumps of hair behind doors. Everything in this near dark takes on the look of an assault weapon. Everything looking like it caused damage. Broken glass and squashed juice cartons behind a broom that gave up and is now leaning against a window.

“I left that there,” Eddy said.

“The broom? Why? You is a cleaning lady now?”

“I thought…I don’t know what I was thinking.”

“To erase the evidence?”

“Don’t be an idiot.”

“So you just come here to clean up on certain nights. Funny, the place still look dirty.”

“I grab a broom and I start to sweep but I never seem to get anywhere.”

“You ever grab a broom in your life?”

“Don’t act like you have.”

“Why you really come, Portia?” I ask.

“I’m sure you’re about to tell me.”

“Man who somehow didn’t get AIDS have a name for it in America. Survivor’s guilt.”

He stared at me so long that his eyes went from shock to fear to sadness to some shit I couldn’t recognize to the most brown I have ever seen them—the first I noticed they were brown—to just plain anger. All they needed was a car to pass by flashing their headlights right in his face for max effect. But there I go off with my faggot impulse for drama. Eddy was furious for real.

“You must be fucking joking. You survived.”

“This arm looking like fucking survival to you?”

“What am I supposed to feel guilty for?”

“Oh, I don’t know, Portia, you’re the one here at night doing housework. Maybe by doing it you put yourself back in the scene somehow. Now you can say you did deh yah. You did your little part. Couldn’t be a victim of homicide, wounding with intent, assault with a deadly weapon, or even a verbal threat, but you can still be a part of the crime scene. Yes, me dear, flex that big throbbing empathy muscle.”

“Bitch, if you want start something, me can finish it for you.”

“Don’t come chat to me like—”

He was right in my face before I could even think when he whispered: “Jordan, shut you rassclaat mouth. Your idea of homeless is slumming it up on Skyline Drive in Jack’s Hill, so stop gwaan like you bad.”

Not goin’ lie, this half-white boy made me step back. Just a little, but still fucking back. Something about him—the squeezing knuckles, the stiff neck, the stare—said that the brethren did want this, been wanting this for weeks, wanting to feel something and good or bad made no difference. Might be a fish but I not biting that damn bait.

“I read The Sexual Outlaw. Again, I mean. This is the third time. John Rechy’s book about what it means to be gay. What it should mean anyway,” I said.

“Oh?”

“John Rechy is th—”

“I know who he is. The only way you find a book like that in Jamaica is by mistake.”

“No shit, one time I peep The Joy of Gay Sex in Bookworld.”

“For real? Some brethren buy it thinking it was a guide to happy-happy joy-joy sex?”

Neither of us laughed, but we did something close to it and that was enough.

“I goin’ guess it’s not like How to Win Friends and Influence People,” he said.

“Ha, in a way it is.”

I don’t know why, but this feeling just dropped down on me. More like a question: Do I want to tell this to anyone and of all people why him? Because he is here, my mind said. Because he is here.

“Sometimes I feel like I reach the end of myself. I don’t know how else to describe it. If you see some of the men I fuck you’d know I reach the end of myself all the time just to do it. But when I read that book, I stopped walking as myself and started to walk like him, you understand?”

“Not sure I do. Maybe. I don’t know…”

“Because all the time I waste wondering why they hate me I could have spent hating them back. If I shout ‘Man gang up and beating a tranny to death,’ police won’t even fart even if they’re killing him right outside the station. But shout ‘Two man ah fuck’ or ‘Two lesbian hitch,’ and they just poof! out of nowhere like Scotty just beam them up. Meanwhile I couldn’t understand why I was so mad.”

“You just explained quite clearly why we are so mad.”

“Yeah, but most battyman no mad like me. And don’t say it’s because most don’t go through what I go through because I know seven dead faggots who would call bullshit. But then this raas book. It teach me this thing called ancestral rage. From day the white god tell them to do it people been killing us. Hanging, castrating, beheading, burning, beating, what else? Stoning, bludgeoning, boiling, from before the Dark Ages until now, they been killing us and still they haven’t killed us enough. So of course, by the time we born either we born angry or afraid. Now add all the shit about being black and we cursed double. Sometimes I get so mad I wonder how one fucking body can hold all of it. So I go to gym to get fitter and stronger. And every time I fuck a closet case I bite him in the ass or neck, or better yet—give him a hickey his wife can’t mistake for anything else. Or I dare them to hit me so I can beat the shit out of them. So fucking mad at so many people I still think my head goin’ explode. Like the school principal who try to expel me but not before he pull down my pants and brief to whip me. The doctor who said that some places in the world still give electroshock, and even some who never lost faith in lobotomy. Or the fucking TV preacher talking ’bout the ‘gay agenda.’ My daddy’s been beating that shit out of me because the principal wants to expel me. Three times a month, twelve months a year, twenty lash, strike, kick, slap, punch per beating. That’s 720 hits a year, from when I was eight till I was sixteen—5,760 times my father hit me. And I swear to fucking God that even if that pussyhole die before I get to him, I going dig up his fucking corpse and smash him bomboclaat head 5,760 fucking times. You ever have rage like that, eeh? You ever get so mad you would desecrate your own father’s dead body?”

“Matt and Orrin gone,” he said.

“What you mean gone?”

“I mean gone. Vanish. Poof, like you say. Gone like thieves in the night.”

“Oh, this is the part where you looking for sense? You want me to repeat everything back slow? Nobody has seen Matt Chin and Orrin Turner since June fifteenth.”

Working Title: The Disappeared

Date: February 14, 1993

Interviewee: JORDAN BROWN

Interviewer: Peta-Gaye Burke (journalist)

Recording method: Tape recorder / Dictaphone

Location: Indies Restaurant, Kingston, Jamaica

Eddy, huh? Courteous Porteous. Let us get this out of the way—that bitch wasn’t claiming he was there, was he? Good. Honest, earnest Edmond, still honest and earnest. Haffi love the consistency though—so uncommon in a homosexual. I’m still not even sure I like him, but say this about Eddy Courteous: He will never lie to you, but he will look at purple and say it’s red and blue.

No, I don’t care to elucidate on that.

You really using that word in a sentence? Just go right ahead and tell me what kind of Jamaican you are. You the kind that says “satiated” when you belly full. No, I don’t care to elucidate.

But if you already spoke to him, what you need me for? People have a way of envying—no, that’s too strong a word, but I don’t know any word milder. Certain people feel a way about people who’ve survived shit, you know? They think it imbues our lives with a meaning they don’t have, like we joined this ultimate exclusive club. Of course, the logic is fallacious. I mean it was a meaningless act, so how the fuck should meaning come out of it? When I last saw Eddy…I think last year. Yeah, he was working in the information technology department of some bank, or maybe he was a consultant doing some cusp-of-the-millennium shit. Yeah, seems all this COBOL computer language business made a huge fuckup by shortening years to just the last two digits because come 2000, no computer in the world will know if it’s 1900 or 1800 for that matter. Yeah, that’s Eddy now, full-on nerd—no, geek turned prophet of digital doom and it’s only ’93. It was all the bredda would talk about. And here I thought he rewatched The Terminator so much because you can see Arnold Schwarzenegger’s cock. Otherwise I would see him at some party up in Jack’s Hill to launch some alcopop. Yow, I don’t create the words, I just use them. I said to the brand manager that this shit sounds like wine cooler and his whole look said, Yes, pussyhole, I too was traveling to the United States in the late ’80s. Anyway, it was either there or that bank where I saw him last. But clearly, you’ve seen him more recently.

Him still cute? Come now, man, white boy—fine, half-white boy with the black boy lips? Nah lie, first time I see him business, I said to myself, Well, now we know which part of you is black, if you know what me mean. Right, of course you wouldn’t know.

Anyway, Eddy told you all this already, so what you want from me? There are no other sides to this story, there is what happened, and Courteous Porteous never see none of it. And what the fuck that mean, sides to the story? You talking to the sons of bitches who nearly killed us as well? Who knew that Omar’s death was just a matter of perspective? Why stop with the sons of bitches, talk to the dogs who raise them, too, so they can tell how them was such nice boys growing up, church every Sunday when them was not busy helping Mama. I tell you one thing though. In every side of this story, Omar Joseph is still fucking dead.

But the boy did look good though. Eddy, I mean. He looked guilty. So we’re at this alcopop launch party and the only thing he says to me was how sick he was of that “What Is Love” song. I say, well, “Rhythm Is a Dancer” is coming up next and then most likely “Mr. Vain,” so if you plan to make an exit you should do it now. He looked at me like I just told him to fuck off and I didn’t try to clarify. So I’m leaving and there he was in the street by a car smoking a cigarette with all his fingers sticking out like he was drinking tea. Like he was smoking menthol for the mint. I knew he was waiting on me. Well, he was waiting for me to bring it up and I sure as hell wasn’t going to.

“What the fuck have you done, Jordan? What the fuck you gone do?” he asked.

“I did what I—”

“Second thought, don’t tell me. Jesus Christ. Jesus Christ.”

But I’m putting cart before horse.

Might as well reach back to 1988, the last time either of us saw Matt or Orrin.

First you should know that one of them called 119. That I remember, or at least that I was sure of since none of us were in any condition to call anybody, and that house didn’t have a phone. My chest felt like somebody swung a wrecking ball right into it and my left hand was a dead fish.

What you mean who I mean by “them”? Who the fuck else? What, you think the Good Samaritan passed by and said, “Oh no, what a sorry pack of battymen”? Whoever called for an ambulance still waited a good two to three hours and didn’t have no problem with his posse taking everybody’s clothes so that whoever find us would think this was some gay sex orgy attacked by Freddy Krueger. All I could think of was Rainford with those two bloody holes in his face walking through the doorway like a zombie and begging somebody to help him.

When the police draw down on the scene, they were so shocked at the whole brutality of it all they forgot to be homophobic. Not even Sodom and Gomorrah was supposed to end like this. They just stood there looking at us. I hobbled over to one of them circling the still unconscious Matt Chin and Orrin Turner on the floor and said, “Nice of you to make an appearance,” and then spat out a tooth. “I would offer you my hand but I think it’s broken,” I also said, and one of the men looked at me like he just hit and run his own dog. Rainford walked right into their car, but not before they shouted at him to move out of the way with their headlights shining on him and turning him into a ghost. Two policemen jumped out of the car with their batons pulled already, because whoever this madman was, a good knock to the head would set him straight. I saw the exact second that they both realized that Rainford’s eyes were gouged out. Rainford still asking for assistance please, while all the cops give him the widest berth possible and step into the house. “Gingerly” is the word you’re looking for. Gingerly. Sure, of course they acted professionally, but why should I give people credit for what they’re supposed to do?

At some point I stopped being clever and ended up being unconscious because at about five in the morning I woke up in a hospital ward, beside an old man coughing himself awake. First thing that come to my mind was Dear Lord God Jesus, please tell me they didn’t take us downtown. It felt like a plan, the mob leaving us for dead and the police finishing the job, though the truth was Kingston Public Hospital is the first one everybody thinks of. But you already know that. Did you know that they didn’t take that tree branch out of Omar’s battyhole until after the wife identified the body? Maybe you know all that. All I know are numbers. Yours truly: twelve stitches, head and right shoulder. Orrin: sixteen stiches, head. Havelock: twenty-six stitches, head, both legs, chest. Matt: five. Clive: seven. Rainford: thirty-seven. Omar Joseph didn’t need any stitches. Two gouged eyes, six broken ribs, two concussions, one collapsed lung, one broken arm, two broken fingers, three fractured arms, one fractured leg, one fractured tibia, two busted noses, two sodomized rectums, one amputated finger, eleven knocked-out teeth, five shattered teeth, one broken shin, one dislocated jaw, three busted lips, zero injured penises. Thirteen assailants, three of them police.

How do I remember all of this? What you think I fill my brain with, poetry? No sah, I mold all of that into a red-hot poker and brand my brain with it.

They scattered us all over the hospital. Nothing much to it, you get a bed where there is a bed. I wasn’t even the first to leave. That was Clive, whom they treated and sent home with a fractured arm and a nose in a slightly different position than how God made it. Havelock also went home, even though the doctor advised him not to, because he is Havelock and we are not. This was the first bed in months that I didn’t have to put up with a closet case to get, so I wasn’t going nowhere. Didn’t matter that the man in the bed beside mine sounded like he was going to die any minute. I’m thinking, I’ve been under men who soon dead, so what’s the difference?

The doctor who came around never took his eyes off his chart when he told me I had a broken arm and two broken ribs, but other than superficial injuries there seemed to be no serious damage to my head. When I said that I must be imagining the massive headache then, my sentence went up into the ceiling and evaporated. He muttered some medical shit to the nurse, who nodded and walked away. Charm he saved for the man in the other bed, who never stopped coughing. The man was old, which meant the doc was speaking to him the way one would a two-year-old, saying, “Let the nurses know before you do a doo-doo again, okay?” They left so quickly, the nurse behind the doc, that I almost shouted, “Mind you trip and land face-deep in his ass.”

At least the doc tried to hide his contempt. The policeman, different story. At least him circle me with three boring questions before moving in for the kill.

“Can you tell me at what part of the evening you and your party made short shrift of your clothes?” he asked.

“I…I don’t understand.”

“I understand this is common amongst those of your lifestyle choice, but please suppress your emotional inclination, sir, and answer the question.”

“Wha di? Listen, young boy. If you think me ’fraid to pull you off that bed, slap handcuff ’pon you, and send you to General Penitentiary for your perverted mouth, then you don’t know what time clock ah strike. Don’t you dare speak no French to an officer again, you understand me?”

He’s jerking me off, trying to bring Mr. Erection back from wherever he vanished to, but I’m lost wondering if I’m feeling something for this dark shadow of a boy, like we shared some sort of intimacy, something raw and strong and painful maybe, and whatever it is—was—I didn’t like it. This man is now yanking me so hard that it hurts and I want to grab him by the throat and tell him, Whatever you trying to get back is gone. It’s gone over there to that boy who fucking took it. Then the boy across the room shifts himself right under the glow of the light and the blue creates his face.

I know him. Less than a stranger, more than some lover. Never seen him before but he feels like somebody I have known or will know forever. No, it’s like I don’t know or remember any part of his body, but his smell is going to wake something up. No no no no no, not that, more like either I know more about him than I should, or he knows me and I can’t fucking remember which. Now I have the shivers and all inside rushes up. I slap my mouth shut and run, looking for the nearest toilet, potted plant, sink, hole, corner, anything. Two feet from the door marked “WC” vomit bursts from my mouth and I keel over. Men shift away from me like a surprise obstacle on the course. Before anyone can say that I’m the one who did it I go, but I don’t make it any farther than across the road. No reason to stay, but I can’t leave. Franchot might come out any second now to tell me ’bout me bloodclaat and not to come back to his club, but I don’t move. I’m wearing a Tom of Finland T-shirt of a white cop in tight pants squeezing his balls, the kind of T-shirt that can get me killed in this city. I don’t move. Above me is the orange that is Kingston now. I hear they call it light pollution.

That man is lighting in me what men who have feelings for me feel. But I don’t have any fucking feelings. And this is not a thrill, or a pleasure, or making my dick stiff, this is making me want to vomit again.

He comes out three hours later, one of the last to leave and with a man. The car is hiding me—well, the dark, because I’m looking through the window and this car isn’t hiding shit. He steps out of the gate into the streetlight with two hands making a belt around his waist. He pushes the man off. The man says either “baby” or “maybe.” They look like how certain battymen look, meaning they look like each other, in the polo shirt with the upturned collar, he in light blue, the other man in light yellow, pastel shorts and Keds as if they came here by boat, not car. The boy—no, the man, because now he is a man—I know or who knows me. He is lighter than I assumed, high brown with lips a black man size but a white man color. A Price Waterhouse middle management haircut. Gym legs, newly-married-straight-man belly, even though he does not look like he’s walking right back into the closet. Why do I know what he would smell like, I don’t raasclaat know. I search for a line from The Sexual Outlaw to stomp the trembling out of my knees but no lines come. This must be a man who broke my heart so bad that my head erased all trauma. Amnesia is a real thing and she’s living in my head.

He pushes Yellow Polo away again, this time harder. “Go ah you bomboclaat yard,” he says. “You not coming?” says Yellow Polo. “I already have a yard,” he says.

I don’t know anybody clever, but I know him. I don’t know that voice, but I know how.

Shadows from the streetlight hide me running to my car, where I wait for him to get into his RAV4 and drive off. I’m on the gas pedal before making sure Yellow Polo is not following him. Seeing this man is an idea that makes me cough into a choke, and I fight down whatever was forcing itself to come up. I don’t know. I must see him. I don’t remember him, yet there is no way he could not remember me. My smell must do for him what his does for me, I think, then I remember that what I have is the memory of a smell. Inside my chest is house music, and my fingertips tremble out a beat on the wheel. There are a million romance novels that say these feelings are wonderful, but I feel like the last song on a Joy Division record.

Right turn off Constant Spring Road to East Kings House Road. Roundabout right around the old cholera mass grave, second exit taking him north to Drumblair. Original white man territory up to fifty years ago, but now it’s the Jamaican yuppie’s Fisher-Price: My First Apartment. I don’t know what I am doing and telling myself that I have followed people before, chased them, stalked them, is not making any of this feel normal. Me telling myself I was never normal anyway does not help either. This of course would be the point where my head finally starts to wrap itself over the whole vomiting thing, as in why would I throw up over a good memory, and why would I forget it if it was good. Then some asshole overtakes me, slipping between us. Yellow polo shirt. I pull back. If I have watched enough spy shows to wonder if I’m being followed, so too has this boy, and now that somebody is actually following him, he speeds up.

Yellow Polo hits the gas.

I wait.

You waiting too long, jackass, my mind shouts at me and I chase after them. The Shortwood Road stoplight is at green, but at least two reporters have called this the most dangerous intersection in Kingston, and not just because an entire family wrapped themselves around a light post two years ago, and in January a truck’s wheels swallowed up a church lady, leaving only her right foot. It’s after midnight and Shortwood Road crisscrosses itself with lanes that spill gunmen. Cars crash because nobody wants to stop at the light. We are all speeding now, and the light ahead just turned yellow. Blue Polo rolls right through, and right on his backside goes Yellow Polo, both of them squealing through the sharp right turn after the light. Red catches me and I brake before my own mind yells out, What the fuck you ah do? Both cars fade even though they are still racing while I stand at the fucking light like an idiot. A gunman should rob you at gunpoint just so this can be the cherry on your stupid cake, my mind says. The light switches green just as I decide to break it. I can see almost for miles, not just the road ahead but what must be a dozen turnoffs. Nothing about that man felt good, but it’s knowing that I might never see him again that makes me feel worse. I punch my left palm and the crack of noise goes straight to my head and shakes something so loose and nasty that I stomp on the brake and the car lurches in the middle of the road. I push open my door and all that was left inside me splashes onto the road. Kingston is asleep and nobody is coming.

I know who he is.

Working Title: The Disappeared

Date: February 17, 1993

Interviewee: JORDAN BROWN

Interviewer: Peta-Gaye Burke (journalist)

Recording method: Tape recorder / Dictaphone

Location: Tom Redcam Library, Kingston, Jamaica

Rainford, of course, didn’t give two fucks about who was missing. You know what him say?

“Everybody missing to me.”

Then brethren point to his shades, where his eyes used to be. I almost thought he was being clever but then I remembered that we Jamaicans don’t fuck with irony. Honestly, I mean for real, what me was goin’ say? We were at downtown Marshall’s on a Thursday night. Different owner who called himself Marshall, but the same eight, maybe nine old queens, the same four women getting drunk, but a different set of three or four young gays wondering if this is really as good as it’s going to get.

“Me back at mi daddy house,” I said.

“Coo yah! Battyman story can have happy ending, who did know?” he says. It wasn’t a question.

“You think we in some ‘Rapunzel’ shit?” I ask.

“Well, if your father allow—”

“My father didn’t allow nothing. Him just not able to stop it.”

“Oh. Okay. At least you and him under the same roof. How much battyman story end so? The only blessing I receive in the past three month is that at least I didn’t see me mother walk out of mi life,” Rainford says.

“Stroke knock down mi papa, that’s why he can’t do nothing. So, trust me when I say that him gone, too.”

“Condolences. Regards. Warm wishes. Whatever people say.”

“If they don’t really care they say nothing.”

“If you say so, brethren.”

“Sorry about America,” I say.

“Not as sorry as me,” Rainford says.

“America” meaning the Immigration and Naturalization Service, which denied his emergency application for political asylum, despite his lawyer citing the homophobic attack, his loss of anonymity, and the increasingly hostile atmosphere for the gays, lesbians, and allsexuals in Jamaica. And despite, well, the holes in his face. Rainford is yet to tell anybody why his application was denied. I wonder if the INS officer took two looks at Rainford and thought, What more could the world possibly do to him? Paul Royale managed to open a door in Spain and somebody clearly with connections is about to say hola. Royale didn’t need prompting from me, but he did want me to know that he made shit happen.

“Pity I no longer need to fuck johns to pay for cigarettes, or I would have thanked you the usual way,” I told him.

How has the attack changed him, other than leave him blind, homeless, and family-less? Sounds like the kind of messed-up, tone-deaf shit Royale would ask. Instead I say, “You drinking whiskey now.”

“Don’t gwaan like me and you is combolo or something. ‘Drinking whiskey now?’ What me was drinking then?” he asked.

“You wasn’t drink shit. Nothing that a four-year-old couldn’t handle,” I say, and Rainford bursts out laughing.

“Me know me coulda trust you,” he says.

“How so?”

“I mean I did know you would be the one person to make me feel normal in this fuckery. I never did like you and you never did like me. Why act different now? Because I can’t see you lie to me face?”

“My mother always said I had a knack for public service.”

“Your mother marry a man who smell like dead people,” Rainford says.

“You know, you’re already a total cunt just by sitting here. You don’t even have to open your mouth. Just shut up,” I say.

“Good, good” is all he says.

He shouts out for another Johnnie Walker. It’s against Marshall’s policy to serve anybody drinks like this is a restaurant, but nobody is going to turn down the blind boy even if he is an asshole. I feel like I missed out. All those years homeless and struggling and I never once used guilt as currency. You’d think I had no idea what homosexuality was for. I want to grab his ears and scream out the lyrics to “Broken Face”: I got no lips, I got no tongue / Where there were eyes, there’s only space, which I know he would not get in a million years meaning he would pick up that I was being insulting but miss that I was also being ironic. Besides, there were about only six Jamaicans who know the Pixies and only three who like them.

“But I guess it’s something when a battyboy go missing, eh?”

“And what thing is that?”

“That—thanks, brethren,” he says as Marshall slams down the drink. “That battyman try so hard to back out of the scene—day in, day out—that who is goin’ surprise that one day he finally just go poof?”

“You trying to say they work so hard at being normal that one day they just vanish inside the pattern of normal society?” I ask.

“If me did want to say that, me woulda say that,” he says. “Me saying that battyman ah try vanish from day one. So why set off alarm when one of them finally disappear?”

“That what you was trying to do when you join a drama group? Disappear?”

“A battyman gone is like sun rising or water pouring.”

I know what he is doing, because I also do it. I will get you to hate me because then you will never forget me. Add the permanent injury and you feel bad about it, as if you have no reason to call a cunt a cunt, which is just carte blanche for him to act extra cunty.

“Don’t act like you don’t know what I getting at,” he says.

“No, I don’t. I really don’t know what the fuck you talking about, Ellis.”

“That when something happen to normal people they leave the space behind. People will fill up a box with funeral program, or put ashes in a spot a tall man or a big woman used to hold and believe that the person take up the same space. Even when normal man leave him mother yard, she look at him room and the emptiness just beat her. But when battyman leave or die he don’t leave no space. He don’t leave no empty bed with a sink in the mattress. He don’t make a mother talk about how he used to not throw out the empty milk carton. He just gone and the world swallow that empty space up like him never did born. You just watch.”

“Eddy and I goin’ talk to some of the relatives this week maybe.”

“Why?”

“Trying to piece a—”

“Trying to play detective, you mean.”

“You think the real detectives going give a shit?”

“Jamaica don’t have any real detective. You two watch too much Murder, She Wrote. You want real work? Find out where me eyes gone. Nuh, that my mother say, that them run ’way from me.”

“Nobody trying—”

“Last thing she say to me. Then she also gone like poof. Can you imagine? I woulda prefer it if she say, ‘Get out of me face, battyboy. Me glad God punish you.’ Instead she give me the quiet, which make me think that even before me couldn’t find her anymore, she did gone. You know what I hope? I hope that wherever she run to, one day she going run right in front of a truck that kill her.”

“We not playing detective,” I say.

“You playing something. Maybe they gone the same place as my mother. You think somebody murder them?” he asks.

“Now who watching too much Murder, She Wrote?”

“Fine, not murder. Holding them hostage.”

“They would be better off kidnapping Eddy…or me.”

“You take a while before you add yourself. Maybe they just choose to get gone.”

“Maybe.”

“Then why the bomboclaat you trying to find them then? If a man don’t want nobody to bother him, then don’t bother him.”

“Because there is a difference between when something ends and when something stops,” I say.

“I don’t know what the fuck that mean.”

“I know.”

This sounds cruel to say, but Rainford’s face says more now than when he had eyes in it. He can’t see people looking at how he looks at people, if that makes any sense. If he could see people watching his hands tremble around the drink, he would have shoved them under the tablecloth. Or that every random sound, like a glass tinkling too loud, makes him jump a little. I wish he had the cleverness to fight the awfulness, but none of us was raised to be clever. The boy not clever, but he not stupid either. Strange that up to now neither me nor Eddy ever thought that maybe they didn’t want to be found. Or might not even be missing so much as they’re done fucking with us.

“The pretty one, Matt Chin-Chin. You know one time him take me to him yard and try fuck me.”

“For real?” I say.

“Why, me don’t look like him type?”

“It’s a surprise, that’s all.”

“You don’t believe me. Don’t need eye to see that. Yeah, man, him have one of them apartment at Waterloo and Hope Road—you know it. Abbey Court. That nuh the first apartment building in New Kingston?”

“One of them.”

“Brethren, me just never in the mood. Plus me never like Abbey Court. The whole place look like where woman get rape and kill and nobody know until you smell the body. And the wall them thin, you see? Everybody might as well be in the toilet with you.”

“I see.”

This bredda must be fucking some other half-chiney boy named Matt Chin, or is some other man by that name living at Westminster Court. Rainford is already thinking that as a permanent victim the rest of us are inclined to believe anything he says. The thing is, I get it. I think. Pity can hit you harder than a punch. Or put another way, it might not hit at all, but it leaves you wounded. Like responding to an open wound by cutting open another one. Bredda, I have been there, wasting no time to get somebody’s contempt because that means I never have to worry about their fucking pity.

After all, “pitiful” and “pathetic” are the same word.

“The only other thing I remember ’bout the man is when we was talking about the shit all of we go through, Matt Chin didn’t say a thing. I don’t know how to treat the man like him gone. He was barely here,” Rainford said.

“But Orrin though.”

“Yeah, Orrin. I can’t explain Orrin.”

Thanks to this man I was never so happy to see Eddy come through a door in all my life.

“Whagwaan, Rainford?”

“Trying to make a dollar out of fifty cent, you know how it go.”

“Zeen. I was—”

“You park outside?” I ask.

“Yeah but…”

“I don’t have all night,” I say and get up to leave.

Out in the street Eddy asks me if Rainford needs a ride, or at least some help.

“Rainford cook and curry,” I say and get into his car.

“But—”

“You want to scratch names off your list or not, Mr. Edwin Jeans?”

So it’s 8:35 p.m. when we get to Westminster, only to see the sign say “Mews,” not “Court.” “Is Jamaica the only place in the world that uses words like ‘mews’?” I ask.

“We the only country in the world that still use ‘artiste,’ so who knows. We reach.”

I swear to God every time I think my stock of sarcasm is depleted for good, along comes some crap to restore it. Westminster Mews announces itself clear as day even in the night. Maybe it’s the relentless white walls that jerk your eyes up to the roof, which is all orange Spanish tiles, the universal sign of new money. Or the paved driveway, or the paved everything since there is no actual grass or dirt anywhere. Grillwork at the front door because even a house in Beverly Hills needs security. Going around the left side of the property—this house is on the corner—is an honest-to-God white picket fence. I want to say out loud that it’s the little things that remind us that the USA has replaced Britain as our cultural colonial power. Upstairs there’s a porthole on the top floor that says “Bathroom.” Eddy can’t even hear my thoughts but looks at me annoyed anyway.

“We the detective duo who hate each other but end up fucking?” I ask.

“They don’t have a doorbell,” he says and bangs on the grille. “Matt? Matt? Matt?”

“You think the man in him bedroom just sulking?”

“You like to think you’re the only one who can think, so I leave that to you.”

“Ouch. Wow.”

“Any reason the two of you calling out man name at me door?” comes from inside. A husky woman’s voice not matching the short, thin Chinese woman who cracks open the door.

“Excuse me, ma’am,” Eddy says.

“Excuse yourself. What can I help you two men with?”

“We’re looking for Matt.”

“You shout out his name three time already, which mean you not looking for Mark, Luke, nor John.”

“Can we speak to him? Tell him Edmond and Jordan—”

“No.”

“Excuse me?”

“No. No Matt live here, so no, you can’t speak to him.”

“You know, Porteous, all them house look the same in the dark. Mind you getting them confused.”

“This is the house. I remember the number. He was opening that lock when I leave him.”

“This lock?” she asks.

“Yes. I know what I saw.”

“Sir, no man named Matt live here. As for opening this lock, it’s a combination, not a key.”

Eddy looks at me like he wants me to tell him he’s not going mad.

“You see him open the lock?” I ask.

“He grabbed the damn lock and was about to open it. Why would I stay around to make sure?”

“Well, trust me, gentlemen, the man inside this house don’t name Matt. And him don’t ’gree with man like you.”

“Excuse me, what?” Eddy says.

“And don’t bother with the rest of this block. No Matt live there. No Matthew neither.”

Eddy jerks, like he’s about to push into the house anyway.

“Him was right here, me say.”

“Go ask Security if any Matt live here,” the woman says.

“Matt Chin,” Eddy says.

“Matt Chin, Matt Chang, Matt Chung Yung Fat. Go ask him,” she says and closes the door with a firm shut.

Eddy is trying to shake the disbelief out of his head. I leave him shaking to talk to the security guard, who let us in easy when he had seen Eddy in the driver’s seat but is now wondering who the fuck let this dark-skin boy through. I wait for him to recognize that I came with the white boy before asking him about Matt. He says him stationed at the gate from the day they open and nobody name Matt, Matthew, or Matthias Chin ever live there.

In the car Eddy suggests that Havelock might know something, maybe more about Matt than Orrin. I tell him that he is free to talk to Havelock whenever he wants to, but I won’t be coming with him. Of course, he now wants to know what the fuck happened, why I don’t want to talk to Havelock, but I don’t owe this boy an answer so I don’t give one.

At Orrin’s mother’s house only his sister is there. No, I’m not going to describe her because I’m tired of making shit people flesh for you. She didn’t have to say it to make it clear that she hopes she never sees us again, not because she have any problem but because the rest of her family do. “The two of you is him kind of friend?” she asks. I wanted to tell her that Orrin was never my friend, but Eddy is asking about their mother, which means that he’s going to pay these people another visit.

“I swear to God I want one of these white people shields,” I say to him as the sister watches us leave from behind the lace curtain blocking her window. He says he is not white. I don’t bother to say that brethren, you took us to Waterhouse, what politicians call a garrison and what an Uptowner should call a no-fly zone. “That’s it for me tonight,” I say and wait for him to ask about tomorrow, but he doesn’t.

Three days later Eddy calls me at the funeral home.

“Always rest assured about your final rest,” I say.

“It’s me,” Eddy says.

I fight the urge to say Me who?

“About to tell this woman why open casket is not the best option for her husband, so talk fast.”

“I called every ad agency, PR firm, even the marketing department of every big bank in the phone book. None of them have a Matt or Matthew Chin working there.”

“You called every one of them?”

“Uh-huh. Two Michael Chins, one Mathew Wong, and one John Chin. No Matthew.”

“And they just give out the information like that?”

“They can see my skin color over the phone.”

“Just so?”

“This a bad connection or you didn’t hear me the first time?”

“Nobody, eh? Why did we think he worked in advertising or PR?”

“Educated guess? He told me one time that advertising was the only creative field that makes any money.”

“He used to dress like every other clerical worker,” I say.

“Meaning what?”

“He could have been working for anybody.”

“Maybe we asking the wrong people. Your people working the street see him?”

“They not my fucking people. Maybe we should try our luck with Orrin. This not getting us anywhere.”

“I starting to think…”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Girl, what?”

“I’m starting to think they erased themselves. Matt, at least. I mean, I can only go by who pass through this place.”

“Usually when a man commit suicide he wants to be found. Hiding is constant work that you never stop doing, and you need to be alive to do it.”

“Neither sounds like either, to be honest,” I say.

Busy night at the Interim Closet. Place packed as if rumor did buss that young meat was coming, which is another way of saying that the crowd here usually skews older. But gay older, meaning on the sunset side of thirty-five. As with every other subculture that you hear about on a college campus, gay shit is youth shit and unless you’re into daddies, anything that reminds you of aging is disgusting. It’s like none of these cunts wants to look at a man and see how he is going to turn out. You’d think with AIDS they would be glad to know that they will make it, but none of us raised ourselves to think about tomorrow as something real. Maybe that’s it, what they see when they see an old fag. Men who look like what they are is all they have left. Some of these men have wives who still don’t know that they’re out here waiting to dance to Donna Summer, because what the fuck they supposed to do with “Mercedes Boy”? Some of these men still remember the one time they make it to Fire Island, or Central Park, or the buck who surgeon them so hard that the wall and ceiling covered in whatever battyman blast out.

I don’t think Eddy has ever been to the Interim Closet. I don’t know if Eddy has ever been this close to battymen who remember when Elizabeth became just another queen. He is casing the place like there’s a list to check twice and why not? Even though it is so narrow that it’s a hallway that does not lead to a real club. A hallway long as an alley in purple light. Somewhere along this purple hallway is a bar, and by this bar usually are the bitter bitch queens and the men and two token women who all pretend to be friends. The thing is, they do love being baited to talk. And I did bring along bait.

“What kind of name is the Interim Closet?” says Eddy.

“One owner catch the other owner playing doctor with somebody else, so now we have two bars named the Closet.”

“Win-win for us.”

“Cool you foot with that. The owner at the bar.”

Sandringham Tucker, Miss Sandy to all the unwashed bitches he likes to call friend. Of course the man see all the way to Eddy’s brain before I bring him in close. Skin somewhere between café au lait and wet dirt, which I know because he was the first person to describe it so. He used to shave his one brow back into two until through some magic he heard about Frida Kahlo. From then the unibrow was the S for his Superbitch chest. From his brow to the two sharp lines of cheek rouge to the bloodred/black lipstick his face always looks like a V. He is the curator of the Pantheon Gallery on Hope Road and is always in the news when there is some exhibition opening somewhere, but he didn’t know what Fluxus was.

“But coo yah. Chocolate and vanilla. All this ice-cream sundae need is me mouth,” Sandringham says.

“Word ’pon the street is that you is a biter, not a licker,” I say.

“Come near me mouth and find out.”

“I give to the needy, Miss Sandy. Not the greedy.”

“Yeah? Me wake up this very morning thinking how me short of vanilla in the house,” he says, his attention long since past me.

Eddy taking a full five seconds to look at me in horror was worth the one-hundred-dollar admission. “Ask him,” I say.

“Come closer, sexy lips, me don’t bite. Unless—”

“Don’t be a corny bitch,” I say.

“How about me be just a bombocloth bitch then and tell you to fuck off.”

Because this wouldn’t work had I given either a warning, I push Eddy right into Miss Sandy, who screams even as his two wide-open legs Venus-flytrap the boy. Miss Sandy is too shocked to blurt out something clever. Eddy is just too shocked. But then he shocks me by not pulling back and breaking into a smile.

“You goin’ lick or bite,” he says. Miss Sandy coughs as his claws retract.

“Is which boyfriend him looking for?” Miss Sandy says.

“Not a boyfriend. Not a client either, and don’t get fresh,” Eddy says, but he might as well have said I don’t have on any panties. Miss Sandy was eating this boy up, his legs still wrapped around him, both of them purple in the light.

“Half-Asian man, about my height, named Matt Chin,” I say.

“Who goin’ give a real name here? Might as well be Bugs Bunny.”

“Very good-looking,” Eddy says.

“Better-looking than you?”

“You’d remember him.”

“Then he couldn’t pass through here then. Sure, we get some mixed mongrels, but me no remember this one. Half chiney?”

“Half Asian,” I say. “Very black bumper, if you know what I mean. Probably dressed like he just leave work, decent dress shirt, decent pants, gray or blue, tie untied. Hair cut short. Dimples.”

“Dimples? No sah, me would remember a boy that delicious.”

“He either keep to himself in some dark corner or pick up somebody like him.”

“He only saying that because Matt never looked at him twice,” Eddy says.

“You have a picture? Of course you don’t. What we really need to do is ask ourselves why,” Miss Sandy asks and loosens his grip. “How we going prove we did even deh yah? So damn frighten to expose ourselves that we doing battyman hater work for them. Now it’s we who making sure we vanish. No picture, no video, no movie, no drawing, not even an Etch A Sketch. We covering our tracks so good that even we can’t find the way back home. You was here for the New Year’s party up in Millsborough? It was like out of a dream. Or a Janet Jackson video. Two dance floors, three live drag shows (Miss Pusspuss straight from Fort Lauderdale!), pretty boys from country and town as well as plenty hot white stud from America. Sexy man couldn’t done me say. Would you believe that was the first time me ever kiss a white boy? But you know what? It was the first time it ever reach me that maybe gay really mean different, me love. Maybe it’s not a ‘We is just like them except for this one little thing,’ for one it not raasclaat little. For two that is the kind of thinking some battyboy pass off as smart when all it do is reinforce that something inside we must did wrong, right? Because we ‘normal’ otherwise, like normal is something you would wish on anybody. Me say to meself, Sandy, you pretty little bitchlette, maybe, just maybe we are whole other way of living as people. At least I did think so. But then nobody take no picture. When even we don’t think our life worth remembering and recording, then reggae singer don’t have to bother telling people to kill we. But what me know, eh? Me is just a cunty queen with a jowl like a fucking rooster. Thanks for coming to my lecture. Please leave a cash donation at the door.”

When we are leaving, Eddy says, “Do that again and I will fucking kill you.”

From there we go to Madames’, which is like the Mayfair Club, meaning all white and high brown, local and foreign, a gay version of an uptown straight club, where nearly all the black people around are either in the kitchen or bar, or banging one of these white boys within an inch of his life, but being on the verge of damage is what they came to the country for. Maybe it’s the presence of all these white and high yellow (as Americans call them) boys why here people are actually dancing.
