“Him no more than a baby right now though. Nuh, that the doctor goin’ say. And here him is day in and day out at the mercy of some pervert. I could call the police right now and tell them that I walk in on you promising to suck your own father penis. He said versus she said, but who you think they going believe? Oh, wait, me make a mistake. Is really she said, she said for true. When police get here you lucky if arrest is all they do.”

This was not the half sister I knew but some other woman I don’t know. Not her mouth, not her brain. And I definitely didn’t know what she would do.

“What you want?” I ask.

“But see here? You think I want anything from you?”

“You the one who say you going call the police. So, what you want?”

She gave me a look that said I won. Anything from here on would be her word against mine, not enough to prove anything or charge me with any crime. But enough for police to believe it and judge and jury execute their own kind of justice. But it’s not just that. It’s that she never really thought she could be playing at this level until I gave her the fucking chess piece. It was a bluff until she realized I believed it. Congrats to her, now she knows one of our knee-jerk words, words that stop us dead in our tracks, like “chop,” “mob,” “catch,” and “burn.” I wait for the smile that doesn’t come but will, maybe later or tomorrow or next week. I watch her think about what she could do to me and I can tell that in her mind there is a fucking ocean of possibility.

Sometimes I wonder why I’m talking to you. You serious?

When?

Working Title: The Disappeared

Date: July 9, 1992

Interviewee: EDMOND PORTEOUS

Interviewer: Peta-Gaye Burke (journalist)

Recording method: Tape recorder / Dictaphone

Location: His residence, St. Andrew, Jamaica

Was that when I lost all hope? That’s your question? Why hope? No, forget that, “when you lost hope” sounds like the point in the movie when everything is lost and suddenly there is a turnaround. That’s not what you hoping for, is it, because that would make you a shit journalist. Are you a journalist? Fuck me for thinking to ask that now. Too late I suppose. As for hope, I mean I don’t know if I ever had hope of seeing him again or Orrin for that matter. Something about his actions just seemed final to me. All of it, even the way he drank through a straw, or that he didn’t eat half of that KFC two-piece meal deal. I mean even when we went to get ice cream that night, he was eating like either he’d never had ice cream before or never will again. It’s not like we had a relationship or something. Yeah, well, you thought wrong. Who chatting all this shit ’bout me, Jordan Brown? Havelock Titus? Havelock wouldn’t know and Jordan wouldn’t care. Meaning Jordan Brown don’t care enough about me to repeat a rumor, true or not. I mean it’s very simple. Is the person you have in mind named Jordan Brown? Then Jordan Brown don’t really give two shakes of a rat’s ass about anybody. And I will bet you that Havelock Titus was your shortest interview on record. He hasn’t agreed to speak to you? Of course. But to come back to your point: No, I didn’t have hope in the first place. At least I had more hope for Orrin than I did for Matt.

It’s no mystery really.

I don’t remember which rehearsal it was, but for some reason I remember Matt mentioning Grecian Health Club on Ripon Road—girl, keep you gay jokes to yourself—so I swing round there. Turns out he was a member, so I asked the front desk when they last see him, who he was with? Who him talk to? For once somewhere did have a record of a Matt Chin. They really weren’t about to tell me a thing until I said he was my brother and has been reported missing. I let my skin color do the rest. The receptionist was family, if you know what I mean. He checked the register. Mr. Chin was last here June 21, he says to me. That was a good eighteen days after the attack, almost three weeks. He said Mr. Chin could barely move and dropped the dumbbell three times. The third time just grazed him foot, but the chiney man bring down all hellfire and damnation on the equipment. Seems Matt was a cusser. One arm in a sling, the other arm trying to do a bicep curl, neither one working. He was on the floor trying to do sit-ups and cussing when some poor girl faas in him business and say he doing the crunch incorrectly. He says, “But you know what me goin’ do correctly? Tell you to fuck off and keep out of me pussyclaat business.” Maybe she was the one who reported him. Poor man must have been really suffering and trying to act like nothing happen. Then him nearly fall off the elliptical because he kept trying to move without holding on—yeah, that’s sensible. After a while it was the owner himself who had to go over and tell Matt to go home. That whatever happened to him he is clearly at the beginning stage of recovery and surely his doctor would have said not to rush things. Matt’s response? “And when me look ’pon you and see me bloodcloth doctor, then you can give me an opinion of my medical status.” That’s when they called security. It seems he never came back.

I don’t know, man, I feel it for him. It’s like he trying so hard to not make this thing throw him off course like it goin’ define him or something. The attack, I mean. If he could do this one thing it means nobody changed anything. You never tried to will your way into something before? I mean that’s our obsession, nuh true? With being normal, I mean. As long as we can do X, Y, or Z, we normal. We do this to be normal but don’t think what being normal is supposed to do. Sorta like boys from high school. One of them said to me I could be normal if only…then stopped. Can I tell you, I would have sold crack to schoolchildren just for him to tell me what I need to do to be normal. Flick my wrist less, walk slower, talk deeper, sit with my legs spread wider, scratch my nuts like nobody is watching.

But the faggots.

Don’t laugh!

I tell you something though. That was fourteen-year-old me. Twenty-two-year-old me don’t think he was ever going to finish that sentence. Meaning I bet he could never tell me what I need to do, when and how much and for how long to become normal. One year in philosophy class taught me that what he dropped was a bad-faith argument, which is a logical fallacy. You know what that means, right? It means an argument or statement that pretends to be reasonable but has no reason, or pretend to be sensible but have no raas sense. Him saying I would be normal “if only” implies that there is an only, except there is none. Shit, man, you have me drifting all over the place. Miss Thang at the reception tells me that him still have Matt’s gym bag behind the counter.

I took it home before opening it and tried not to act like it’s some kind of gift or key or something. Without saying it, me and my brother realized that the best thing we could give each other was distance, so I knew I didn’t have to worry about him barging into my room or giving a shit what he would find in there. And Lord knows it’s not like Daddy was going to make a visit anytime soon. My sister was suddenly all about church summer camp, which means a Pessoa, Shoucair, or Azan boy was now all about church summer camp.

I don’t know why I’m delaying this shit with you. So, I unzipped the side pockets first and found travel-size toothpaste, no toothbrush, and a receipt, a rent receipt from a Miss Fontaine Kong for six thousand dollars. For 36 New Kingston Mews, unit 37. That must have been where he really lived, but New Kingston Mews is just as expensive and stush as Westminster, so why go through all that to hide it? I mean this bredda made it his mission to throw me off his scent. June 1, that was the receipt date.

A pair of sour-smelling blue Converse socks. White Adidas shorts, blue Nike shorts, and a plain yellow T-shirt, all smelling of old sweat and cologne. Speaking of cologne, a half-full bottle of Cool Water. Flip-flop slippers. A greasy bag with two Tastee patties, both of them with one bite. Yuck. I almost forgot the zip on the other side, which opened to…well, that was unexpected. A full set of clothes, gray jacket, gray pants, brown—no, tan belt, tan shoes that if he wore even twice would be a surprise, light gray shirt. I mean he left the bag behind, which mean he clearly had other clothes on. But honestly? I not no detective, but I don’t think him did wear any of the formal clothes. And I mean didn’t wear them, not to work or anywhere because there were no creases or nothing. None of the creases you see at the bottom of a tucked-in shirt. Oh yeah, condoms, K-Y, and an enema kit in one of the little pockets. Did I mention the job ID yet?

Huckleberry Investments on Oxford Road. Mat Chin-See. Here I was thinking that “Matt” was short for “Matthew” when it was long for “Mat.” Turns out he wasn’t a marketing exec but an investment portfolio manager. Nah lie, that was kinda disappointing, but I should have known from the clothes he was always wearing, I mean it’s not like it screamed “art director.”

Portfolio manager. Imagine that.

And you know, because it was like three-ish in the afternoon I say to myself, might as well check out where him work, right? Huckleberry Investments. What were the odds that he might be at work today? Took Daddy’s car. Here is what I was thinking, that if I show up in a Jaguar, they couldn’t just dismiss me, right? I figured I would use the same half-brother line as before. Well, here I was thinking I would be lucky to get as far as the receptionist before they ask me to leave. Wrong-bong, as we used to say in basic school. Them people had me all the way up in the boardroom, the way they all wanted to see me. “You talking to your brother? All is well? Is like he just pop off the face of the earth. Him buss ’way like beigey kite—him was in an accident? We called all the hospitals. The human resources manager said that the last check they mailed out was returned to sender. It was always strange that he never did direct deposit. His address? Of course: 333 Longford Close, Kingston 6. His phone line was at first dead, but then it started ringing again, for somebody else. Oh my God, I really hope he is okay and there is some explanation.”

He used to talk a lot about California, a sad woman I could tell was in love with him told me. Or some kind of feeling maybe—I mean I don’t know what in love look like! She showed me his desk, which was in a corner on the same floor as reception, their workstations facing each other. Yes, I wanted to check the drawers but didn’t think I was allowed. He used to bring two doughnuts, plain for her, strawberry filling for himself, and then joked about how at least when him finally get fat he will beat the curse of chiney butt. “Between you and me, though, him chiney butt was fine,” she said. But he said to her that this year, this year, this year he was going to California. When she said California sound like a big place, so where in California exactly he mean, he would just repeat “California, California,” like he just find the word on the street one day and pick it up.

“Your brother though, as soon as you call him his smile would light up the room, but if he was off on him own, even when he was deep in work, him face look like somebody lock him up in the dark. Sometimes it was a little scary how Mat could just switch it on and off, like when a client come by, even the crankiest old bitch he would have her cracking up, promising to send him a slice of potato pudding that the helper cooked and then joke that she have two daughters. Man, woman, child, that man could put anybody at ease.

“But yes mi love, as soon as the client gone, him face seized up again. I don’t think he did know that we could see it, because it’s not like him used to withdraw or anything, even though he never once come to the company socials.

“Him married? A man like that too good to be single. Nobody round here ask because most people don’t look at chiney people that way, you understand? As if chiney baby come via stork. But as me say, all the older clients just wanted to marry him off.”

Even though everybody was glad to meet Mat’s brother, me being there made nobody happy. “You call the police?” somebody asked me. Another asked if they should make a Missing flyer and post it all over Kingston. Then they asked how his parents and family are taking his disappearance and I almost choked. “They are praying,” I said. “They think wherever he is, communication not too great, and maybe he has been trying to contact us.” I’m not sure that convinced anybody, but it was enough for them not to ask me anything else. When I was leaving three women in the secretary pool asked me if it was okay to spend a few minutes in prayer and I nodded before realizing that they wanted me to pray, too.

Oh, right, I wasn’t done with the gym bag. Let’s see…what more did he have in there? A phone bill but I didn’t recognize any of the numbers. I’m sure one of them was Havelock’s. Another tie with ketchup on it.

You want to know why I checked out New Kingston Mews on my own. Maybe I want to keep all the mews to myself? You know, no mews is good mews. All the mews that fit to—fine, I goin’ stop. The truth is I didn’t really think much of it, other than I didn’t want to turn this Jordan and Eddy into some sort of dynamic duo or, worse, one of those TV couples like Bruce Willis and that other woman, or Pierce Brosnan and that other woman, or whoever. Is not just that Jordan suck the air out of a room, but you hear him huff and puff. I’m just saying that he have a way of making everything about him, even the search for somebody else. It’s like I need a week’s break after I see him. You know he showed me child porn once? Yeah, at some old pervert’s house, and yeah, he knew where all that shit was, European, incest, animals, little pickney. Whose house? Take a guess.

But I could feel my mind stopping itself from trying to make sense. Three different addresses, four if you take Rainford seriously. Strike Westminster off the list since he didn’t live there. I still don’t know why lie about it, worse, be so elaborate with the lying. That means I’m not the only person he is lying to, don’t it? Was lying to. I mean if you take so much time and effort to build your lies did you build something else? Aren’t faggots always building something—I don’t know, a safe place, a room of one’s own and world where you can let your hair down so to speak? And what if that world is not one place but a bunch of places put together. That church’s confession booth. That gym’s shower. That public bathroom. The last aisle in the library’s seventeenth-century reference section. That man’s bedroom in the back of that house in the hills. Anywhere in America. Put four rooms together and you have a house, but who say they must be under one roof?

But there I go trying to make sense, when 36 New Kingston Mews don’t make any. This place looked like he actually moved out. And recently, too. The landlady (always a lady) said he came to her one day, all chip-up (meaning bruised up) and gave her notice. Then he and two other friends move out three days later. She says all of this was three weeks ago, maybe a month.

“Friends?” I say. “What friends? Did you see what they looked like?”

“They look like him,” she say.

I asked her how she know they wasn’t family. She says that family don’t move that way with each other. I mean of course he has friends, everybody in the world has friends. But Matt Chin cuts up his life into all these portions that I wonder if the people in section A know anything about the people in section C. The landlady thought I came by to clean up, so that’s exactly what I did.

I took down the dirty curtains that used to be white lace years ago. Matt didn’t strike me as any kind of lace person, but he did come off as somebody who didn’t give a shit how he found an apartment. As long as people couldn’t faas in him business. Dusty floor. I forgot to ask how long he lived there, but either it wasn’t too long or he didn’t give a shit about turning this into any kind of home. This must be what it looks like to always have one foot in and one out. I’ll bet that he left this place in under an hour.

So in the closet was all this paper and one book, Two Girls, Fat and Thin, by Mary Gaitskill. It took me a while to see that all the loose paper was a manuscript. Maybe. Well, it was a lot of pages typed up. On this page a white man is saying hi to the neighbor from the bed and the sheets shift to show that he is naked yet doesn’t care. Nor does the man in the house with him. On another page somebody is narrating how now that he looks through the window, nobody is there anymore. Pages 236 to 249 come before pages 16 to 75. Matt was writing—had written a novel? autobiography? I didn’t know—or that he was a writer. On page 222 the narrator is looking through the crack in the window as two beautiful men have sex. Loud sex. He closes his eyes because the sound of fucking is more real than the sight of it. Page 240, blood and blood and blood everywhere. From what I’m reading, a shy boy in his first apartment is watching his neighbor and a visitor have gay sex. Then they both vanish. No, one of them vanish. Murder, there is a murder. A body. Somebody here now gone, somebody missed, somebody that he thinks about too much. Obsession, masturbation, memory.

I wanted to know everything about this book without reading it, because by reading it I knew that I would learn too much. There are pages scattered on the bedroom floor including the title page. I by C. H. Matthew. Pseudonym. So, Matt takes everything but leaves this?

I scooped up all the pages and stuffed them in a paper bag.

Other than the pages, the apartment was empty. Just empty packs of milk powder, boxes of Lipton tea, and rolls of toilet paper. A dark brown crucifix on the wall. I searched the closets again, hoping to find something to tell me how he lived life. Did he fuck anybody here? Hurt anybody? Did he miss anybody? Is this the place that family knows about? If I stay here long enough will his sister visit, or his mother? And will we try to compare notes while I try to figure out how to dance around him being gay—that is, if they don’t know? When is anybody going to call the police?

Well, wow. No, I’m not surprised him was keeping that to himself. You still surprised that a gay man can keep secrets? But it’s not a secret about himself, you right about that. Kept them from me? Listen, I not his brother or his father or his lover, so him don’t owe me a damn thing.

Working Title: The Disappeared

Date: March 3, 1993

Interviewee: JORDAN BROWN

Interviewer: Peta-Gaye Burke (journalist)

Recording method: Tape recorder / Dictaphone

Location: Miss Minnie’s Ital Restaurant, Kingston, Jamaica

Sorry about last Saturday.

No, no. Jamaica don’t get to beat us, kill us, then vanish us. And we don’t get to stop paying attention. This is important. What you’re doing, I mean. This is important.

You know what I was thinking of yesterday? That if we were ever to do a Day Without the Gay, one morning where none of us show up for work—but where it’s both gays and straights who support us so that nobody could tell who from who—this country would grind to a complete halt. Can you imagine? Battyman and lesbian cleaning their house, cooking their food, teaching their kids, curing their sickness, and literally saving their lives every fucking day. You think they would see us then? What a fucked-up situation, eeh? The only way for them to see us is for us to disappear. What would it take to do it? Bravery? Guts, as the Americans say? But is not we who need the guts.

You should know what happened the second time we check up on Orrin. It was Eddy’s idea. After so much time with Matt, Matt, and nothing but Matt, he was just interested in Orrin all of a sudden. We were kind of relieved honestly. Because the more we try to find Matt, the more that man just came off as lost. He was just making a point of not being found, which pissed me off. I mean why you think you so important that people would pull out stops to find you? Anyway, Orrin.

I drove this time. No way to give this bredda a heads-up so I just showed up at his house and said, “Let’s go.” Eddy was like, “We should take my car,” and I was like, “To Waterhouse? You drinking mad puss piss?” I mean. My wreck could make it without anybody noticing. But Daddy Porteous’s Jaguar? Now if only he could tone down the battymanness we would be fine.

Of course the whole ride over he was talking about how the new Terror Fabulous song wouldn’t be out of place in a gay club. No, I haven’t heard it. You don’t see what him really saying? Him bitching because me car didn’t have no CD player.

Anyway, we make it to Waterhouse and pull up by that wide dust bowl football field that used to be a park in another vision of Kingston’s future. Don’t look too hard and you would think you’re in America with all the two-story houses squeezing beside each other like New York brownstones. But then you notice that even with prefab concrete, they all look like shipping containers stacked together. Pink, green, peach, and yellow as if cotton candy colors could stop tribal war.

This teenage schoolboy caught somewhere between smart and smartass passed us.

“My youth, where Miss Turner place deh again?” I asked. I thought my ghetto chat was with it, but he eyed me and Eddy for half a minute.

“Who you?”

“Her nephew.”

“And who this?”

“Her other nephew. Syrian side of the family, you know how it go. Yo, we ah go surprise her, you see me?” I added.

“Zeen, 3422.”

I didn’t want to say that none of these houses had numbers.

“Pink house.”

“Zeen.”

Or that every fourth house was pink. But then I finally remembered it. The women of the house were home. Meaning Orrin’s sister Maylene and his mother who I just called Miss Turner. At the door the neighbor peeked over the fence.

“You two is police? So unu care ’bout ghetto people after all.”

“You have a good day, ma’am,” Eddy said, ignoring that I was clearly scowling at him.

“Them say me boy involved in foul play,” said his mother.

“If foul play mean him is the victim, how come him involved? Me would never say murder victim involved in him murder or that rape victim involved in her rape. What ‘involve’ mean?” Maylene asked.

All I could think of was how much this question needed an answer. But gay men are always considered to be involved in their own outcomes, no matter how fucked up, for real a mob could put two car tires over our necks and burn us alive and we’d still be “involved” in our demise. God help you if you are a lesbian and nine men were waiting outside your door, because that is a corrective gang bang—not a rape because like Mama Turner said, you can’t be involved in a rape if is you them raping. I want to tell her that she in the right wheelhouse but can’t see our wheels. Any minute now I was expecting her to tell us how many grandchildren her one son was going to give her.

“Why they say he at large?” asked the sister.

“At large? But he’s not a suspect in anything. He’s the victim,” Eddy said.

“Victim? Lawd you think him dead for true,” the mother wailed and I glared at Eddy.

“Pastor Trey say to hold on to hope, Mama.”

“Is all we can do,” she said as she looked at me. I want to tell her that I don’t have any answers either.

“They not going do anything, these idiot police. They not goin’ search for my brother. And is not because he from round here, if you know what I mean.”

“What do you m—”

“Eddy,” I said and cut him off. I realized that Maylene Turner know enough to speak to me without speaking. She know what her brother was about. And she know that is why the police will never look for him. The mother is still whimpering about the grandchildren she is not going to have, annoying her daughter.

“Why you so sure he didn’t just check out? Country? Miami? You don’t think he just up and leave?” I asked.

“Orrin don’t have no passport. Also leave and go where? People not always kind to my brother and he don’t even have to do nothing for the unkindness to show. But like me say, leave and go where? That boy can’t take care of himself. Who going cook for him? Who goin’ clean?” Maylene said.

“Lawd, me boy,” his mother said.

“Is all right, Mama,” Maylene said.

“How it all right? Mi boy involve in mix-up? How you two know me son? You involve in mix-up, too?”

“They know him from work, Mama.”

I don’t think this answer satisfied her, but she quieted herself anyway.

“When was the last time Orrin come home?” I asked Maylene.

“Thursday, near a month ago. Anybody could tell he was coming from the hospital. ‘Orrin, what the hell happen to you?’ me say, because it was near a week now since anybody see him. I mean he just disappear like that. Maybe he was practicing. I don’t know. Him say it was some minor accident with a bus and that everybody get treated and sent home. But four days? Mild mean same afternoon, not most of the workweek. And how come nobody hear about no crash on the news? But the more you ask him is the more he clamp down until is like him did born mute. I remember when I try to hug him he bawl out ‘Owww’ and rub him chest. ‘The crash fling you from your seat?’ I ask him and him just nod. All Mama could see was her little boy all mash up. A big white pad bandage to him head back and another right over the left eye. Mama threaten to kill whoever cause the accident, which make him laugh, but when he do so I notice that most of him left teeth gone. Orrin always did have pretty teeth. Always. Me ask him if is rough man do this to him. If him did think he was going get one thing but him get another and him just look ’pon me. Me never see a look like that on him face ever. Is a look that say a whole mess of things, but it was also a look that just say You too? Honestly it make me mad ’cause it not me who is that way, is him.”

“Girl what you talking ’bout?” Miss Turner almost mumbled.

“Nothing, Mama. Me soon set out your afternoon pills. You want stew peas or fish this evening?”

“Ooh. Stew peas, me love. You goin’ put in likkle pig’s tail?”

“Me will see what me can do, but don’t tell you doctor, Mama,” she says, which seemed to satisfy the mother.

Maylene then took us around the back.

“You two just like him? Or just you?” she asked and nodded at me.

I wanted to ask what the fuck about me comes off as gay and how come this half whitey don’t have a whiff of it, but I reminded myself why we were here.

“But that wasn’t the last time you see him, right?” I said.

You don’t look shocked. I must be wearing on you now. Can’t surprise you anymore. I’m assuming you spoke to Orrin’s sister? She get less ignorant with age or is the term “more aware”?

They not telling lies, they building fictions and no, it’s not the same thing. “Telling lies” implies that they have some kinda reality to distort, when the truth is they have nothing. Can’t judge it at all—I create a fiction every time some vile man gone inside me.

But seriously though. Four different houses under four different names? You have to wonder, did this bredda just wake up every morning and then decide which version of himself he was going to be? I goin’ guess that three out of the four Matt Chins were straight. The question is if straight Matt Chin did have a girl. I mean, think of how many men out there whose boyfriend is a girlfriend. Working Title: The Disappeared

Date: July 14, 1992

Interviewee: EDMOND PORTEOUS

Interviewer: Peta-Gaye Burke (journalist)

Recording method: Tape recorder / Dictaphone

Location: Burger King, St. Andrew, Jamaica

You know I used to keep a journal? Yeah, man, one of them leather-bound books with a buckle that you can get in like a Borders in Fort Lauderdale or something. You buy one of those and think to yourself, I goin’ be a writer, and even buy a special new pen to go along with it. One of them pens with three colors, you ever do that? Okay not goin’ lie—there must be at least seven journals with exactly one entry under my bed right now. Me sure by now Mummy file them under children stuff to hide from the children. You think she read them? I think mothers want their children to stay exactly as they see them, so no. How the Bible verse go? When I became a man, I put away childish things. I only mentioned it because if you were to read the last one, you would know why Matt Chin stayed with me longer than the other one. Orrin, yes, I remember his name. Jesus Christ.

But Matt haunted me longer. Too long. I don’t know, man, shit did get weird. And after a while I just stop spar with Jordan Brown. Too much, man. How such a skinny little fuck can be so much that he is too much I don’t know. I know, that sound like something he would say. Plus, him fat now, right? Hey, I would be the first to say that somebody don’t have to be close to you to leave a mark on you. I mean Jordan, not Matt. Chin didn’t leave a mark, him leave something else. That’s why I say “haunted,” man, I don’t have no other word for it. I should have gone to the police with my mother. Instead I went alone and that was a…well.

So check this now, I take myself to the Cross Roads police station. I don’t know why, and would you believe I passed three stations to get to that one? The corporal on duty look me up and down when I said I want to report a missing person, but you should see how he burst out laughing when I said the victim might have gone missing two months before. “It take you that long to miss him?” him ask me and laugh so long that I didn’t hear him ask for Matt’s name until the third time.

“Matt Chin,” I say back. “Also known as Mat Chin-See.”

“Two name? You not one of them old lady who just give ’way all them savings to them ‘nephew’?” Him ask me and I could just tell he was expecting me to find this funny. No laugh from me so a scowl from him. Relations? No relations that I know. I mean I don’t know if he was or is an orphan or only child, or foster or whatever. No, I am not related to him. I am, well, an associate. I know him hear that one before. All it take was one look for me to realize that “associate” must mean “lover” or “partner” or “sister” in the homo sense, meaning code for battyman. “Business associate,” I shout too loud and too late. “Late of which address?” he asked me and when I tell him the three I know, he look at me funny again.

“You goin’ have to consider that he do this deliberately,” he says, and before I ask why he says, “It look like he been trying to get away from you or at least live without you for a while now.”

“No, I not living with him, I not anything to him but friend, and barely that.”

“But the man have three address and you couldn’t find him in one,” he asks, and I say, “Well, I not a detective. But in one of the three it look like he just left and the other two I didn’t see.”

“Then it look like you solve your own mystery,” him say to me. “Maybe he just up and leave, and maybe he don’t want to be found, but bad things happen to people like that all the time.”

I ask what if he in some gully or dump somewhere rotting to nothing. This cop had the same face no matter what I said so I don’t know if he thought I was bullshit or some hysterical gay boyfriend he’s going to laugh about later.

“How well you know him?” he asks me.

“Not that well,” I say. I read the newspaper. I hear the rumors. If police suspect that a faggot is in their midst they don’t even wait for the mob to start the beating. Don’t they beat the shit out of you just to put on a show? Anyway, now I’m sure this police think me is this man’s boyfriend, or that we have some sort of thing, after all why would I be reporting missing somebody who is not related to me?

“Because he doesn’t have anybody,” I say, and he says, “Except you, eeh? Where he work?”

“Huckleberry Investments.”

“What kinda car him drive?”

“A green Suzuki Swift—no, I don’t know the license plate.”

“Do you think he would have reason to take his own life?”

“No…I don’t know…I don’t think so.”

“But people like him take them life all the time.”

“People like what?”

“Him.”

“But I didn’t tell you want kind of people he was.”

“So what kind then?”

“I don’t know.”

“So you can’t tell for sure that he is not that kinda people?”

“What kinda people you talking ’bout? What him look like?” This is a trap, I just know it. He’s listening not to what I describe but how. “Light skin almost white, no, not like me. Black hair cut low like a buzz, Chinese-looking eyes but black-looking lips, tall—I mean taller than me. I guess some people would call him—” I cut myself off before handing my backside on a platter for calling another man attractive.

“Call him what?” he asks just to show that he caught me.

“Professional,” I say.

“Anything else?” he asks me, and I say nothing I can think of.

He said okay and let me tell you everything else he was not going to say: that he was going to type only a few of the few notes he took, and then he was going to file it to a file drawer and then move on to the next case, and that would be that for police work on the matter.

What I wanted to do right there? You know what. But what was he going to say if me did ask if he would have paid more attention if it were a straight man? All I know is that I was angry. Then I wondered what would happen if Jordan Brown was the one asking the questions. I mean he is good at getting shit out of people.

And then Jesus Christ, it hit me. This police might think I had something to do with his disappearance. I mean, no so it go? Anytime something bad happen to a gay man they think another gay is responsible? Mind you I never said he was gay. But I guess a man can’t in any way miss another man in this country. Not without people questioning why. Imagine that, eeh? When a man go missing in Jamaica the only safe thing for another man to do is let him go.

It’s hard though, isn’t it. Missing a man who was barely there. Did I like him? Sure, I mean there was stuff about him you were bound to like. Charm was one, I think. But I remember one time, this was week in the rehearsals when he just get cold on everybody, just withdrawn and cold and honestly kinda bitchy. Of course we never did know why or if it was about us—I mean if it was about us, then all he had to do was stop coming, right? But he would be short with everybody, especially me, and he was the first to leave. Then one day he stop being mad and started being Matt again. At least the Matt that I met. Maybe he was going through man problems? Woman problems? I don’t know.

Thunder too piercing is usually lightning too close—that I remember. Women drag their children from tree to tree and shed to shed. Two little girls scream and three little boys can’t believe their pirate ship sailed right into a storm, mateys. Raindrops so thick they sting.

We run to a gazebo and squeeze in with at least fifty just as drenched as us. Both of us have lost our cones and he thinks it’s funny, which I guess it is. I’m watching women clutching their children and their bags, girlfriends squealing about their hair and boyfriends looking at blouses that suddenly went see-through.

He sees me before I see him.

“Jordan?”

He is behind me so I pretend not to hear. A hand grabs my shoulder and I turn around.

“Jordan.”

“But wait. Eddy. Ah you that?”

“Uh-huh.”

“Didn’t recognize you.”

“Good thing my mother can identify my body.”

He laughs at his own joke. Every time I see him he looks older. Better-looking, what I want to say is better-looking.

“I don’t think I see you since—”

“Yeah,” he says. “Few months right? But who ah keep count.”

“Almost a year and a half,” I say.

“I want to insert a David Bowie joke here just because you the only person I know who goin’ get it.”

“I dunno, brethren. Liking rock music in Kingston don’t make you special anymore. Even reggae sound system playing ‘Mmm Mmm Mmm Mmm.’ Plus, I really just into fag music now. Call me Mr. Vain.”

“Brethren, for real?”

“No, bitch.”

“Ha. I thought about you when news come on ’bout your Nirvana boy.”

“Hey, give a white boy a gun and sooner or later he goin’ blow him head off with it.”

“Jordan Brown, still have to be the cleverest man in the room. Always. You telling me you never did sad?”

“Why? He sing three or four songs that I like. I also like Joy Division and their lead singer kill himself, too. Americans call it the stupid club. Yeah, for rock stars who off themselves deliberately or otherwise. Usually by age twenty-seven.”

“I really don’t care that much about America. Except for OJ. That is some fucking madness, star.”

“What OJ do?”

“Bombocloth, you serious?”

“I don’t watch TV. What him do?”

“Who that?”

“Who is who?”

“That. The man right by the railing on the other side whose eyes land on you a minute ago and stayed there,” Eddy whispers.

“What make you think—”

“Did a lot of growing, Jordan Brown. Lot of growing. Make up, break up, loss, grief, and other fuckery mean you grow up fast. Nowadays I can just look at two people and tell if they fucking.”

“Brethren, what the fuck?”

“Exactly.”

“Why not just get a raasclaat bullhorn so everybody can hear you?”

“We’re whispering.”

“We’re not—”

“Denial. Still a river in—”

“I know where the fucking river is.”

He stares at me in this silence he seems to like before breaking into a grin. More people try to leave the gazebo but stop when a woman slips and lands on her backside.

“Jordan Brown discombobulated. Give me a minute to take this shit in,” he says, laughing.

I’m back at the end of James Joyce’s “An Encounter” where the narrator discovers that he always despised his friend a little. We about to do this dance? I ask myself. Where gay people try to be gay in the presence of thine enemies. Except there is no Jamaican Polari, no secret Jamaican gay language. I’m sure there is some battyboy code, but I never hang around any society long enough to learn it, except for the sex stuff because that language is business jargon. Gareth is looking for some kind of signal that it’s safe to walk over, and me looking out at crawling traffic is clearly it. The rain has eased up but everywhere is a river. I think he is coming toward me but he does not stop walking.

“Going get back another cream,” Gareth says, not looking at me.

“And you must be? People who like me call me Eddy.”

“Oh.”

“And your name is…?”

Gareth looks at me as if for direction, or permission or something.

“Is okay, me friend. I’m family,” Eddy says.

“Me never see you at my mother house,” says Gareth. That he wasn’t at all making a joke makes me laugh all the harder. Eddy can’t tell if this is funny. It’s been so long since I’ve caught people in an awkward moment that I want to just stand there or sit and let it unfold as long and as uncomfortably as possible.

“This is Eddy,” I say.

“Oh,” Gareth says.

“Gareth,” I say.

“Gareth don’t have permission to talk to other people?” Eddy asks. I want to say, Don’t be a fucking asshole, but the words don’t come out of my mouth. Gareth takes it to be a joke and half smiles.

“Jordan and me was in a play together,” Eddy says.

“Jordan can act?”

“Make-believe not a stretch for any one of us, right? When was that, ’88?”

“Four or five Prince albums ago,” I say.

“I just drop Mummy off to some social club bullshit. You two on a—”

“Rum and raisin. The flavor. You was going to get us ice cream,” I say to Gareth. I don’t know why it irritates me that he thinks I’m familiar with his mother.

“Right. Zeen. Nice meeting you,” Gareth says and walks off.

Eddy stares at me for a long time without saying anything. I want to make some sarcastic crack but can’t think of anything savage enough that wouldn’t cost me looking calm.

“Did you know those gully girls live under the bridge in New Kingston now?” he asks.

“Urban drift even hit the sewer. This country fucking wild, I tell you.”

“Yeah, I was dropping off some clothes at the old spot and somebody told—”

“You go seek them out?”

“Well, clothes and food wasn’t goin’ drop off themselves.”

“You drop off clothes.”

“I mean it’s just some old shirts and some food. Maybe some money. The gesture more symbolic than anything. But you know how B-boys love a symbol.”

“The gully running through New Kingston?”

“It that. Most of these girls new. But we never short of that, eeh? Every day another boy get kicked out by his daddy, neighbor, the whole community.”

He is hitting too much and too fast. All I can think of is to shout “Savior complex” to shut him down. I don’t know why all his do-gooding is irritating the shit out of me but it is, and I won’t figure out why until about this time tomorrow.

“You come here with somebody?” I ask. Nobody comes to Devon House without their tribe.

“Solo. Some of we stumble on the way to true love.”

“I don’t even know what that means.”

“Not sure I do either. But look at you, out with your man for an ice cream at Devon House.”

“He’s not my man.”

“Sure as fuck not your girl. Listen, I celebrate any love in the time of ‘Boom Bye Bye.’ ”

“Oh, now you have me in love with the man.”

“The more Jordan Brown call the sky red is the more I know it’s blue.”

“I don’t know what the fuck that mean.”

“No? Here me was thinking that is exactly the kinda thing Jordan would say.”

“You have me as—”

“It’s good though. It’s good that you making things work. Every fucking thing in this country seem to engineer itself to end us these days,” he says and it takes me a while to register that he’s not making a joke. “Can’t believe me out here wishing a happily ever after for Jordan Brown.”

“Whoa, brethren, you gone all the way to Jupiter with this shit. Make we come back to Earth, please.”

“To tell the truth I was here just to cruise the bathroom. But you, you of all people making me wonder if I should keep believing in something else.”

“Fuck why? This some ‘If Jordan can do it, anybody can do it’ bullshit?”

“Maybe, but look me in the face and tell me that three years ago we wouldn’t have been on the opposite sides of this argument.”

“I don’t know what you see between me and that boy—”

“You the only who don’t see it, brethren.”

“See what?”

“Mock ignorance is not your skill, boss. Or maybe you really don’t know. At least you really don’t see it.”

He laughs. I want to kick him. I know what he’s talking about and he’s fucking wrong. And the more I act like he’s fucking wrong is the more he will believe he is right. I wish Gareth takes an hour with those cones. A whole fucking year.

“You know pretty much anybody else in the world would say love is making an honest man out of him. You the only person where it’s making a lying man out of you. Giving me hope, brethren. Bombo-fucking-claat, Brown, you of all people giving us hope.”

“Fuck off.”

“I mean fuck I love you. Jordan found the man who will ask if you want sprinkles on your vanilla.”

He laughs again. I’ve never hated a laugh more.

“Not that way. Can you believe that? This boy tell me last month that him like me but not that way. After four months of me fucking all the way up to his liver. Well, trying to.”

So he was laughing at himself all this time. I’d almost say that this kind of talk was unlike him. Clever and smart-ass, sure, but bitter and vulgar? That didn’t seem like him to me. But I need him to know that there was nothing between me and Gareth Coombes, no matter what he was thinking. But he wouldn’t listen to me if I said it, because he is the one who needs to believe it. Fucking fabulous—now I am the last remaining hope for the possibility of gay happiness because I went to get some fucking ice cream at Devon House. And yet I only tell him to fuck off in my mind.

“If you tell me that I’m giving you something to believe in I will fucking spit in your face.”

“Calm down, horsey, you not Jesus,” he says. “I’m just saying that living well might really be the best revenge.”

“So you think this is living well. Oh. How Havelock doing?”

“Why you think I would know about Havelock?”

Because this life of survivor’s guilt turning you into Mr. Responsible can’t fucking work if it doesn’t include Havelock, I don’t say. But I do stare at him what-the-fuckly until he gives me an answer.

“Clive still putting on plays,” he says.

“Havelock’s plays? That fucking Fortune and Men’s Eyes?”

“I don’t know. The last one was a roots play about a dancehall-dancing uncle.”

“So no fucking way Havelock Titus involved then.”

“I didn’t say he was. And why you think I know what’s going on with Havelock?”

“You seem to know what going on with everybody else.”

“Nice, Jordan. Nice. He was the one always saving you, so if anybody should know where he—”

“Havelock Titus never fucking save nobody. I don’t know why we talking ’bout him.”

“Him always talking ’bout you.”

“Yeah? You going give me an update on blind-as-a-bat Rainford next?”

“What that supposed to mean?”

“Pop story give me. Mat Chin-See raising sheep and Orrin is now a woman.”

“Brethren, what that for?”

“What you for?”

He is about to say something but then shakes his head and laughs. I’m officially in the territory of not being worth it. For the life of me I can’t see why we are talking this long or what we’re getting out of it. As for this bullshit about Havelock saving me…

“I goin’ leave you to your boyfriend.”

“Him is not me—”

“Fine, you boyenemy then,” he says and then mutters, “Fucking asshole” as he walks away.

Gareth reappears, right on cue, and all I can think of is punching him right in the face. Had this play went on it would have died the natural death as a flop it was always meant to be. Instead, it was interrupted—no, aborted, and now it will live forever in that fucking purgatory called “could have been.” And this fucking man holding a fucking ice-cream cone is the reason.

“Throw away that shit and make we go home so I can fuck you,” I say.

In my father’s room I do him hard on the armchair until he yells for me to stop. Gareth is too young in gay years to dismiss all this shit and piss as just the trappings of gay sex, but he says nothing. At no point does he see my father under the covers, watching us with one eye. When he leaves, I dial a number from muscle memory. He picks up on the third ring.

Of course he does.

Working Title: The Disappeared

Date: October 29, 1994

Interviewee: JORDAN BROWN

Interviewer: Peta-Gaye Burke (journalist)

Recording method: Tape recorder / Dictaphone

Location: Hope Gardens, Kingston, Jamaica

I just thought you bit off more than you could chew and decided to hold your corner and chill. Nothing like a little mercy killing to throw a wrench in the best-laid plotlines, eh? That’s not what made you stop. Oh right, you did talk to me after that. Maybe I wasn’t that memorable. Or maybe you thought your story on the disappeared would have ended with you finding them. You should lay off the TV still. People go missing in Jamaica all the time and nobody will ever find them. As for gay people, and by “people” I mean gay men, look at the many ways we vanish without a trace. From when our families kick us out and pretend that we never born, we been going through being erased.

A therapist once asked me how I felt about being gay. Nebulous, right? I mean what a fucking question. Then he told me to separate homosexuality from all the baggage around it, the baggage that I and everybody else bring. Strip away all context and tell him how I feel about being a gay. I said to him okay, if you strip all the fuckery that God lay in my way ever since I started sucking dick and just focus on the fact of faggotry, how do I feel? You know what the answer was? I fucking love it. Maybe not love so much as fascinated by it. Enthralled? More like spellbound. Yeah, spellbound with being gay from when I was eight and didn’t know what it meant or that it would have anything to do with sex since I also didn’t know what the fuck sex was. But I did just know I was different, and it was like realizing I was twelve when everybody around me was still eight. Being different made me feel like a superhero, like one of the Teen Titans. That knowing that I want to live inside another boy so I could feel what they feel, even if it was pain, was the most electrifying thing in the world, man, that was something I started living for before I even knew I was doing it. Every time I hug a boy the softness of him would shock me. The rush, Jesus. Seeing a boy and realizing how he was making me feel was proof that I was alive. Look at his bulge like it’s both threat and promise. You ever watch a boy run, how everything flops on right thigh, then left, then right, like wow. Boys who just sprawl out and don’t care which side they hang, shit I could look at that for days and weeks. And still prefer when they have too many shirt buttons loose. The first time you hold a cock in your hand that is not yours, it’s like you disconnect from your body to see yourself, but it also feels like you have never been more you because you have laid part of yourself in a man who has the same things you do and he has laid himself in yours. Erection is just a bonus. I can’t imagine a kiss where a mustache is not tickling my lip and a beard isn’t scrubbing my cheek.

I might have wished that people didn’t hate me because of it, but I never wanted to be anything else. I pray for the world to change, not me, because fuck that. Then one day I stopped praying.

I don’t know why I’m telling you this.

Has anything happened in the past seven months? You tell me. I must have a sign on my forehead because everybody feels the need to tell me that the guy from Nirvana killed himself, as if it’s proof that they know what is going on in the world, and I clearly fucking don’t.

How about you? I guess you decided not to give up on the story, but you give up on the boys? I was watching an American detective show where police said that if the missing person is not found within the first forty-eight hours then they will never be found, certainly not found alive. So how about six years? And what it mean if nobody miss them? Me? I didn’t even know them. I leave all those feelings to Eddy Porteous. How him doing? Yeah, I see him from time to time but I wouldn’t say we talk.

Forgive my dense ass, but I’m not sure what you doing. You trying to piece together what happened to those two or are you writing about the aftermath? As if either man left any sort of stain on the people left behind. Maybe Orrin was not the sort of man that ever leaves an impression, Lord knows I can’t even remember what he looked like, and maybe Matt—well, Matt is just a pile of maybes, not true? Even I am starting to think he didn’t exist, though I was right there with him when…when…

Where is all this interviewing leading you? This must be way too long now for an article, and who would be printing it anyway. But isn’t it too short for a book? Look at me, as if I fucking know. So what do you think this story is really about? Loss? Well, loss is a room a thousand years wide. That’s from Soundgarden, they’re a band. No, not a group, a band. A rock band. You won’t like them. Loss. I thought you would be writing something special to the gay community but everybody on the fucking planet has experienced, will experience, or is experiencing loss, so that means you’re telling people how mundane and like everybody else we are. Kudos, as the Americans say.

I wasn’t going to tell you but fuck it. I saw one of them. Found them—no, that makes it sound like I was looking. I don’t know. Let’s just say “saw.” One of them. No, not the two or I would have started the conversation with that, wouldn’t I? The men. The men who did it. The gay bashers. The beaters. Jesus fucking Christ the fucking murderers, I saw one of them. See him two times before I could figure out why the sight of him was making me feel sick.

I do better than that. The second, no, third time I followed him all the way to his workplace. Why would I tell you that, so that you can warn him? Then again how the fuck you goin’ know who? Fourth time I went right up to his fucking face and he didn’t even recognize me. People just don’t understand, you know. It’s not that they fucked with you that gets to you, it’s when they don’t remember. You want to know how I got right up to his face, don’t you? Worried about him or me?

I’m not trying to be fair, where would you get that fucking idea? What him did look like? You know what a salaryman is? Sorry, pretentious me out here thinking the average Jamaican is up on the latest manga. Well, he looks like a salaryman and that is all I goin’ say.

Revenge, karma, no, I’m not thinking anything.

I wish I had nightmares about them. Sometimes I wish they would haunt me, but the truth is I’ve forgotten what half of them look like. But the half that I do…you want to know what happen to them? One of them was a Rastaman selling fruits across the road. Do I think he had any part in conceiving this shit? Of course not. Brethren just saw a good thing and decided to join. You ever see a mob? Yeah, well, me and Eddy do one better by running from one. My point being that everywhere that mob went it pick up three or more because a mob is a walking infectious disease and everybody catch it despite themselves.

Ask yourself a question: How many of those who beat us up were gay themselves? Or struggling through a thing they think that was going to fix? Easiest way to beat up myself is to beat you instead. So I followed the Rastaman and his cart full of mango. Follow him for over five miles, all the way to back side of Barbican Road. That’s the thing about Barbican Road, the only main road to the rich up the hill but littered with poor people. Man park his cart, then go down some alley or gully or something, I wasn’t paying attention. But I did have my lighter, and his cart did have a lot of flammable shit. Hey, I didn’t tell him to use tarpaulin and cardboard. Of course, when I got back in my car I started to wonder if that was the same Rastaman.

Problem is I see them in everybody, which might be a consequence of forgetting. Did you know that from 1988 to 1991 I used to drive around at night, looking for somebody, anybody I recognize, just so I could mow them down and run my wheel right over their fucking body until they turn into street pizza? After a while, I realized I was just driving. That time, ’88 to ’91, was also when most of the gay clubs closed down and more private parties started to spring up. I mean when Madame’s closed that was the beginning of the end, I mean Madame’s was around from before Michael Jackson turn white. Then you have what is still basically a house but the private parties get so regular that they turn into a gay bar by default. And all of them have sell-by date, here today, gone later today. Like the one where I run into him.

Right there in the back room under backroom lights while some fool was sucking him off. And you know when I finally realized who he was all I could think is just how fucking perfect this was. Of course one of the attackers was a cocksucker himself. Asking him when he gave up the fight and learned to stop worrying and love the cock is a movie I don’t want to see.

You would think that it would paralyze me in some way, recognizing him, but that’s because your whole vocabulary for all this shit come from movie and TV. It happening was just so…correct, like one unremarkable sentence following another to a conclusion you kinda saw coming.

I think battymen like to hold on to the idea that we’re remarkable. I mean, if the reason people are going to hate us is us, then that reason better be something great, right? Or at least fabulous. But when you saw this man you had to look deeper to find the gay because the keys to faggotry are all in the details—yes, I am going to spell it out for you.

Normal gray pants, probably cotton or wool because we don’t care that we sweat like pig in white man clothes. But the waist just half inch too high and he not around enough straight men to know the difference. Also, nobody around to tell him that it too tight round the backside.

What else? Red socks. Not because it’s red but because he’s trying so hard that even the socks was from thinking about it too long.

How about the shirt? Just like every other shirt, which is the problem. Man with nothing to hide or nothing to prove can go a little glitterous with them shirt because who goin’ stop them? To be that every day take concentration.

Corny clothes, corny shoes, corny socks, corny drawers. And every single one he takes off, left then right. I swear to God that there must be a school that teach men how to behave when the door is shut and the lights are off, which is why they all behave the same way. And it’s nineteen ninety-fucking-four, so why people still wearing twenty-dollar Drakkar Fucking Noir, like it’s 1983 and some girl from Holy Childhood High School decide to grind on you because the DJ just serve up Al B. Sure!’s “Nite and Day” so that you can pretend that it’s an erection rubbing against that girl’s dress. Because it’s all just a dance, isn’t it? Just a dance—no, a ceremony. No, a ritual, and we all do it just to get through it, but closeted battymen most of all because everybody knows normality is just a process, it’s an achievement, there’s even a certificate you get at the end of it. I mean even with a man leaving ChapStick on him dick he was still going on like he straight and this was just some horrible misunderstanding. Misunderstanding my vers ass. Three squirts of baby oil and that bitch was on a voyage of discovery going where no man has gone before like his little asshole was Star Bomboclaat Trek. But I goin’ show him. I goin’ show him. I goin’ show him.

What?

Drakkar Noir or Cool Water, or some other shit. How am I supposed to know what he smell like? You think I have to be licking a man skin to know what cologne they wear? Maybe I just know cologne.

What you mean by what I mean? I don’t fucking know. I’m not confused no matter how much you try to confuse me.

That’s bullshit.

What you mean by what I said. I know what I just say. I don’t even know his name.

No, he don’t have a mole on his right…Son of a bitch. You son of a bitch.

Yeah, well, maybe you are just an idiot.

You want to analyze me analyzing him? You’re not a psychiatrist. I’m still not sure you’re a journalist.

I said I didn’t say nothing like that. Fine, play it back, I don’t care. Play it the fuck back.

Stop.

Stop.

I said fucking stop it. Just say it then, just fucking say it. Say what you think. Oh, it’s not what you think, it’s what I just said. Look at you thinking you clever all of a sudden. So raasclaat clever. Everybody should be a clever dyke like you. If you want to know, I have plans for Mr. Fucking Coombes. Big plans. Plans that when I done he…Shit.

Coombes Coombes Coombes, you happy now?

I don’t have to answer another fucking question from you. You know what? Me done with this shit. Bombo-raas-claat done. So fuck this and fuck you.

Done, me say.

December 1994. Get yourself afraid / Get yourself alone. Close the windows, sit in the dark and let the television tell you what’s outside. TV is realer. It’s looking outside one’s window that takes you to never-never land, to a world that keeps moving no matter what. Don’t you just hate it when the world keeps rolling like cars outside even when it stands still like death inside? Sunrise is force shifting to noon to afternoon to sunset no matter what we build or destroy. A sunset can’t tell you that the day is fucked, it just barrels on into night. But TV can stop a day cold, and a VHS can rewind it, which means I don’t have to believe shit just because it is happening on the other side of my window. It’s not true if it didn’t make the news, not even if it happened to me, or maybe I have this wrong. Maybe the TV reduces everything to two feet by two feet and in that frame even a massacre is manageable. Besides, I cannot switch off what’s outside.

There is no switching anything now, whether on or off. It has already happened. So I stop the day and relive it in reverse to make it make sense. I can’t breathe. No, my mind is telling my throat to shut down air. Or I am having an asthma attack. I’ve never had an attack. Real or dream, I can’t decide where I want to live, no, what I want to live in.

On the third ring, every time all the time, never one more or less, is how you know Paul Royale is on the line. Anybody answers his phone, and sometimes the voice sounds younger than somebody in high school. But only Royale answers after three rings, because he thinks it gives him some fucking mystique. Just as how he always orders a Dark ’n’ Stormy with four slices of lemon. Not lime, lemon. He says to me, “What the raas do I look like? Tinker, tailor, soldier, or spy?” as if his line is bugged. So I go around to his house. It’s a colder than usual Monday night because of some tropical depression passing through. Before I get to the door “Theme from a Summer Place” rushes out because nothing about that shit is subtle. I steel myself for whatever is behind that door before it opens, but when it does it is Royale alone and covered up from neck to shoe.

We talk in the garden by the fountain of little cherubs pissing. Heading out to an official dinner with some prince who is the brother of the sister of the cousin of the queen, he says, and I want to make some crack that all those people calling him Ambassador will make him think he really is one, to which he would say some shit like “It’s like a husband’s surname you get to keep after the divorce.” I didn’t have to say much for him to catch what I was saying. And even though he said a job like this is its own pay, he will make me pay one way or another.

“It’s not a job,” I say, to which he says, “But it’s work though. I’ll call your daddy’s house when it’s all set up. What about you?”

“What about me?” I say.

“You don’t do business if you get—”

“No.”

“Sure ’bout that? Because we can—”

“I don’t fucking care,” I say, and he leave me alone in his house.

Eddy wanted to know why I never want to talk about Havelock, as if he doesn’t already know. Then again, maybe he really doesn’t and if so, I don’t know how to tell him. Last year I came back from Miami with a book from this homo named Paul Monette. I knew he had AIDS and I knew why I wanted to read it. No, I don’t have HIV or AIDS. Yes, I fucking know. HIV is like the shit going on in the house next door, meaning it’s not my house but I can see inside so clear that I can smell it. But the only thing I’m going to learn about it is what white man will show you because they seem to be the only ones brave enough to teach. Or maybe the black man who would write is instead going home to the wife he is about to take to bed and kill.

Anyway, in this book Monette talks about real suffering versus ghost suffering. That there are people who are suffering shit for real, right down to physical pain, and people who think they are in pain, but are just constantly feeling bad. And it made me think if that is what me and Eddy have in common: that we think we have problems but we don’t have any fucking problem. My ghost suffering makes me want to scream. Sometimes it makes me want to walk out in traffic or sink to the bottom of a pool until I can’t stand it anymore. I look at people and still want to murder the fucking world. But then I think of Havelock Titus and wonder if all I have is imaginary pain. Ghost suffering.

The second to last time I saw Havelock was in the hospital three days after the attack. His smile was pink as if his mouth was still bleeding and all I could think about is who give this raasclaat man something to laugh about.

“I spit in at least three faces,” he said to me. “The more them punch me in the mouth, the more I spit that bloody shit in their eyes, nose, mouth—everything. The guy who cut me, I slap him, with that same cut. Bitch? Call me a little bitch, eeh? Then this bitch wipe him own blood and scratch the shit out of all of them. All of them. They wanted to spill blood? Then blood got spilled on every single one I could touch. You look at me like you don’t understand.”

“You want to kill them, don’t you? I see it in your eyes. You want to do unholy things to them,” I say.

“But I already kill them, you understand me? I already killed them.”

It took me an entire month to get what he was saying.

What that movie say? Well, fuck me gently with a chainsaw. Havelock, good old chap, I would never thought you had it in you. To think I was watching you shed spit and smear blood all over them and nothing registered with me. Chances are most of them getting off with a clean bill of health, but maybe, just maybe, one or two goin’ get the most shocking news of their lives from their doctor. My dear Mark,

I thought you’d appreciate me beginning the way your favourite novel begins, though I have to say it’s been three times now that I’ve tried to read Memoirs of Hadrian and for the third time I got as far as page 150 before asking, “When is this bomboclaat novel going to start?” Story, my boy, we need story. We will not be denied it, and I say that as someone who has always found that a little denial can be, as the boys say, hot. This I will give you: As an aging homosexual the opening pages of the novel now hit closer to the bone than I would like, as I too must grapple with a body that without warning discombobulates like my old Ford Escort. I groan when I stand up, hiss when I sit down, and these days cannot say from which cavity came that hiss. Seriously, what is the purpose of a young mind in an old body? Mentally I’ve never moved past thirty-nine. To think there was a time when we both swore on Oscar Wilde’s grave that we would never become savage old queens, but here we are.

This goddamn business of getting old though. I, Havelock Titus, submit that those who lose their minds early are luckier because they are no longer aware of a mind to lose. They certainly don’t have to be aware of the constant indignities that come with losing one’s body. Add to that, my friend, what was fact only five years ago: that neither of us was ever supposed to die of old age. I’m not even talking about AIDS. I mean that as queers, stately old homos, faggots, (or for some Jamaican flavor) battymen, our life expectancies should have run out at least ten years ago. We’ve all seen that Madam George, who did not die when she should have, before her friends and lovers, and who now haunts the bars smelling like Vicks VapoRub with nothing to offer but old dollar bills and bitchiness.

I for one thought I would go down blazing, and by “blazing,” darling, I do mean in the most literal sense: with a car tire lassoed around my neck and my bound arms and beaten body set afire by a righteous Jamaican mob. We always thought God had already chosen the person who would come to kill us. If not with the mob, then the police. If not the cops, then some boy who will love us, murder us, then tell the police that we grabbed his balls, God is his witness.

And what reason do we have for old age when our own kind throws us out with the rest of the garbage? Nobody makes an old gay feel like a dead gay like a young gay. As we get older, the age where one is considered old gets younger, which makes me wonder who is behind all this considering, a vampire? It gives us a blankness, don’t you think? The same sort of blankness we used to see in the eyes of the hall master and some of the professors at Oxford. The lost stares of the Lost Generation, the bright young things with their lights all blown out. Here I must speak like an American in saying that in me at least there is a fuck you, to the people, the church, the world, the bullies, the righteous ones, even Jehovah himself.

Cheating death. I’ve thought long and hard on this. In Jamaica we have a saying which you might have heard me repeat. “Duppy know who fi frighten,” meaning a ghost knows who to scare. This will seem blasphemous, but I have come to realise, darling, that death is simply afraid of me. I can’t remember how much of 1988 I have told you, but suffice to say, there is nothing like an actual brush with the thing to erase all fear of it. And for me it was more than a brush, for one it happened all night. Spend an evening being called an abomination while you are punched kicked slapped tortured sliced burned and a little bug working its way through your body’s defences feels like just another thing.

You warned me of this. You warned me from as early as 1952, though I’m sure you don’t remember. You always said that a sentence is only half of the thought. The rest of it, or perhaps the true meaning, the subtext behind the text, was all in the eyes. And the Jamaican eyes all around us, around Noël Coward, Alan Wilson, Graham Payn, were all saying We would kill you if we could. Side note, and speaking of homophobes, I don’t know if you remember Graham Banks. He was the one who used to carry that sign at the Negril beach that said “Sodom and Gomorrah Is Here” (but spelled it “Go-More-Yah”). Police caught him a few years ago in flagrante delicto, allegedly just as he had impaled himself on another man’s flagpole. It’s the ones who hate us most that fiercely love us. Or kill us.

And yet when I came to London I really did come to die.

Yes, to see you, but really to die. Not the sort of thing one tells a person, not even a friend from whom I’ve hid nothing, which is why I never told you. You would not be remiss to ask why a return to London of all places, given that death is everywhere and this is the last place I ever expected to end up with my end up. I do believe that when I left London that door most certainly clapped my backside on the way out and our divorce could not have been more mutual. Well, my dear Mark, there are deaths and there are deaths. Once one has accepted life’s only inevitability there comes the wish to die either suddenly or with dignity. To suffer long and alone on a filthy stinking bed as mosquitoes draw my infected blood and nurses refuse to touch me was not my kind of death. Worse, to die not in that nasty bed, but some alley, or ditch, or the insane asylum, the only place that will take us. I have faced all forms of hatred all my life, so I was not going to deal with that fuckery in death. Not that Britain is some sister of mercy, after all Inglan is a bitch.

This was the first time I used the airport because truth be told I was too weak to even sit up straight. A solid guess would be that my T-cell count was below three hundred when I boarded that flight. My tongue felt like a scouring pad against my teeth, and I wore a turtleneck in ninety-eight-degree heat to hide the little one-inch sarcoma on my Adam’s apple. One can only guess what my breath smelled like. Truly, dying is such a disgraceful show. I will never be a fan of the thing whether in myself or other people. It didn’t matter how much I tried to puff my chest and stick out my neck, the deathly sick look deathly sick. I finally shouted to the flight attendant who was clearly not about to let me on the plane that I had colon cancer and would die without treatment. Not exactly false given what we used to call this plague. The first time I set for England (on the SS Reina del Pacifico no less) I thought I was going to colonise it in reverse. The first time I left I thought, Well, Jamaica is where I belong. Or maybe what I deserve. That it was home never crossed my mind.

Dear heart, here is the thing. The friends who sent me off had no reason to believe I would be coming back, not even in a box. You’d think Jamaica was the disease I was trying to cure myself of. You never agreed with me returning home in the first place. I wish I could say I proved you wrong, but the truth is that I belong nowhere. Saying I’m too British for Jamaica and too Jamaican for Britain sounds simplistic. It’s that neither country ever thought to throw a line so in both I was drowning a little. You will read this and think I wasn’t happy, but I’ve drawn a measure of happiness in both places. It’s belonging that eluded me. Exile from one home, alien in another, only to return home and feel like an alien there, too. Blighty never really welcomed me, but it ruined me for anywhere else. But you have heard this colonialism lesson before. Can we just think about dancing to the O’Jays and Three Degrees and seducing cute boys who are now all safely married and leading the country? And getting fat. Let’s not forget them getting fat and gross and still thinking of us as they make love to their horrid wives. I think in the US this is called being cunty. I fancy that we are indeed a pair of old cunts.

The young man who picked me up from the Kingston airport, a Mr. Eddy Porteous, looked at me both bewildered and dumbstruck, which of course struck me as how one realistically looks at a ghost. He asked me what home would I be going back to, as if I had somehow forfeited my present one. The little bitch could have said “which.” He did have words for the next time he saw me, except that all his remarks would have been in memoriam, and he expected to deliver them to a gravestone. For a second it looked like Noël Coward’s house. You do know, darling, that they have left his house exactly as it was when he died? So it remains. That half-full bottle of ketchup is still on the counter, and two desk drawers are still half pulled out. Photos of the Queen Mum are sunblasted out to blue.

Love always,
