“Eat some chicken, Ever.”

“I will know what you mean.”

“For fuck’s sake, Everton Caulfield. Those nuts you’re intermittently grabbing under the table aren’t chestnuts,” Barry said.

Everton leapt from the table and was at Barry’s throat before any of the girls could scream. One of them looked at me as if I was supposed to pull them apart but I was not about to do any such thing. Two night watchmen rushed in to pull them off but not before Everton broke Barry’s nose. Of course, everybody stayed to finish dinner while they cleaned themselves up. Another boy whose name I forget said, “What dreadful business this is, but funny to watch,” to which he laughed and infected the girls, who also started laughing. “I mean seriously, for what other reason would you be here,” he said and it took me a bit to realise he meant me.

“I mean, nobody here is fond of you. And it’s not because of the complexion the Lord gave you if you think that’s it. Everton’s bed has long been a colonial buffet of colour.”

I could only look at him with the stupid look of struggling to make words come.

“As soon as he ditches chocolate for say, curry, you will be swallowed and shat out.”

The night watchmen came back for me.

Class shut me out before race came into play. Barry stayed because he is Everton and Everton is him. And they are all us, but I am them. Between you and me that would have been enough, for I hated them just as much, especially the women who seemed to think they were Joans of Arc for eventually marrying men whose holes have been through far more use. But he humiliated me. Imagine security escorting you out (of your own college) as if you were some dirty animal that had wandered in by mistake.

Did you know that the concept of public health comes from the British? Long before working women in Jamaica found themselves with pamphlets encouraging two children instead of too many, the British orchestrated the whole thing for the common good. The common good of the British that is, and by that I mean white. A plan created to locate and prevent the spread of disease was a plan that assumed that disease, plague, the undesirable stuff always came from someplace else. Syphilis? Blackies. Gonorrhea? Coolies. Sickness by itself was “not of us” despite the long tradition of Europeans obliterating millions just by turning up. Soon any nuisance declared foreign was subject to the same treatment. This is why AIDS simply must have come from Africa, darling, but I digress.

The money came second. He came first to my flat four months later and way too drunk even by his standards. Demanded that I take out that rifle of mine and subject him to most grievous bodily harm. Of course, I responded to his request because I’ve never turned down a free meal. Or maybe I didn’t care. That I hated him made us both enjoy it. What followed came quick. The school year ended and while my grades were high enough to graduate with honours, they weren’t exceptional enough to merit a postgraduate scholarship. Then money came but not from him. Two envelopes to be precise: one fat with pounds (I’ve forgotten the sum), the other thin with a ticket back to Jamaica. By ship. I made use of the former and burned the latter. Not only was I unsure about when I became a nuisance, I was also unaware as to when his parents found out. For the money could only have come from his parents. Seems it was time for Everton to ascend to his place in society and the last thing he needed was a four-year detour in prison for buggery. I don’t know how the parents found out about me, but Everton had not, at that point, caught on that they knew. Right before summer break he was again in my room, again demanding that I ravage him with my blackamoor shift stick and then saying after the dull business (because he was dull) that he had grown tired of me. I would have liked to have said that I wasn’t the one trying to get himself raped out of his own self-hatred, but did not have quite those words at that age, only the feeling behind them. But when someone of society breaks with you the entire society breaks with you.

What followed came quick. None of the bars would serve me, not even the ones for us girls. Not even the Royal Vauxhall. Friends stopped being friendly, acquaintances passed me by as if we had never met. As for lovers, well. Can you imagine, showing up at Dickie Flowers’s house only to be told that the service entrance was at the rear? That little shit was friends with everybody even though nobody I know could stand him. It got to the point where only you would speak to me and I’m still not sure why. It was the beginning of the season of weird. I came home to another envelope of money, which I’m ashamed to say that I was in no position to refuse, especially after the landlord confronted me a few mornings prior because he was very concerned about the alarming complaints of importuning he had been receiving.

Evicted! I had no place but one of the few hostels that would take West Indians, one of the few West Indian hostels that would take blacks, and one of the few black-permissive hostels that would not have beaten and thrown me out were they to discover that I was not like the other young men. I mean, an invert among the coloured sort was unheard of, even though the coloured sort was just about the only kind that white men bought. Us sailors and soldiers still bruised from the war. But it was a weekday hostel and weekends I had to figure out for myself. It’s funny, and by “funny” I mean deeply strange, how one falls into the transactional simply as a response to need, if you see where I am going. But life was still a party, and one could party one’s way to Monday, which I believe is when we met.

Despite no permanent address another letter found me anyway, one I never showed you, warning me of how my status in the UK was precarious as a ledge and a boot could come from any which way, which bothered me as much for its unsophisticated batch of metaphors as anything else. It made me think the note was written by a subordinate. Of the parents maybe? One night in King’s Cross a car swerved and nearly ran me over. Seriously, I lunged for the hedge the way a leopard would an antelope. I thought it was the everyday drunkard driver until the car appeared again a few nights later. And again. And again. Always right before dawn, always as I left some generous gentleman’s home through the service exit. You’d think I would be frightened but I was just monstrously curious. The car would follow for most of the way, then drive off as soon as I was near the hostel. One night the car hopped the sidewalk and chased me right up to the stoplight. Of course, there in the driver’s seat this time was Everton Caulfield. I thought he would be flashing this wicked grin, but instead he looked at me with malice and I do believe hurt. I was about to bend over, pull my pants down, and give a full defiant taste of my backside when I remembered who played what in our affair. Instead, I shouted my best regards to the future spouse. So lightweight, I know. So un-Jamaican of me.

Then new letters started coming, this time from him. One could read the unease in his choosing every word. His public schooling going up against his anger and his inability to express it. But what a total cunt I am for judging what must have been the hardest thing he had ever done in his life. The letters were long, I mean the first two pages of each was him trying to figure out how to write a letter. Stuff from the fifth grade about the shade in the clouds and how happy flowers make him. But the outbursts would come out of nowhere: Why won’t you see me? Why the fuck are you so cruel? I wish I could hurt you right now really I do. You really are a monster. I sit here crying because I want you to fuck me until I scream. Am I a total girl now? Have you done this to me, you bastard? Turn me into a fucking girl? We could go to Paris, or Munich, or some ghastly Latin American country. Two letters went into shocking (even by my standards, can you believe it?) and minute detail of what I was doing to him with every thrust. Another made it quite clear that his balls were mine, they were not his anymore. I think he was trying to be romantic.

You helped pull him off when he tried to beat me up at the Quatrefoil. Fall of ’54. What I never told you was that we had sexual relations right before in its disturbingly pristine toilet. You will undoubtably ask in your next letter why I couldn’t stay away. I insist that I did not love him. I did not even like him. And he was the one who always found me. But no, I have no reason. Nor was it the last time. But three days later a reckless speeding car came straight for me, again riding the sidewalk, nipping at my ankles, chasing me even through a stoplight, and driving off only when I slipped into a closed store’s doorway. It was Everton’s Jaguar, but not him behind the wheel. The same car was waiting for me at the hostel as well as two gorillas masquerading as men who looked like they were about some serious business.

Everton would kiss you like he held a grudge. Like he was about to bite your lips off for making him do it. Or maybe he was simply a terrible kisser, but this man made every act of affection feel like violence. He couldn’t even touch your shoulder without digging into the muscle until it hurt. Once, and this was just weeks before his wedding, he asked me if I ever did anything without considering it first. Did he mean if he ever found himself acting just for action’s sake without thinking about it? This was in a friend’s flat in Shoreditch where nobody really lived, the kind of place one takes a person you would never take anywhere else. He took me there five times and each time there would be a moment in bed where I would catch him looking at me the way a teenage boy would, meaning somebody who is starting to feel that there is something else but wasn’t sure what that was. “French cinema is so tiresome,” he said.

And then he let it loose. That he has never done a single thing without considering it first (which was a total lie from a man who never thinks). How it would look, how it would feel, what it would mean. And not the big stuff, like marrying a woman he will never love or breeding the next earl. But the simplest of things that no normal person ever has to think about, like should one cross his legs at the knee or the ankle, and which look says Here I am, Dorothy. Should he wear blue. Should he tell himself to watch his hands so that his fingers never fidget in that delicate sort of way. How long should he hold another man’s look, meaning how long in actual seconds. And always, always, always, how it looks to other people, especially his parents. So much work to just stand around in place that he hated everyone in the place with him, a hatred that made him want to squeeze a living thing until it burst in his fist. He was talking into space because emptiness was the only thing that couldn’t judge him—at least that is what I think. When he turned around and saw me in the bed with him it took him by surprise. I thought about telling him of the long campaign his family had been waging to get rid of me, but I didn’t. Something about him being oblivious made perfect sense to me. Then he told me to get the fuck out.

Yet you still think I have feelings for him despite me once telling you that I’ve had no great love before, during, or after. This all ties into your grand theory about me, that I pre-reject with the same indiscriminate consideration that some people prejudge or pre-surrender. I always knew where I would have stood with him and would never have put my heart in the hands of a man making a fist.

I might have dreamed about him once. Twice. Three times but the third time was a daydream. You will ask me in your next letter about how he made me feel. Not how you felt about him, Lochness, I asked you how he made you feel, I can read you in my thoughts already. So yes, there was one weekend when he bought me fish and chips, played with my fingers at the Dominion Theatre on Tottenham Court Road, made me do him missionary, joked about my coils of hair, showed me where his family hid during the Blitz and told me just how scared he was of his father. A genuine fear considering that Everton wouldn’t know drama to have a flair for it. And that weekend he gave me the curse of thinking about possibilities. Yes, possibilities bigger than men like us dare to dream, even now. Sometimes I think that was the worst thing he ever gave me, this from the man who did give me more than one scar.

You want me to admit to you that I miss him. That in whatever one could call our psychosexual business, love must have been somewhere in the mix, which is shocking since he never told me he loved me nor did I him. The last time I saw him he called me a sickness and a bewitchment. I said, “Only that? Not also bothered and bewildered?” This was at Brothers in Arms, the only men’s club that had not designated me persona non grata because of him. The fucking nerve of this man, really, to get me banned from nearly every spot in London, only to drive himself mad trying to find me in one. Because he was searching for me that night. I know you remember that night, oh Pimp. I say that without the slightest trace of malice—you know that. He was already drunk but he was a lord. I was not in the mood to leave given that I had nowhere else to go. You were going to introduce me to the most successful confirmed bachelor lawyer in the West End. For some reason I stood there, seven men down from him, and took his abuse. For the first time he called me the most wicked kind of lover, which shocked me. Not because of where we were, among queens and princesses used to such talk, but that it was coming from him given that he used his fists for his eruptions not his mouth. I knew he was to be married a week from that night and so did everyone in London.

“Not also bothered and bewildered?” I asked again, and he walked right over and slapped me. I know in the movies that I am supposed to touch my cheek in shock, but I slapped him back so fast and so hard that he staggered backways and fell, grabbing for a table but getting the tablecloth. Down went him, the cloth and pints of beers somersaulting in the air. Everton could barely pull himself up and slapped away every hand that tried to help him.

“You’ve never shown me the slightest kindness,” he said and left me there with my jaw on the floor. Shook, positively shook. Everton Caulfield, the most brutal man I have ever known, telling me that I had no kindness. I thought kindness was what people showed to each other. Am I wrong? You talk sometimes of my Jamaican reserve, as if affection, regard even, was something we parse out in very small quantities. All I remember of his face was that he was so sad and sure when he said it. The club closed its doors on me at four thirty in the morning, and I decided to walk off five beers all the way to the hostel. I barely turned a corner before the headlights switched on and the fucking Jaguar came after me. And since the busiest city in the world chooses to go to sleep at night, nobody was around to witness, help, or scream. The road was wet from rain at some point in the night and I tripped twice. Imagine a city with hundreds of lanes, some barely three feet wide, and yet there were no turnoffs on this street. I ran for a good hundred yards before my mind said, Fucking hell, and stopped me. Childish, I thought. Childish that he was revving the damn car like it was a spoiled brat throwing a tantrum. That was when I walked to the car. The driver did nothing. Getting closer, the car revving less and less until I was right by the bumper. The street was too dark. Whether it was Everton or not I would never know.

“You are a fucking coward,” I shouted and walked home.

The car did not follow. They were in the post the next day, his love letters with my name of course redacted. In two days they would reach the Daily Mail, and by weekend it was the biggest scandal since that Nazi-loving king and his double-smashed American found love or whatever they called it. You know the rest. The bride fled to Spain. The family retreated from London and never went back.

A week later it might have been, I’m not sure, but the police arrested him for importuning with an immoral purpose in Piccadilly Tube station. Milord the magistrate said there had been such a decline in morals, particularly in young men since the war, that one must wonder who in fact won the war. Only the year before a baronet squashed his own conviction by claiming that he was too drunk to drive so he sat himself in the station until he sobered up enough to either return to his car or board the tube. Everton went the other way, following who knows? Maybe the mad idea that if you keep turning right you eventually end up left. He insisted that he also saw and did business with the undercover patrolman’s cock, and if he could describe it perfectly then there was all the proof one needed that the policeman broke the very law he was supposed to uphold. The court was not to have such a thing, which only led Everton to scream that the copper’s cock was nothing to crow about, but it did refresh his memories of the sea in both its smell and taste.

He was about to get four years in prison—three for indecency, one for contempt—when his father, stunned that the horrible business had gone this far, intervened and got him sent to Bromley instead. Three meals a day without the price of castration. His father sent him, bound and gagged I hear, to the madhouse. Between you and me they committed him for the same reason the royal family commit their retards: to erase them from memory. They could have sent him to some place in the colonies or to France or Switzerland where nobody thinks much of the faggot. Nobody can tell me they didn’t force him into Bromley then had him fed drugs of some sort to keep him at the brain capacity of a melon. Word is they lobotomised him, which I have never been able to confirm or deny. I knew the family would come for me sooner or later so instead of waiting for an expulsion I pretty much deported myself. The rest you know.

Yours,

Lochness

March 15

I am sidestepping it. Maybe even avoiding it. Your question, I mean, because to be honest I wish you had not asked it, and I can’t say I’m answering it willingly, but there are myriad ways in which I owe you and if answering your question is to be considered payment, then so be it.

Nineteen eighty-eight, what of it, and what do I remember? That movie Willow, which was a not great film that I wanted so badly to be better, mostly because it had the prettiest white boy I have seen in three decades, a man with a name that sounds like he might hunt you down: Val Kilmer. What else? It was one year after my diagnosis. (No, I was not Jamaica’s patient zero.) The children were all taken up with this dancehall thing. There doesn’t seem to be much to it, none of the rocksteady that we used to dance to at the Blade or the Scissor Sister. Why, these children get excited by a song exhorting them to take a bath (“Hol A Fresh”), to scorn women with the foulest of breaths (“Yuh Breath A Baddi Mi”), and to stop telling this white man named Dominic that he looks like Boy George. Well, youth must be served. I know, I am sidestepping again.

There is this young man named Eddy Porteous, who I know I have mentioned in a previous letter. His name really should be Eddy Earnest because somebody told him (maybe a Sunday school teacher) that there is meaning in suffering and Lord knows he wants to suffer. He wants to relive a moment he never experienced while I have tried my best to put it past me. Not the same as forgetting it, mind you, I could never do that.

So, June 1988. I’m not sure what you want to know. And I must say I resist this because to dwell on it is to admit it was a definitive moment and I would sooner define myself by HIV than this. I have nothing to gain from it, nothing to learn from it other than to never put my faith in the essential goodness of people. Or in the blank-mindedness of mobs. My experience of a mob was nothing close to mass psychosis. These men knew what they were doing and each one brought their own little ingenuity to the mix. To call them a mob is to let them off the hook. Those were grown men fully intent on doing what they did, each in their own way. For example, consider the weapons they brought. A lot of clubs, but also unique and terrible (and occasionally handmade) instruments each according to that person’s individual desire for damage. Maybe each victim has his own working definition of evil. I think evil is a choice, and an ongoing one. Even in the midst of committing wickedness there are choices of how wicked one will be, which is made by the minute. I saw it every time one of those men bludgeoned me with a blackjack, paused, looked at the weapon, then at me, and swung again. That moment in between each hit was all about choosing and they chose.

Eddy was one of the boys in my little play and, what seems to be his regret, the only one not present that June night. I said to him, “Dear boy, don’t regret that you were the only one of us with some sort of life you chose to live rather than turn up, because you might have not made it out of that night alive.” Omar Joseph certainly did not, poor man. First he was killed by a mob, then murdered by the press. I saw a TV reporter shove a microphone in his six-year-old daughter’s face to ask if she knew Daddy was a sodomite. You can tell I’m refusing to gain perspective on this. “Perspective” implies that you have learned something, and I refuse to believe there is any lesson to be learned from suffering an atrocity, other than always to be on guard for the ways people turn on you. And yes, “atrocity” because we need to stop calling atrocities tragic. The Titanic was a tragedy. What happened to us was not a tragedy, it was appalling and vicious. I read an observation made at Nuremberg that at the core of evil is the absence of empathy. The thing is, I don’t want empathy, nor am I convinced when people say they have it. Because they will never have it. I want to believe that those men are all out there raging and stealing and burning things down, but as I write this, on this cooler-than-usual evening, I bet they are kissing their little daughters good night. That night was not a failure of empathy. The men simply had empathy for those who want to beat and kill us. You want me to say that I think I confronted the very worst of humanity, when what I confronted was humanity itself. Call me pessimist, I will call myself realist, and we’re both right and wrong.

But maybe to tell your story it is essential to turn oneself into a character. Become a fly on your own wall to watch you being you. The thing is, I have tried that. Not through some psychiatric advice, but in the sense that I feel the only option for me is distance, and maybe that equals perspective. The problem is that without perspective, I become the millionth gay man with a huge stash of anger and nowhere to shelve it. Why did you ask me this question?

Yes, I lead a quiet life, but it’s not because of the June thing. Dearest, you know that my life has never been short of atrocity or tragedy but you insist that 1988 was the turning point in my life when it could have easily been 1981 or 1957 or 1949 for that matter. I mean I just unburdened my whole Everton Caulfield story to you and your response is “But what about 1988?” Fine, I will say this. That was not my first attack, after all there was that time when two men climbed over my second-floor balcony because they “hear from them woman that me was a battyman, and them man must get beat up.”

The first had a nose that collided with my dining chair, which I admit I was swinging at the time. The second thought he was chasing me into my own kitchen, not realizing that I was leading him to my own frying pan and my decision at the last second to fry his chest, not his face. Then I threw both men over the balcony—I think one broke a leg while the other landed on top of the first—and moved out the next day. But 1988 was the first time I ever feared for my life. There you have it. Ever been hit in the face? It’s like being slammed with a flash of lightning. We were all clothed except for one actor who was in character, but the mob needed to feel disgusted in order to justify their brutality so they forced us to take our clothes off, then pretended they had walked into some kind of orgy. A few of them were even demanding that we “do what we usually do.”

At one point the whole thing felt like bumper cars, each man circling then ramming into me, all of them taking turns, all of them trying to draw blood. They didn’t expect us to fight back. We didn’t expect them to overpower us, even though they were over twice our number. Plus, we came to act in a play. They came to kill us. But this one man, I think he was a preacher (and not the only preacher), he kept swirling me like a mosquito and I wondered if this was how Jesus felt in the wilderness being tempted by the devil. “Just say you repent and let the Lord into your life,” he whispered to me, but it would be “just say you…” over my left shoulder, and “repent and let the Lord…” over my right, and I swear “into your life and sin no more” by my crotch. Following the man’s whisper was giving me vertigo especially when he wasn’t talking and somebody else was punching, or kicking, or scratching me. He was mosquito-squeaking Jesus even when they finally knocked me down to the floor. “Repent and let Jesus begin a work in you,” he said. “Please, my brother, say it and I will get them to leave you. Not all of you, just you.” “Is this the fortieth day or the fortieth night,” I asked, and he spat in my face. The punch that split my bottom lip came from him. So I did what needed to be done. I licked off enough blood from my HIV-infected lips and spit it right into his eye. God didn’t have much use for him after that. Every time a man made me shed blood I made sure he tasted it. In that room I was patient zero. Whether or not they were going to kill me I was going to kill the whole fucking lot of them.

They took leave of us only after one of them gouged Mr. Rainford Ellis’s eyes out. I hear that the sniveling son of a mongrel bitch is a reggae singer.

Havelock

April 4

Mark,

Also this: The first news story was of a gay sex orgy that had turned murderous because everybody knew that if a homo (no matter how stately or old) ended up murdered it was from another homo’s hand, his own or at least his own fault. Or a degenerate tried to pass his filth onto an upstanding gentleman and got what he was looking for, if not what he deserved. Because how many perverts does it take to stick a tree branch up a dead pervert’s bottom? Inquiring minds would love to know.

What I do know is this. One of our assailants (certainly there were no witnesses) called the police. At some point we were loaded into an ambulance, singular because I distinctly remember being on the floor. The ambulance took us to Kingston Public Hospital, which even then seemed like an act of spite. I had two head wounds that required twenty-six stitches, but two of us, Matt Chin and Orrin Turner, arrived at the hospital unconscious. Clive and I they treated and sent home, even though neither of us had the cognitive abilities to get there. I am pretty sure I spent that night on a bench under a tree in some park until some form of wits came about me the next day. Two days later they transferred the rest of the cast to a more private hospital. I don’t know how long everybody spent there though I heard that Paul Royale took care of the bill. Remind me to tell you one day about Paul Royale. I regret to say that to a certain extent these men were my responsibility, after all they would not have been there were it not for me and my stupid idea to stage some prison play where gay men get beaten up.

And yet as soon as I landed in that private hospital, all I could think of was how soon I could leave. My thought was my own escape. I am so ashamed of this, of how I’ve spent all my life conquering fears only to be so terrified that I walked out of this hospital before I had the wits to know where I was going, hence falling asleep on a bench in a no-man’s-land park. I just left them there. Poor Rainford, a man who lost his eyes because of me and to prove what point? That Jamaican poofs can also be cunty little faggots in prison? Oh my Lord, Marky, what had I done? Oh my Lord. There is no forgiveness for me, I can tell you that much. But the awful truth is I ran as soon as I could, without thinking of those I left behind, and when it came to actually saving them, that fell on a pedophile with no redeeming qualities except that he rescued who I had condemned. Honestly, when you made the offer for HIV treatment, my first thought was How could I possibly deserve it? Who deserves to die more than me? It’s not death I deserved but suffering. I just…left.

Days later—who knows how many—there was Omar Joseph’s picture in the newspaper, an inset passport photo of his face and a full splash of his bare feet on a slab with a tag on the big toe, and between his legs the massive tree branch shoved up his posterior. I will not humiliate him any further by sharing the gross headline, not that I can remember it. Worse was the fact that there were my men and I knew as much about them as the public. But I did not dare go back to the hospital. Look at me, a man who would shout “Do your worst” because it certainly can’t compare to my worst, as if I was that fucking queen Quentin Crisp, and yet here I was again a twelve-year-old, as boys took their turns beating me, and me so furious at my own fear that I would run into the walls at top speed to beat myself as punishment. I took myself home after finally regaining my wits and there in the mirror was that boy who told no one what happened to him. The boy who begged the other boys to beat him in the chest and back and spare his limbs so that he could hide injuries in his school uniform so nobody would know. Do you know what it feels like to flinch when your father puts his arms around you, flinch from a pain you can’t reveal but letting him think that he disgusted you? This man who used to let me step on his toes while he held me and carried me in a dance. He used to look at me, at his children, in amazement, somehow stunned that we came from him. There I was in my fifties, all but murdered, hiding my wounds under my fucking green jacket and thinking of my father. It was Eddy Porteous—a mixed-breed Flemish Jamaican boy and the one cast member who skipped that night thus saving himself, who told me two weeks later that two of them, Orrin Turner and Matt Chin, had vanished. Gone like thieves in the night. Eddy was the last of us to see Matt Chin alive.

Orrin was from a neighborhood called Waterhouse, which hovers between working class and ghetto. Matt was from—well, who knows where he was from but it was as befits his appearance, meaning somewhere in Upper St. Andrew. No reason to believe they vanished together but they were both indeed gone. Eddy knew because he and Jordan had been looking for them. Orrin seemed to have left for work one day never to return home. Matt was the wilder conundrum, since he seemed to have three different homes and at least two different names. How can somebody be gone if he was never here? Together and apart, Eddy and Jordan spent six months searching for the two to end up with nothing. I’ve never had so much as an intelligent guess. Murder? Suicide? Migration? All three leave some sort of trace, I would like to think. The only part of a suicide that is private is the killing. Why does it feel more plausible to me that they simply wasted away?

It was harder to associate their disappearance with their gayness. I know I felt guilt over not missing them, until I realised that was a fault of me not knowing them at all, in Matt’s case not even his real name. Between you and me the reason why I could not see either as dead was that I half expected I would see a ghost. You want to see gay ghosts? Go to New York City. Gay men find their own way to haunt you, and in this I deserved a haunting. Because each of us find our way to live here, whatever that way is, and the only thing we have in common is how a delicate existence is always on the edge of a knife. This is what I destroyed. I do wonder if those two men are in a place better. But that would hinge on a belief in some afterlife or worse, some god, and the homosexual has no business in believing in anything so preposterous. The same Jordan I mention above, Jordan Brown, once told me that he stopped loving and began to actively hate those who hate him, beginning, I assume, with God himself. I know you have a fondness for your Anglican rituals, but surely God must be the most unpleasant cunt in all fiction. Only a week ago some Jehovah’s Witness asked me if I knew God was the answer. “The cancer?” I replied and repeated it every time she corrected me until she wished me a happy Thursday.

My guilt haunts me so much that I keep trying to give it shape, and at first I thought that shape was the play. I tried to revive it. I contacted my stage manager, Clive, who thought it was the right thing to do, otherwise that bomboclaat mob and every mob after it wins. Neither Clive nor I had it in us to invite those who remained of the original cast. And if that was so clearly a bad idea from the get-go, it took going back to Lady Musgrave Road to realise that staging it there was a worse one. I’m sure some well-meaning psychologist who uses words such as “trauma” would have advised on the foolhardiness of returning to the scene of pain to reclaim what you lost. Worse to do the same play, Fortune and Men’s Eyes. I bring this up to say that while my own actions haunted me, the two men did not. I wonder if this was their plan, to vanish not just in physical space but mental as well. God help me but as I write this I have forgotten what they looked like. I have never been good with loss. Not with family or friends, not with AIDS, nor gay bashing. Loss always struck as a page that one turns, never to return to.

Eleven years. I have never observed an anniversary, nor see any reason to. Sometimes I wonder if the world simply swallowed them up. Other times I question if they were figments of the gay imagination, Lord knows we have several members who are indeed fictitious. I know nothing of Orrin’s family, only that in trying to find him both Eddy and Jordan were nearly murdered by mob. That said, I’m convinced that is not what finally drove those two apart, but then who has time for the petty squabbles of petty poofs. I had enough of that back in Blighty.

Once, back in the ’70s, I had the misfortune of finding myself among a group of white men at a party on the north coast. A very ’70s party—meaning most of them were American, already naked, strung out on cocaine, and waiting for a semiliterate black stud to split them in two. Fascinating times. But I remember that one of the men, a fat, rude, and drunk queen who paid for the villa, had several books on his desk; one of them had Groucho Marx glasses on the cover. How to Disappear Completely and Never Be Found by Doug Richmond. Eleven pages was as far as I got with such dull prose but it did make me consider that disappearance can be a deliberate act, done with much thought, careful thought even. And here we have one man who may have simply decided to hide in a place that most of us never see (in Jamaica this can be across the street), and another who was a ghost all along. Sometimes I imagine them being alive and in Cuba, but then I remember the Mariel boatlift and all the homos Castro shat out. I know men who went to the Soviet Union on scholarship whom I never heard from again. What I’m trying to say is you can vanish if you want to badly enough, and if disappearing becomes a daily act, then nobody will ever find you. Moscow is a big place and so is New York, Bonn, Bombay, or Kathmandu. But I also believe that sooner or later people who are living show some proof of life. Or maybe Jamaica is a place that one never gets out of one’s system and everybody eventually returns.

They could also be dead.

Lochness

April 19

Mark,

At first I thought I was writing furiously because I was running out of time. Today I’m not so sure. Maybe now that mortality is no longer playing so assured a hand in my fate, the fact that death is up for grabs makes my writing feel more urgent, not less. Well, maybe not so much up for grabs but more like a progression than an act of desperation. Mind you, tomorrow I might get hit by a bus.

I never saw Joe Orton’s play but I did know a rather entertaining Mr. Sloane. Forget that narrative of the homosexual simply being starved for love from his father. My father adored me and I him. I know this because back in the ’40s it cost twenty-one shillings per term to send a boy to high school, especially if that school was Wolmer’s or Knox or Munro. Even then you stood no chance of getting in if you weren’t one of the thirty children island-wide to pass the scholarship exam. And Lord help you then because everyone knew you were the scholarship boy: one, because you were darker; two, because you wore the same shoes all week, sometimes even to PE; and three, because no Austin, Jaguar, or Ford Deluxe came for you after the final bell.

Given that Jonathan Stiebel’s family tried to shut down the school a mere 140 years before for admitting Jews, I never assumed we would be anything less than antagonists, but we became fast friends in the way two burgeoning friends of Dorothy see sisterhood in each other instead of attraction or enmity. Among our obsessions the chiefest was Mr. Sloane. I don’t know if every Jamaican school had one, but we did: the improbable teacher straight out of a book from Muriel Spark but sporting far more pleasing anatomy. Mr. Anthony Sloane, who looked like he had walked right off the pages of Jules Verne’s Mysterious Island into our school. Understand, my boy, that at the time most of the teachers were white expatriates in their endless search for something and the odd brownie still stunned that he found it. Blackies were who cooked our food and cleaned our relentlessly foul toilets. But Sloane. Too brown to be white, too white to be black, and possessing that black-man-lost-at-sea accent that said “educated abroad.” And here he was at our school like magic. There was no before Mr. Sloane because neither Jonny nor I had any memory of it. Sloane just was. Usually such a man is the literature or philosophy teacher who talks about wars as if he was in one and tries to lure us with “Dulce et Decorum Est,” but Mr. Sloane taught biology. He said there are only two things, young sirs: things that science can explain and things that science will explain. There is no third thing, which sounded like a buckshot at Jesus. Everybody else dressed in starched and pressed white and blue shirts, bow ties, high-waisted linen pants so wide in the legs that nobody could tell if they were wearing shoes except for the tip-tap walk. It’s the look I still see on the British man in a foreign country. Dressed as if always ready to leave.

Sloane, on the other hand, dressed as if these were the clothes in which he woke up. Never pressed, never neat, always smelling of cologne, always cream, never grey. Gary Cooper with bigger lips, woolier hair, and smooth skin that had been in the sunshine too long. Boys like us in that time looked for and hung on to the slightest gesture or ambiguous phrase. Him calling me Master Havelock. Both hands in pockets as he turned to the blackboard meant seeing the imprint of the most perfectly formed bottom I’ve ever seen on a man. Rolling up his long sleeves right above the elbow. Calling Jonathan Bonny Jonny. Sitting cross-legged on his desk instead of in the chair and slapping his knees when we finally got the concept of homeostasis.

But I will never forget Mr. Sloane, or that Tuesday class on the nervous system when he hopped on the desk, clutching a live white rabbit. This is what he said: “Just because something is immoral, or ill-advised, or considered wrong does not mean it is unnatural. We think nature’s prime purpose is to create. Some of us think God does all the creation and let’s say he did. God built nature or nature built herself. But Nature’s prime purpose is also to destroy—God’s prime purpose is also to destroy.” He said this while stroking the rabbit, his fingers caressing its neck. I wasn’t even the first student to gulp. The rabbit started to fuss and fidget as Mr. Sloane wrapped his fingers around the animal’s throat. “Take, for example, a mother killing her young. It is despicable, morally disgraceful, but as an act it is not unnatural. Society looks at the urge as a flaw in man to subdue, but perhaps that most animal in us is what makes us, us.” One of the boys whose surname was already on school buildings said he did not know what he was talking about and wondered if rabbit stew was for dinner. Mr. Sloane laughed and said to be ready for whatever our King asks of us next.

To be of my complexion in a posh Jamaican school one had to develop a little bit of magic, and, more than any other trick, the ability to appear and disappear. Put it this way: a boy of slender means could never survive the humiliation of being seen hopping off the bus or worse, walking from any distance that would cause a sweat (casually walking on a street named after your great-grandfather was of course allowed). Which means this boy had to appear every morning fully formed like magic. Unless the agent of your appearance was a car more expensive than a house, no one could know how you came to school or where you came from. For me that meant catching the Spanish Town to Kingston bus at five in the morning to reach school at six (school prayers at eight), or hopping on a food truck.

So between six (sometimes five forty-five) and seven the school was mine. A wild kingdom of sorts or more like my own mysterious island where the booty was the detritus of posh boys. My lifelong love of Trollope, for example, came from whoever couldn’t be bothered to take home The Way We Live Now. The red leather belt that still fits—a forbidden colour, by the way, so whoever was the original owner can thank me for saving him from suspension. Shoes, once, though I never dared to wear them at school, countless shorts, a watch, a ring, a model car, several pens, and a love poem carefully stashed between two pipes in the changing room and clearly meant to be found by its subject: another boy. Which is to say that treasures were everywhere, but mostly in places where boys could afford to take something off and never put it on again. I think it was a Friday morning, me sneaking toward the changing room even though there was nobody else on the grounds and surprised to hear the sound of a shower going but not surprised that some spoiled little shit would have left it so.

What can I say. The shower, third in a line of nine, was blasting water jets all over Mr. Sloane. His back to me, the sound of the gushing water masking my very audible gasp. I still tell myself that I was just two eyes locked in a stare with a cobra. There they were, two perfect letters U bouncing into each other to form his flawless backside. Me making out that sculpted double U as he released himself from his soapy grip and there fallen in the gap between were his balls and cock, bouncing up and swinging pendulous. Furious rubbing of his shoulders led to soapsuds that cascaded down his back to a scar that looked like a blasted sun. So he was in the war. Standing under the shower was a perfect X, broad shoulders held up by the V of his back meeting at the narrow centre of his waist then spreading wide into the stance of his legs, packed with the muscles of a footballer. The army really did make the man. Another scar on the back of his left thigh, a jagged line as long as a muscle, demanded that I choose a direction to look, either down to his bulging calf or back up to his ass.

Maybe this was all in my head but as Sloane continued he started doing everything so slow that each gesture filled itself with uncertainty. Will he lather the left side of his neck now that he was done with the right? How long will it take to circle his right elbow? How far down will that same hand go and what in God’s name was the other hand up to? And then he turned around and jumped as he saw me, stared at me whipping my bag around to hide my painful bulge, his eyes easing away from surprise into a suspicious narrowing complete with a raised eyebrow. I couldn’t tell if it was the water rushing into his eyes that made him blink or if he was winking at me and I would not have dared to entertain the second notion anyway. I saw what his second hand was doing, and it did so oh so slowly. Uncertainty again, meaning I couldn’t tell what I was seeing for real and where my imagination was filling in the blanks. Happy to see me looking at him, or naturally swinging such length and girth, who was to say. I watched him soap himself up again from neck to calf, diligently stroke and scrub between his legs and between his bum, then lean under the showerhead to wash the suds into the drain. From that day I came early every morning, but he appeared whenever he felt like it, so random that I could never figure out a pattern. I wondered if this is what he wanted, to subject a teenage boy to such delicious torment. He never smiled, I never moved any closer, he soaped himself somewhere between thick and hard and I always left after he toweled himself dry but before he put on his shorts. This went on straight to the end of Michaelmas term, but he never returned after the Christmas holidays.

And that was that. Word was he was caught with a student. Caught where and doing what was never said. It was all very cloak-and-dagger. Hilary term came and went, and the school went on with school business, boys went on doing what boys must do, and nobody saw Mr. Sloane again. But there he was, his face imprinted on the pillow that I put through all sorts of sexual distress. Mr. Sloane grabbing himself as I grabbed myself. Mr. Sloane with me in the bathroom taking up my time and leaving my mother banging on the door. Me, him, the same old lotion. From thirteen to nineteen I was turning into something and I needed him to do it.

It’s not that it was the love that dare not speak its name because there was no name for it. But I might be misleading you into thinking that I did not recognise that I was an odd one until adolescence. Darling, I’ve known I was gay since eight.

Always yours,

Lochness

May 4

Marky,

Everything in this country seems new, even the things I recognise. I don’t remember every intersection having a stop sign. I don’t remember Liguanea back roads having streetlights. I don’t remember the official house of the prime minister being abandoned, and I certainly don’t remember when Madame’s, Andante, and the Closet all closed. I can feel it already, your response that will mention Proust, that it is not new places I am discovering but new eyes that I have. My dear love, we are now the age when there is no new anything (speak for yourself, says Mark Armstrong-Parker bitchily), so it must be me that is new. I don’t want to seem ungrateful, but I do have mixed feelings about this and yes, I am shocked that a new lease on life would result in mixed feelings.

Living, or whatever we are going to call this, feels like something I need new instructions for. Indeed if living is what we are going to call it. Do you remember Ambassador Paul Royale? I’m sure his fingers found a way to slip into your pants on one of your visits back in the ’70s. As he gets older and older he pays for younger and younger so that at this rate he’ll soon open a whorehouse and kindergarten at the same place. Or become one of those men eventually murdered by trade. Methinks I might be protesting too much.

Eddy Porteous, the same one who picked me up at the airport, has taken to fussing over me, which I find endearing and annoying, mostly the latter. Long out of university and doing God knows what for a living since it gives him all the free time to sit in my house in the hope of learning something by osmosis. Dear Lord I hope the poor boy is not still learning how to be gay at near thirty. Worse, learning from me. I’ve made such a terrible mess out of being a homo. More likely is that watching over me gives him something to do. Driving me to the pharmacy, taking out my garbage, getting my groceries, pickups from the dry cleaner and the bookstore—it’s way too late in life to have a secretary. And so goddamn earnest. I mean the boy thinks he’s already found true love. The true love? Some black Cuban named Miguel Gabriel who makes me think that mocha is this white-ish boy’s favorite flavor. He said they went up to the top of John Crow Mountains and exchanged rings. It was just them, the clouds, and the god who did not approve but fuck him and fuck his prophets, too. They shack up—pardon my French—live together in a town house in Liguanea. Both only have eyes and loins for each other. They seem to be truly married, meaning they went through an actual ceremony in New York. Truly this domesticity that battyboys are grabbing for is frightening. Did we risk getting murdered by fucking under bridges and in toilets just so they could buy “his and his” bath towels? It’s just an extension of straight people envy if you ask me. And usually from boys who look at themselves as perfectly normal in every way except for this one little sinting, like it’s a quirk. Always hated that take on homosexuality; for one the obsession with normalcy makes my teeth ache. Then you have the rejection of desire itself, or the reduction of it to make it seem like a blight, some sort of wart instead of the core of our existence. I knew I was gay before I knew I wanted cock. For all their liberation these boys seem to have latched on to the homophobe’s idea of homosexuality.

I do think I am happy to be alive, and I am grateful to you more than ever. I imagine not many men have as a friend someone who can get them into very privileged treatment. Not many men have a friend who has literally saved his life.

You said this in your last letter that men like us have been left in a permanent state of flux. Is this what you’re talking about?

Love always,

Lochness

May 22

Dear Mark,

So, I took your advice and stopped griping about Mr. Eddy Porteous taking me on as his pet project even as I remain dubious to the boy’s motives. Attraction, you say. That ocean liner has sailed off far into the sunset and I for one am relieved. What the gays never tell you about gay culture is that it’s just a tedious nightly gathering of young cunts and old vampires. I have neither the beauty to play the former nor the money to play the latter, and neither realise they are in a game older than ancient Greece. You will love this. So, Mr. Porteous takes me to some gussied-up garage called, with no sense of irony, Back Door. In true homosexual fashion, the sight of fresher versions of his kind meant he promptly abandoned me to engage in pursuit. So, he and Miguel Gabriel aren’t lesbians after all. Made my way to the bar and who should be there but a fair-to-middling little black thing, thoroughly convinced of his magnetism, who spoke to me through his friends.

“Gay bar or retirement home? Me can’t tell the difference no more, y’know,” he says.

I studied this boy and his friends and said, “Well, look at you. Having neither the intelligence nor the vocabulary to wield sarcasm, nor the looks to excuse such a fuckery attempt, but you did give it your B-minus best. No, no—not another sentence, me dear. ’Cause right now every word coming out of your mouth just screams ‘little penis.’ ”

I left him to pick his jaw off the floor.

But the last time I was another man’s project yours truly was a broke student with an ended scholarship and barely twenty quid to his name but an already infamous reputation. And the Ol’ Puddin’ in that transaction was not me. Confession: Now I regret writing this letter in pen because in graphite I could have erased “transaction” and nobody would have been the wiser. Freudian slip by pen? Just call me naughty and be done with it. We were indeed a naughty bunch, I admittedly being the worst. But what can one say to people who after centuries of vanilla come across this thing called chocolate. Remember Dr. Barrett? That old pervert Life Fellow in Corpus Christi? I don’t think I have ever told you this story.

Picture this with your smudgy spectacles, old man, me trying to down a pint at the always dank and dim Royal Vauxhall, pretending to mind my own business, checking out the queens and queers but never daring to talk to one. And of course nobody daring to talk to me, the sole negro in the room. I lie; my mouth would never have encountered something as ghastly as beer. I do believe I was drinking tea, which I guess makes me even more of a queen than the queens. So, there I was, at the window near the door, looking outside and feeling outside when along comes the Right Honourable, who sits down in the chair beside mine.

Up to this point I had figured him the type who seemed stunned every time he came across a negro face on campus. Then he started smiling (shockingly nice teeth) and said, “What a remarkable credit to the race you must be. Simply extraordinary.” He was so pleased with himself, that he could exalt my common negro spirits. He said nothing for a while and I certainly wasn’t going to talk to him, but then he leaned over to me and said, “You do like men, don’t you?” Yes, I know we were at the Royal Vauxhall, but I was still shattered, horrified even. I don’t know why. A man in a bar preferred by men who prefer men and I am rattled by another man stating the obvious. No, not stating, asking. Maybe that was it. Maybe I thought that merely being at the RVaux was the answer to any probing question somebody could ask. Surely being there meant not having to come out, as the children say. I could go to a back room or dark alley and entertain a jolly man and return to a sort of normal. But to speak it into being was to change how we saw things.

I didn’t answer. He took silence as a yes.

There was something very Richard Burton about Dr. Barrett, I mean the man was not unattractive. He had fired his first shot and now moved in for the kill.

Wish I could have said it was horrible and the sight of naked Barrett with his pale skin, Father Christmas belly, and balding head made my skin crawl, but honestly, he was wonderful. A man who knows how to use his body is ten times sexier than a man who simply has one. Or maybe I’m a fool for a white man who smiles from the heart. It was also the first time experiencing that “little death” with no help from my hands at all, indeed I had no clue such a thing was possible. And I never had to endure the awkwardness of having him in class because I saw no better living through chemistry. But it did feel organic when he started to leave me sums of money, especially with Everton out of the picture. Not that I have ever asked him for money. Are you surprised that when you ventured to be my pimp I was already seasoned in the business? What I did not have was access to your blue-blooded clientele. You are now saying: “I was never anything so ghastly as a pimp, I simply connected demand to supply.” Also it was 1956, and seeking out your own petit mort in the street was becoming increasingly fraught after that awful business with John Gielgud.

And there I was, graduating that year, doing my damnedest to stay in Blighty and Lord knows my grades were not going to win some extra grant for postgrad study. And yet I could not return to Jamaica. I might not have known where home was, but I certainly knew where it wasn’t, and even with a clampdown on queers, London still felt like the only place where I could live life as myself. No, returning to that colony was out of the question, but making a living, simply surviving, was impossible, too.

There is a certain alchemy to homosexual communication, where certain messages never have to be spoken. I still remember when Dr. Barrett gave me a phone number and an address, expecting me to figure out the rest. And figure it out I did, even before I got to the theatre dame’s flat in Marylebone. Truly I never thought I was anything special until His Royal Highness took one look at me with my pants off and sat at the edge of the bed fidgeting, genuinely worried that he was about to grievously injure himself. And what would he tell the hospital?

Gas, grass, or ass, one must make a living. At least I was never what the Americans called trade, for I will say this, the seasoned fag is wired for pleasure. That was the beginning of it, dear heart. You might already know all this, and if so consider this a reminiscence from an old bugger losing his grip on reality. One night a horrid old tosser with a mouth like beheaded fish called me a blackamoor, then thought it cute to split the word in two. By the time of my next appointment, the name, like my reputation, had preceded me.

Black Amour.

Lovingly yours,

Lochness

June 4

Mark, my boy,

We were queers who had no business being pale shadows of the straight world, or worse parodies of what was already parody, but I could also say the world’s oldest profession tied into my ravenous penchant for penis. Make ’em laugh, make ’em cry, make ’em wait. Now you’re accusing me of being Dickens, ironic considering I’ve always disliked him and preferred Trollope. You know why but let me repeat. Put another way: Trollope knows how real life works. Maybe you needed to come from the colonies where you never grew up with the luxury of separating politics from everything else. Trollope knew politics poisoned everything. But how’s this for irony: He despised Jamaica.

There’s an assumption about the black homosexual that even some black homos make: that to be in the thrall of queerness is to be at the command of whiteness. Sometimes I wonder if they are right. I have certainly slept with more white men than any other race, which I attributed to there simply being more white men. But the theory goes further, assuming we are in white thrall not for pleasure but submission. Ay, there’s the rub. The cock as the instrument of subjugation and conquest, a theory that knows no orientation as it comes from men who are ten times out of ten sexist. Turns out they don’t care about sexual attraction at all, much less homosexuality. What they care about is domination and they do so from the waist down. What blows me out the water is how they see the white penis. Because the real surprise is that gay and straight but especially straight are in terror of the white cock. It’s an instrument for forcing pain, a staff to beat you into submission. This is why straight men always assume that the black man is the bottom. Nothing wrong with that, of course. I am talking about the fear/desire response in the straight man that lets him project his fantasies and then react to them instead of real people. Fantasy number one: Not only are we gay but we’re attracted to them.

But you wanted to know more about my quiet life. How forensic. Let’s see, I wake up at six thirty, climb out of bed, yawn, stretch, scratch, fart (not always in that order), and put on the kettle. My little house (cottage to you) is so far up Red Hills that I’ve run out of hill. I am surrounded mostly by clouds and the three mountain peaks higher than mine. The nearest neighbour is nearly a mile downhill, which means that my shower is outdoors with no walls or doors and smooth-cut stone for a floor. No hot water, of course; this is the tropics and yes, up in the hills I might as well shower myself with ice. So I get up, walk into the sun peeking out, listen to birds, and wake myself up with the shower. Sometimes I rub one out and think of Jim Kelly or Richard Chamberlain or either Starsky or Hutch.

As much as I abhor you British, I have never been able to let go of your customs, in particular tea. By seven I am having the first of five cups, sometimes seven. Coffee makes me think people are after me. I listen to more birds. I take my time before putting on clothes. The sound of traffic floats up to me. On Sunday it’s the praise and worship from the Pentecostal church on the flat. Indoors at my desk I pick up the cleanest yellow pad and write. Yes, there is an electric typewriter and an old computer with WordPerfect, but I like to write as slow as I think. Yes, I’m still writing the same play. Two Gentlemen United for Northside. Yes, it is still based on Joyce’s story “Two Gallants,” which I know you have never read. That’s when I’m not sexing up some old Pinter or turning the queer subtext of Cat on a Hot Tin Roof into actual text (don’t tell the Williams estate!).

My life is so much about words but most days I don’t actually speak until the afternoon, if at all. About three p.m. I head to the Little Theatre to earn my life as a stage manager / light and sound expert / dramaturge, which is just another way of saying I am wherever they want me to be. Sometimes that means directing a rehearsal. It’s not much of a job but it is permanent, there isn’t anyone who can do all that I can do, and it comes with Blue Cross. Sometimes I am at the theatre until 8:30 p.m., sometimes 9:00. If rehearsal ends early I might get a drink with somebody, usually one of the sassy girls in wardrobe. At home I reheat whatever I cooked on Sunday for the week. Sometimes I put on Tchaikovsky or Grieg or some cantata I’m trying to learn. I would love to say I pick up a book, but it’s usually TV, even if I can’t tell one show from another.

Then I shower again, and let crickets lull me to sleep. So yes, a quiet life.

Love,

Havelock

August 2

Havelock Titus, the world’s only living heart donor. I could never tell if people thought I either couldn’t hear or didn’t care when they said this sort of thing. The funny thing about this—and by “funny” I mean fucking strange—is that I don’t have to tell you about this country. You already know. You sing about it all the time how you’ve never encountered a place more homophobic. Ignore that Miroslav—your little Russian toy boy—went back to Russia and was never heard from again. Your reductive reasoning is offensive. Why darling, just migrate to somewhere better. Well, good golly, Miss Bomboclaat Molly, why didn’t I think of that? Surely all I need to migrate to America is to simply tell Uncle Sam that this queen would like to go. Maybe I should take a boat to Panama and then land somewhere in Georgia and ask for political asylum. You think the choice is so simple because your life is fucking simple. Let’s see, do I want freedom or do I want a decent job and a house with more than one room? Lord knows there is such a shortage in America of stage managers and hotel concierges with knowledge of the ’70s. What if he doesn’t even know how to turn on a computer? You remind me of people who go, Wow, if she is in such an abusive relationship, why doesn’t she leave, failing to realise they have already answered their fucking question. Maybe I simply dislike people. You act as if I have no reason to, as if you’ve never seen how shit men could be. Or did you think life as your dilly-boy was all a rollicking sex farce by Mike Nichols? And yes, we joke about it, but the lack of threat of physical violence is all that differentiates you from the whore-beating pimp on the street. I mean you were literally selling me for sex, although for you I’m sure it was all shits and giggles. Don’t get me wrong, I was a willing participant and not just because it covered the rent and kept me in London, and it did seem like a good adventure at the time. Maybe. I was twenty years old and hardly at the age to think anything through. But I came back to Jamaica because I was all but forced out. And I came back with nothing to a country that didn’t even notice I was gone.

I came back to a father who was dying and a mother who always looked at me like she was surprised I was here. But you know what? I made do. I got myself hired at the Myrtle Bank Hotel and if it was because I was a docile, well-bred negro who opened his mouth and a white man came out, then so be it. I have never been ashamed of work, not even once. I organised those gay parties with tourists and locals in the ’70s and never made the mistake of confusing life with work. I helped take this country’s theatre from a fucking minstrel show featuring field negroes to its own thing and still got to do Macbeth. And whatever you think about my life, I have lived. And I will keep on living, cocktail or no. You know why? Because I have seen how awful this world can be, and how fucking terrible people are, and I’m still fucking here, that’s why.

Back in my teens the most awful thought was which of my parents should die first. I thought my mother was so self-sufficient that she could move on, but without her my father would up and collapse. Then he died and I realised who was leaning on whom. His death made her distant, more bitter, in one-hundred-degree heat but a total ice queen. And even then I refused to become one of those Jamaican queens devoted to their mothers even as they had nothing but contempt for these women because they prevented them from living life fully. Also this: Mummy them from having to try. And I never let that happen to me. I never went back home, never allowed her to reign over me, never even gave her my phone number. Seven days after she died was when I got the news, and all I could think was Well, there could have been no other way. I told myself I would never turn out to be one of those sour bitches, those mama’s boys who ended up rudderless when their mothers croaked. How homosexual. How sad, faggot. How pathetic.

Miles Motherwell. No, you don’t know him and why the fuck would I tell you? I was the director of a production of Tartuffe and he was the conductor. We had what would be called a relationship, though we never had a name for it. We never dared. Maybe it was superstition. He hated Grieg and thought all music in the world came from Bach. He thought the love of Beethoven was proof of the accepted and exalted mediocrity of white men. I told him that Beethoven was one-sixteenth black.

He is the only man who ever topped me and even that we simply stumbled into. Miles was my partner, maybe my other half. The person I called not to say “I love you” but “Did you eat? Don’t work too late. Don’t forget your optician appointment.” We never talked about what we did out in the street or when we were away from each other, mostly because I didn’t fucking care. Then one evening out on the Palisadoes strip the police drove by a small car with foggy windows. He called me from the police station begging me to come get him out and to bring some money. I didn’t dare. To be in any way associated with him was to admit I was like him. They would have locked me in the jail cell right with him just to see if we would kiss or make love or say something straight out of a doomed romance novel.

The police locked Miles up for four days. By the weekend his name was in the news. First just “Jamaica’s preeminent conductor,” then his full name. He even made history as the last man in Jamaica to go to court for buggery, but everyone was so humane and civilised. They told him to do the hard work of curing his illness, and he took that as a sign to migrate to Canada. To half of the country he was a sick joke and to the other half he was just sick. In all of this he not only stopped speaking to me but acted as if I was dead to him, which I was because I would not bail him out. That when push came to shove I thought of myself first. He hung up every time I called and in the end he changed his number. He made it clear I should never fly to Canada to see him. It’s not that he didn’t forgive me, but that he realised in the end he would be all alone. None of this was choice. An ultimatum is not a choice.

So maybe I choose to be alone. Or maybe life chose to take everyone from me, the way it has with so many of us. As it has even done with you. But you are right about one thing. Losing you? Yes, that’s a fucking choice.

This is not a letter I shall ever send you.

Havelock

Sometimes I try to picture that year had the play been a success. It leaves me confused. I don’t know what success would have meant anyway. What nobody tells you about tragedy is that it lowers your expectations of people and yourself. Lose your toes and success means still having a fucking foot. So, success became a rehearsal that did not leave a body count, a reading that did not leave one with his eyes gouged out. I don’t know if failure is something that never succeeded or was never tried. Maybe a woman mourns an abortion the same way one does a stillbirth. Somebody out there is saying that communism never failed because it was never tried. I only say that because that is how I feel about this play. Fortune and Men’s Eyes. It never had the chance to become a failure so instead it became a ghost. You wouldn’t know this but in the Caribbean the stillbirth becomes a peculiar spirit, menacing because it is so innocent. It never grows old enough to know that it shouldn’t wail in the early morning like some hacksaw jagging and cutting through the darkness. Like somebody had cut its throat. The only thing a ghost can do is haunt you.

Could have, would have, should have. Sometimes I wonder not about failure but success. A Jamaican proverb says the higher monkey climb, the more hawk see him in the tree. Maybe I should be grateful, after all what does success do other than put a bigger target on your back? Like I said before, straight people make our bar so low. A day without a beating or being called a faggot is a success. But I am repeating myself. Maybe the truth is that I have nothing to say to you. My measure of a successful play is now one where nobody gets murdered before opening night. This is one of the little ways that people like you make me hate you.

Is that what you people have been trying to tell us? That the black faggot was never meant to have ambition? I mean look at what you all did to Wilde, a nigger if there ever was one. How dare the faggot think of a future when the only thing the homosexual has is the present.

Sometimes I think about restaging the play just to reclaim as something of my own that I lost. You are one of those people—I can tell—who thinks that if you revisit the place where your luck ran out, that is where you can get it back. The place where you lost your power is the only place where you can regain it. Well, nobody who thinks that has ever tried it, because the only thing waiting for you there is nothing at all. Once I dug into an old chest looking for the script but stopped when I realised I could not bear finding it. This was ridiculous, it’s not as if I was trying to hide it or bury it. This is not a letter I shall ever send you.

H

Last night I dreamt of Omar Joseph. We were at a party just like the one where we met, but “I Love to Love (But My Baby Loves to Dance)” was blasting out of the speakers, which meant it was 1976, and we met in 1972. He kept winking at me even though he was right beside me and kept saying “You remember?” without saying what. Everybody was white or light-skinned but us.

You remember?

You remember?

You remember?

“Remember what?” I asked, but he kept repeating the same thing over. All I could think about was that party in 1972, just like this one where we were the only men with dark skin. Omar thought we had fucked, because he woke up the morning after on the floor with his pants and briefs down and me with my back against him. That party had turned into an orgy, but in this dream all the dancers moved in slow motion, and nobody took their clothes off. His winks slowed down and I saw he had no eyes, just two blank spaces of dark.

You remember?

A time better than this, yes. Parties greater than this one, yes. When tomorrow had a different shape, yes. Before a big mass of people and a small disease killed us off, yes. Before Omar came to the next party with a wedding ring on his finger, yes. When he and I were closer because we bonded? That never happened.

“But we bonded now,” he said, and I woke up.

Unsent.

November 9

Mark,

I know that despite my joy in writing to you again the tone of that last letter was still sombre. What I did not tell you was that even though that envelope was postmarked in Jamaica I wrote that letter in Ottawa, Canada. I had a valid reason, you could even call it an alibi, but the National Dance Theatre Company was touring and they needed someone who knew the lay of the land, how the culture worked, and basically how to get people out of trouble. And that is why I went, that and because I knew Miles was living there.

I envy people who know what they are feeling as they are feeling it. People who can sense something growing when I can’t even sense when it’s there. When people say things like “I’m falling in love with you,” as if love is something slowly creeping up your skin, like humidity. I want to talk about love but I really mean all human things. It took me decades to realise that I still have a grudge against the nine-year-old girl who told the other schoolchildren not to talk to me. I’m still waiting on Leandra to get hit by a country bus. Maybe love and hate really are two sides of the same coin because it took a long time (I’m too ashamed to say just how long) for me to realise that I loved Miles. It hit me so off-the-cuff and matter-of-factly as I rose from the couch and struck me so hard that I stumbled back down. Oh shit, I did love the boy. I realised that I loved him more than anything, not because that is what people say but because I scrambled in a panic trying to find someone or something that I loved more.

He agreed to see me, which took me by surprise because I had set myself up for him saying no. That he would say yes never entered my mind. But I suppose time really does heal. Sometimes I wonder if it healed anything in me. He was in a long relationship but not anymore. It says everything about us that he had to clarify that they broke up, not that he died of AIDS. I told him I was positive, and he cried. Seems news of miracle cocktails had not yet reached him. Besides, he was negative. There is so much about my life he never knew, and not getting the chance to tell him made me feel like I was robbed of something so, so awful. “Awful” is the wrong word. I was robbed of something wonderful. It’s the theft that is awful. The thing is, I knew he had broken up with that man. Not that I was expecting anything—after all why would I dare? Why would I think I had that right? Why would I think I even deserve such a thing? Except the heart wants what it wants. I don’t want to say it. I don’t want to say that I was just so fucking sick of being alone. He said that he always knew I would age well.

At one point I thought we were heading back to his place to make love, because though I read cues for a living I am always getting them confused. We hugged, we shook hands awkwardly, and when I turned to leave he pulled me in for a kiss. This was at an all-you-can-eat Japanese restaurant—I know that sounds ridiculous but they exist. I wanted him to take me home and fuck me. I wanted to suck on his rawness and lick his honesty. And howl from a pain I know I had earned. But we were so civilised, and I was proud that two older men were not afraid to speak truths to each other.

Except if I were to tell him the truth I’d have said that I thought about him all the time, and I don’t dare imagine anything because if my heart were to break one more time, there wouldn’t be much of it left. Back in my hotel room I cried for so long that somebody came to the room to check if I was okay. Of course, I am Havelock Titus, so I gathered myself together.

I always gather myself together.

Love,

Havelock

You had the misfortune of running into him back in 1979 at Andante, that jazz-club-cum-gay-bar I took you to once.
