I think the Queen Mary’s captain thought it was his nephew. Or his aide-de-camp. One time in the ’70s he and another homo I do not speak to disguised themselves as condom salesmen and spent an entire weekend driving around Jamaica’s south coast to get men to try on their condoms and then jerk off in front of them to prove that they work. On the one hand I think he consistently rips a hole in this hypocritical bullshit that Jamaicans pass off as sexual morality. And he proves that there is no rule about normalcy that can’t be bent with the limp strength of a dollar bill. On the other hand he’s still a villain, a pedophile who fancies himself a pederast, and all those boys get from him is lunch money and syphilis.

So, I ran into him at Finistère.

“Well, busha, at least you finally look like somebody feeding you,” he said to me.

“Royale.” I sighed.

“And how you keeping the other skinny boy?”

“Not in the practice of keeping boys, skinny or otherwise,” I said to the barely postpubescent boy behind him.

“Jordan Brown me mean.”

“Oh. He always had a bed, well, floor in your house, so I’m surprised you’re asking me.”

“You right. I forget. Your job is to save the boy, and it look like him don’t need no more saving. That why you don’t see him.”

“I don’t—”

“Wasn’t asking a question.”

“Well, he is not much of a boy anymore, which might be why you haven’t seen him either.”

He laughed.

“Every boy on scholarship end up with a distinguished career, you end up with an acrid mouth. I tell you, something is off. Something is happening. Something warning me in the spirit.”

“You going church now?”

“You know what I mean.”

“That would imply that I understand your mind, Paul. I don’t.”

“So, you don’t know.”

“And probably don’t care.”

“What the fuck me do to you, busha?”

“You don’t think your skin too dark to be using that word?”

“Still a posh uptown bitch minus the class and the money. And the job. And the friends. I was a Rhodes Scholar, Miss Tight-Ass Titus, not the bargain basement scholarship them give you. All I’m trying to tell you, Your Royal Highness, is that him sell off the family business and vanish.”

“Vanished.”

“Yeah, it mean disappear.”

“I think I know what it means.”

“People don’t just disappear.”

“I beg to differ.”

“What? All I know is that him gone. And yet in a weird way I see him everywhere.”

“You going have to be less nebulous than that.”

“You seem to forget that I paid the hospital bill. For all of you. Anyway I’m trying to tell you that Jordan Brown didn’t even wait until his father was dead to sell the business and go. Maybe he didn’t disappear, but nobody—well, none of his usuals—see or hear from him or could reach him if they try. In the meantime, don’t you see it?”

“See what, Royale?”

“That certain things happening in this city that have…I don’t know. If not a mark, then certainly a whiff.”

“Of?”

“Jordan to raas. Jordan Brown. I surprised you don’t notice nothing.”

Then he told me a wild story, which might or might not involve the young man. First he asked me if I ever read The Count of Monte Cristo, which I have but that was not making anything clearer. Seems back in 1994, six years after the incident, Jordan broke into Paul Royale’s house not to steal anything but to tell a story. Funny, Jordan never struck me as the unburdening-his-soul type. Anyway, four months after the bashing Jordan recognised the Rastafarian mango seller across the street from the house on Lady Musgrave as one of the men. Gay bashers, that is. The best guess was that the Rasta saw men with cutlasses, clubs, sticks, and knives and knew that a fun time was to be had. Jordan, who in a surprise to no one, had been haunting the house, recognised him two nights before National Heroes’ Day. Recognised him and the red-yellow-and-green-striped food cart he was pushing. As Royale told it, Jordan followed him to a place off Barbican Road, waited until the Rasta secured the cart somewhere and left it. Then he set the thing on fire.

That was the beginning. Jordan also told him about swerving his car to hit another attacker as he was bicycling across a bridge, knocking him off a thirty-seven-foot drop. And then there was that nasty suicide of that man from the phone company right around Christmas ’94. The weekly tabloid scored video stills of him having sex with another man and splashed them all over page ten. The man threw himself off the roof of the Bank of Nova Scotia downtown. I asked Royale what Jordan have to do with a suicide and all he said was: “Did you see the photos? Him face really is the only body part you know? Trust me he might as well did push him. Beside this is what Jordan Brown was himself telling me after I wake up to see him squatting at the foot of my bed like some vampire. I tell you, Havelock, I screamed like a bitch being dragged to hell. And he wouldn’t leave. Also he did smell so so so bad.” Two days later after Royale finally regained his composure he called the funeral home to give this boy a piece of his mind only to hear that the place was under new management and nobody by the name of Jordan Brown was working there. He only ever gave him two contact numbers and the first, some family member, maybe his mother, said that thankfully she hadn’t seen him in weeks.

“The second number I didn’t bother call,” Royale said to me.

“Why not?”

“It was yours.”

“Why you telling me about 1994 in 1999?”

“Because Jordan is more Jordan than ever before. That is what me telling you.”

I think Royale was trying to tell me that since then, Jordan has become some sort of spectre.

I had nothing to say after that and I still don’t. So tell me more about that barrister boyfriend of yours. Write soon.

Love,

Lochness

December 6

Dearest Mark,

The spectre did come to see me back on New Year’s 1995—also a break-in, something I didn’t tell Royale. “This is an anniversary celebration,” he said to me. Two and a half million Jamaicans and somehow he was the only one to be cursed with irony. And can I tell you, he is none the better for it. “Funny thing this fuckery that we call trauma,” he said to me, trying to sound older than he was. “What nobody tell you is how it flattens time.” His friend who was attacked still talks about it, not in the present so much as struggling to make it past, meaning it is always happening to her. “When people do cruel shit” (his words) to you it never stops being a current event. Get hit by a car or shot in the belly or struck by your husband—it’s the same thing, because nothing freezes you in time like violence. It leaves a mark inside and outside that slams the door shut on the past because in the past you did not have this mark. It arrests the future, stagnates it because wherever you go you take that mark with you. He is not the only one who knows a thing or two about that, but Jordan decides to tell me anyway. Honestly what I noticed was that he was again thin after packing on some prosperity fat from working his father’s job.

“That damn attack was almost seven years ago,” he said, “but it might as well be seven days, even seven minutes. I know that look on your face. It is telling me that you’ve moved on.”

“Moved on where?” I ask, but he ignores me.

“I like being right where they left me. Fuck moving on. Moving on is shit the perpetrator gets to do, not the victim. You think me feel bad that Gareth Coombes is dead? Fuck that bitch and fuck his corpse, too,” he says.

“Who is Gareth Coombes?”

“Somebody who didn’t know that when you dig one grave you should dig two.”

“Got that one from Clint Eastwood?”

“Like you ever see no Clint Eastwood movie.”

The newspapers told all Jamaica who Gareth Coombes was before Paul Royale felt the need to tell me. I just didn’t expect Jordan to say it and confirm everything.

“He that young man who killed himself?”

“If you know already then why you ask?” he says, surveying my apartment like he’s either discovering something about me or confirming it. “Always did like how you only keep the things you need and nothing else. Three thousand books but no TV.”

“What you have to do with this man’s death?”

“Suicide usually a one-man show, Havelock.”

“If you think only one person is responsible when somebody kill himself, then you don’t know a damn thing,” I say and watch him tremble then hate himself for doing it. The looking away, the rubbing of the back of his head, the clearing his throat, the scowl he returns to me quickly before smoothing his face into I-really-don’t-give-a-damn-ness. Performance, all of it.

“Why you didn’t press charges?” he asks.

“I go through a million indignities every day, Brown. Be specific.”

“Go fuck yourself, Havelock.”

“I do quite enjoy—”

“No. No. No. Stop clevering your way out of every fucking thing.”

I leave him in the kitchen to go in the living room. He follows me.

“You know I mean your fucking play. The motherfuckers who attack us.”

“Motherfuckers? What next, ‘jive turkey’?”

“What?”

“Brown, is seven years now.”

“Really? Feel like fucking yesterday to me. But you make them get away. People like you still think we have that shit coming.”

“I am pretty sure you don’t know any people like me, Mr. Brown. Now I would like to go to my bed, so get out.”

“Or what? You call the police? We just establish you don’t do that.”

“Who is people like me, exactly?”

“People who take any fucking shit straight people do to them.”

He slips into silence and I hold it. Black T-shirt, black jeans, black what looks like Puma or Nike or whatever.

“Get out of my house,” I say as calm as I could but I shivered out each word. He wants something from me.

“You could have charged—”

“Charge who? Charge who, Brown?”

“Streggeh Don for one. You knew he was one of them, you knew it. Every fucking Jamaican know who the fuck Streggeh Don is. Yes, Mr. Batty Is Not Pussy. Blinded Rainford with him own two hands. You know who the fuck he is. And you know at least three of them was police.”

I laugh.

“Either you mad or me mad,” I say. “So you want me to press charges against Jamaica’s most popular musician and three members of law enforcement. In this country. Work it out for me, Brown. I going to the police to accuse the police of retaliating against some men who were breaking Jamaican law, because that is how they’re going to frame it. Why stop there? I can give them a head start by beating own self to death to save them the trouble.”

“I wish somebody would take a fucking stand.”

“You wish somebody would take the fucking hit, you smug son of a bitch. I didn’t see you go to any police. And charge who? And when the police beat me in the same station, first for being a battyman, then for daring to come spread AIDS to them, then for slandering the musician, what next? You picking up the cause after you find me dead in a ditch?”

“I know—”

“You don’t know a damn thing, Jordan Brown. Man murdered right in front your face and all now you can’t see that is Jamaica that kill him. Not one man or two. This whole fucking island kill him.”

“You think me ’fraid to—”

“That’s exactly what you is, you little shit. A ’fraid little boy. What you going do, pun me to death?”

That’s when he staggered backways as if I punched him.

“You know we did look for them, right? Six fucking months we tried to find them. Orrin and Matt, I mean.”

“You…”

“Me and Eddy. We search everywhere more than once. Uptown, downtown, ghetto, gully, my own morgue. Family, friend, work. We even go back to the scene of the crime. Barely escaped a mob trying to kill us. That was a night. Poor Eddy never experienced his life slipping away before. I tell you I wish I had a Polaroid of his face. That is a story that even have fairy godmothers. How people just vanish so? Just gone like them never did born? Nobody disappear like that.”

“Jordan.”

“Unless somebody disappear them.”

“What you saying?”

“You know what I fucking saying. Maybe those same men find them and finish the job. Maybe they will find me next, or you. Maybe their own neighbors figure out what they get beat up for and decide to dish out some more. Maybe they lock them in a room or stall or car trunk or whatever and burn it up. Maybe police in the crew track them, find them, and tie up the loose ends.”

“Maybe they emigrated?” I say.

“They didn’t fucking migrate. And they didn’t seek no political asylum neither.”

“Then what, Jordan?”

“You think I mean they both disappeared the same way. I mean, maybe. And fine, maybe Matt Chin did migrate. If his name was even Matt. The man had like four different houses, three different jobs, and five different names. All that man need to do to vanish is drop a name. And you didn’t go to Waterhouse with me and Eddy. You didn’t see these fucking people. The way they wanted to butcher us. Nobody can tell me that Orrin’s own neighbors didn’t kill him. And his family still in there smiling with them and chatting to those motherfuckers and making plans for church brunch or whatever as if nothing happened or worse, they did them a favor. But it’s fine. Your generation not used to doing anything.”

“My generation?”

“Yes, your raasclaat generation. The only thing you do well is flee. Well, if people like you not doing anything, I doing something.”

“You a regular Miss World. Beauty and a purpose.”

“Go suck yuh mother. I doing something.”

“Yes, Mr. Take a Stand. What you doing exactly.”

“I make them hose Gareth Coombes off Port Royal Street. That’s what I doing,” he says.

I had nothing to say. His words slapped mine out of my mouth.

“Lured him, seduced him, whatever your romantic novel imagination want to call it. Never liked the bredda. That shit was not real,” he says, but I know what the eyes of a man who has lost someone looks like.

“Tell me you stopped with Coombes,” I say.

“Don’t be stupid. I still doing something,” he says. Then he asks me if I have a problem with him crashing here tonight. Three times before dawn night terrors took over his sleep and left him screaming and crying all the way till morning. Between five and eight he slept in my arms as we both sat on the floor by the bedroom window. Still such a boy. Still such a fucking boy.

There is a moment between when he woke and before he showered when that lost boy was wandering around, still looking adrift, asking permission to make ginger tea, too bashful to request a towel. And I said to myself, There he is, the Jordan Brown before life decide to scoop him up, take him to the highest height, and then let go. A sweet boy, perhaps too eager to please and far less cool than he thinks. If I had a television he would be watching cartoons. I wanted to grab him and ask, Who interrupted you? But then he took a shower and who emerged but the Jordan I know. The performance of the boy who puts on the armour of Jordan, the helmet of stubbornness, the sword of sarcasm, the shield of loss of faith, the whatever of vengeance. All of this is too big for him, so it drains him. No wonder he is so meagre.

He made a joke about me using local soap. I considered cooking him breakfast, then handed him a box of three-minute oats and said milk is in the fridge. Milk taste like mucus, he said to me and turned on the kitchen tap. We sat and ate in silence: him and his dry cereal, me and a mango. From the corner of my eye I saw him look up to see if I was looking. Five hours later he was finally bored enough to leave.

Most days I just sit at home, waiting for my pension cheque, and wonder if I should try to stage that play again. And that was before I found the script lodged between two albums on my bookshelf. Fortune and Men’s Eyes, by John Herbert. The truth is that I think about restaging that play all the time. I want to say it’s unfinished business but feel it’s more than that.

“And what do you see when you bend over so far backward that you eyeing your own asshole?” he asked me.

“ ’Bout time you eye that front door,” I said.

Yours,

Lochness

December 17

Dearest Mark,

Well, we are certainly in it. Pre-Millennium tension, existential dread, or maybe it’s just my backside twitching, waiting for the Rapture. I wish we weren’t taking AIDS into the next century. Yes, poverty, cancer, and ghetto politics, too, but it was getting to the point where every gay in Jamaica knew somebody who knew somebody. I hear they (and by “they” I mean Americans) are saying that it came from Africa, meaning somebody thinks a bushman had sexual congress with a chimpanzee. How it got from chimp to blackie to whitey is anybody’s guess.

Sometimes I think I was never loved. Maybe by my father, but certainly not by my mother, or teachers, or priests, or other boys. I imagine there were men who thought themselves in love with me but I can’t say I ever felt it. Except for you, my dear boy, which is an odd thing to say for the man who pimped me out. I’m joking of course; rent needed to be paid, I had no skills that were of use to a black man in Blighty, there was only one thing about me that others wanted, and one must make hay while the jawline holds. I have never known domesticity either and have started to think they, domesticity and love that is, have something to do with each other.

I was expecting (by which I mean dreading) Jordan but instead I got Mr. Always Willing to Please, Eddy Porteous. The little shit brought me a present and I call him a shit only because the present was a clock. Because that is just what a gay of a certain age wanted in his life, another reminder that he was running out of time. The problem with pretty young faggots is that nobody has told them that gay years are like dog years, except people tend to love the dog more as they get older.

I asked the boy, “What are you doing here really?” and he said, “Helping you put up your sorry-looking Christmas tree.” He knew that I meant Why the fuck are you back in my life, Edmond Porteous? When are you going to realise that there is nobody here to save, especially now that I have saved myself? That in a way he was no different from Jordan Brown in that both are frozen in 1988 and are still doing everything in reaction to what happened and what did not. And no amount of plant watering, lawn mowing, National Dance Theatre season tickets procuring, and cable-channel buying (though I do appreciate the gay porn) will account for dodging a bullet, because a bullet is not something anybody should be sorry to miss. The future is here, so why am I the old bitch, the one who is still running out of time, natural time that is, why am I the only one all set to see it. These two young boys with everything to look forward to instead choose to run backwards and to be honest it offends me. Of course I said none of this when I told him that he was not the company I was expecting tonight so get the fuck out of my house.

I look at the boy, the one who has a future marked on his face. The one who will most likely find something like love, something like marriage, something like a family, and the fact that all he wants to be is a damaged faggot makes me want to strangle him. But the only cruelty I have is words. So when he asked me what I know about this company that is coming, I said he both spits and swallows.

“You don’t have to go on like some cunt about it,” he said.

“Oh, my mistake. I thought abuse was what you came here for.”

“Okay then.”

“Seriously though, Mr. Porteous, why are you here? Again. We’re not friends, you know.”

“Why? Why you saying that?”

“Because, young man, you have this idea that surviving trauma makes us some sort of brothers, or friends, or whatever, but you never experienced the fucking trauma. You didn’t even witness it. You didn’t hear about it but read it.”

“I was at the hospital the next day.”

“Chasing the news or the ambulance?”

“All right. Okay. So this really is it, when the old battyboy turn into a real pussyhole.”

“Turn? Boy I was the sourest sourpussy from I was nine years old. But you still haven’t answered my question.”

“Which is—”

“What. The. Fuck. You. Doing. Here? To find out about me? That not what the phone is for? You want glad tidings of great joy? Send a letter. You want me to count the many reasons why we are not friends, boy?”

“Me not trying to be your friend. Nowadays we call it being a good person. Maybe a human being.”

“For who?”

“What the fuck?”

“For who? You being a good person for who? So you come in here in the goodness of your heart and can you believe it? When you leave I will be in the same place as when you came. I won’t be richer, I won’t live longer, I won’t see better, and my faith in humanity will be where it always fucking is. But you, when you leave, you must be bomboclaat high.”

“Oh. So you think I come here to feel better about myself. That I go home and tell me mummy that I do a good deed today.”

“No, not like that. I don’t think you tell her anything. You just walk back into your house feeling so much lighter, like you on a fucking cloud.”

“Maybe I just feel sorry for you, Havelock.”

“Fuck off. No, for real, fuck off.”

“Maybe you flattering yourself,” he said, and I saw a look in his eyes I never saw before. I can’t describe it, only that it made me feel cheated and desolate.

“Maybe all I feel for you is pity.”

“Me say get out of me bomboclaat house!” I shouted.

He turned away from me so that I wouldn’t see the look on his face when he walked out.

Havelock

December 31

Mark,

We might as well begin with his visits, for after that night in 1995 Jordan Brown broke into my house all the time. Never using the front door because the homo is allowed one moment of drama and that was his. Two things: First, I thought of just leaving a window open but that would be an open invitation to every thief in Kingston, not just him. Second, I really did begin to wonder how safe I was with this non-burglar so easily breaking into my house. Sometimes it would be every two weeks or so. Other times it would be two, three, even four months and I would assume whatever he was doing finally caught up with him until he appeared sitting at the side of my bed, laughing as I screamed out. At least Eddy used the front door.

So, 1996. Eight years since the thing. I think it was August. I began to wonder how this boy was supporting himself. No career, no inheritance, some proceeds from selling the funeral home, or maybe Paul Royale was again whoring him out. Jordan must have been in his late twenties now, almost twice the age of the kind of boy that Royale gives Devon House ice cream to fatten him up. I wondered where he slept, knowing that he has laid his head down in cars, on floors, in trees, and in the bed of countless men. But when he slipped into my house that August night what I saw was exhaustion. He gasped out every word to the point where I wondered if something was going on with his heart. I had not seen him for four months.

“Thought you shuffled off this mortal coil for real this time,” I said, thinking wit would hide that this boy had scared the shit out of me.

“Fear or wish?” he asked.

“I am not getting up to make you tea.”

“I know where it is,” he said, and I met him in the kitchen. He made some sarcastic crack about my pyjamas, a warning for the full onslaught that might come later.

“You keeping yourself good, Havelock.”

“Can’t say the same for you, young boy.”

“What you call the opposite of good, clean living?”

I honestly didn’t have an answer, but I noticed how the silence was eating him up. I didn’t say a thing as he put three different kinds of tea in a mug and turned on the hot water.

“Kettle is right there.”

“Don’t like waiting.”

“Since when?”

He smiled. Awkward moment over. He was so shifty and nervous, as if home space was something alien and he had to tell himself this is a counter, this is a table, this is a chair, and you can sit anywhere. “Sit where you want,” I said to him, and he propped himself up on the counter. There he was, Jordan Brown, but even when he was just a boy you only saw it after somebody hurt him.

“Something about crossing a line, no true? Make you realise that line is just shit somebody write in chalk. No line at all,” he said.

“Boy I come through the ’70s.”

“Meaning what?”

“Hippies, Bahá’í, Rastafari, Moonies, Children of God, Heaven’s Gate, Jim Jones, enlightenment can come from anywhere and anything, even inside a bubblegum wrapper.”

“I don’t get what you—”

“Cut the pop psychological bullshit and say what you want to say.”

Either it was too easy to shock him back into the child he still is, or he came here looking for it. For himself, rather. Remember I am the one he comes to when he wants to cry all night. He’s been doing this since the late ’80s.

I know what you have been dying to ask but can’t find a proper way to. The answer is no, I have never known the boy in the biblical sense. Squeeze a cracked cup and all you will do is shatter it. That is all I have to say on the matter.

“What is the evilest thing you ever think of doing, and then you do it?” he asked.

“Did it.”

“Fuck off.”

“Set out to break a man’s heart.”

“Only that?”

“Then I did it.”

“Look how—”

“I sold his love letters to the Daily Mail,” I said. “Right before the police arrested him for cocksucking in Piccadilly. Everton was his name. Family committed him to an asylum, I mean it was either that or prison and doom for the entire family. The judge said his case was ‘not without hope’ and that he could indeed ‘rescue’ himself, so they put him right in the Bromley madhouse among retarded royals and Nazi ladies-in-waiting. Oh, the family tried to pay me off. Then they tried to threaten me. Then they tried to kill me. Then they figured out how to get me to leave while still keeping my thick nayga lips shut. Poor Everton spent so much time in Bromley that he really did go mad. They didn’t let him out until the Patients in the Community Act forced them to. Want to hear the second one?”

“Ball is yours, might as well serve.”

“The other one I left to rot in a jail cell after the local police arrested him for fucking another man in his car right out on Palisadoes. I loved my safety more than I loved him, so that was that.”

“I swear every time I talk to you I want to sing that song, Bwoi yuh a boy and yuh no man yet,” he said.

I think the Coombes death unhinged Jordan in ways that he did not have words for despite being both chatty and convinced of his own brilliance. It did to him what breaking a taboo always does, which is to make you feel condemned and invincible at the same time. Remember when doing anything queer, even touching another man, felt like going too far? When everything you did after that came with an inside voice screaming, I fucking did it? Jordan was still on the counter. Maybe he was trying to look alluring, not the first time he tried to inject that kind of tension between us, but to me he looked skinnier and hungrier. And sadder.

“People think past is past and you can’t go back and fix it. Bullshit. The one thing I remember from history class is that the past change all the raas time. All the time. You can go back, Havelock. You can fix it.”

“What you talking ’bout now?”

“Ever read Song of Solomon? The Toni Morrison novel, not the Bible story.”

“Can’t say I have.”

“You should. There’s an ah…what you call it…ah…a side story. Not even the main plot. So this part? It’s about these black men, seven of them. I don’t remember how they come together but what they do is, every time white people commit some atrocity on a black somebody, they commit one back on white people. Part of me wish the whole novel was about them. Don’t matter who, when, or where. Don’t even matter if the white person is guilty of the actual crime. Beat a nigger to death in Columbus, we goin’ bludgeon a honky to bits in Boulder. Don’t matter who he is, hell he or she might even be a nigger lover. This is not in the book, but say a white woman throw boiling water on a black maid. We drive up to the first white woman we see and scald the fucking bitch. They don’t have a second thought when they kill one of us, don’t care that the man was a father, son, husband, deacon, so we don’t give a fuck who we kill either. Let his fucking family starve because the breadwinner dead. The main character tried to make it seem like a bad idea, like the kind of idea that will kill your soul from the inside, in fact that is exactly what it does. But he didn’t count for the person whose inside dead already. See, on the surface it’s random, reckless, but in the grand scheme of things it balances out.”

“Jesus, Jordan. I don’t think I want to hear the rest of this.”

“Oh, don’t worry, Titus. I am anything but random. I mean, that would just be chaos.”

“Jordan.”

“Meaning the people I hunt might not be guilty of the crime, but they guilty of something.”

“Hunt, Jordan? You serious?”

“Rebut it then, Havelock. You look like you used to run the school debating club. Give me one line and I might even stop. Eye for an eye we all end up blind? Good. It’s what we see that make us judge, so fuck sight. We better off without it. It solves nothing? Me look like me on a bomboclaat solution mission? Revenge leaves you hollow inside? Who the fuck take on revenge to fill themselves up?”

“I wasn’t going to say anything.”

“You always have something to say.”

“I don’t have anything to say.”

“Bomboclaat say what you want say, to raas.”

“You the one who come here to talk. So talk.”

I don’t have much of a living room. A daybed and two dining chairs too ornate for dining. But he sits himself in the room and makes it look bigger. I am still in the kitchen, looking over at him. I want to say, Little boy, don’t you see how all of this is making you smaller? But instead I listen to him.

“You still don’t watch news, right? So let me stage-direct the scene for you. Up curtain, the scene is the men’s bathroom of the natural sciences building at the University of Technology. Early morning, leaves still wet from dew, sounds of traffic already. Enter from stage right, two boys, maybe eighteen, maybe nineteen, but two boys. They were most likely just pissing at the same urinal and shared a joke. Or they might have never seen each other before this scene. Looking for a regular thing—m4m. Discreet—m4m. Good-looking married guy looking for fun—m4m.

Bingo.

Married means no ties, no strings. Married also means he will go at it like this is his last time on earth. Married means a whirlwind that will sweep himself up with all he came with as soon as it’s done. Pictures are sent. He demands face pic first.

You Asian?

No.

You look Asian.

That sounds like a problem.

Not to be racist but I’m looking for a top…

You send a dick pic.

Holy moly.

Good enuf?

You must have some black in you.

You haven’t sent a face pic.

He is just as you pictured him, somebody who girls thought was the most handsome boy in high school. Face too thin, maybe drug-user-thin, cheekbones too sharp, lips too wide, mustache too thick, but in his brown eyes is that thing some people call a twinkle.

My wife hasn’t…well…in months.

You send another dick pic.

Jaysis. You up for now or later?

Now.

Condoms?

Have to.

You know sometimes when we do it, my wife’s hands touch me back there and she doesn’t know that just makes me lose my shit.

West Flagler and Northwest Le Jeune.

He doesn’t want to kiss. That’s a no-no, which is fine, because his breath is a no-no, too. He smells like somebody not allowed to smoke in the house. Tall and skinny, but missing-too-many-meals skinny, so let’s call him lanky. You thought he was mixed because his dick pic was, well, it just was. But he really is a white man and missing his left canine. Not gay-acting except for the slight hint of a swish and calling you girlfriend. Gay white men aping the sass of straight black women, the ridiculousness of the whole thing makes you chuckle. “What’s so funny,” he says. Then he lays out all the things he ain’t gonna do and two-thirds of them you’ve never heard of. “No, I don’t have poppers,” you reply when he asks.

Six Feet Under has a scene that plays in a parking lot but is exactly like this. You could never bring yourself to watch Queer as Folk. Gayness still had to feel as if it came on the screen by surprise or at least by accident, like you were watching an otherwise wholesome program when up jump the faggots. The thought springs a chuckle and the married man wonders what’s so funny. No answer so he says, “Are you laughing at me?”

“You want to do this missionary?” you ask.

“You always this boring, honey?”

It blows your mind that there are women out there mistaking this bitch for straight. Then he said some shit about never getting a word in, in the great state o’ Florida, and a man should be able to do what he wants to do.

“Texas.”

“Huh?”

“It’s the great state of Texas. Nobody calls Florida great.”

“Well, shit, ain’t you got a mouth on you. Now you gonna shut it and fuck me or what, darlin’?”

You expect him to add that Little League practice is over at four or something else that screams American dad, though grandpa could also apply. The sun abandoned you both hours ago and he’s talking again despite just telling you to shut up and the whole thing sounds ludicrous because it is ludicrous, but here you are, and he pushed you down on the bed and yanks your shoes socks pants briefs off, says “Holy moly” again and winks. You declaring again “I’m a top” competes with just lying there for whatever because these are the things that must happen to you. “I’m not a bottom” vanishes into the hum and rattle of the old air conditioner, set to maximum but failing to stop sweat. He won’t do oral. You didn’t ask and want to say, Bitch, I’m not in this room to make love either, but all that comes is “Okay.” He watches you as he undresses—this is supposed to be sexy, and it really should be but it isn’t. “I’m still waiting on the bitch to notice my tattoo,” he says, pointing to a mark on his left thigh that looks like an arrow. “You know I’m gonna ride the fuck out of you,” he says and crawls onto the bed.

And then this, he grabs both ankles. “I’m not a bottom” leaves your mouth but again it vanishes into the hum and rattle. And he squeezes them until they hurt, which makes him smile when you wince, and laugh that you’re still hard. “Holy moly, Chinaman,” he says, and you say that you’re not a Chinaman but it comes out like a whisper. Why is everything coming out as a whisper? The louder voice is in your head and he says how about if you just surrender?

“I didn’t clean out.”

“I don’t care.”

Still holding your calves he pushes your legs up and over and knee pins chest near the crook of your arms. This is really going to happen, he is really going to take it anyway. Your knees at the armpits crush your voice. “I don’t…I’m not…What are you…Okay.” Somehow he is on top of you but you are inside him. He is the bottom but still the top. “Oh yeah, sweetheart,” he says over and over, then squats down harder, heavier. Hurt, this is beginning to hurt, this squat on you in happy baby pose. Fuck him for making you think in yoga terms because the burn in your muscles is beginning to irritate. “New position,” you say, but he is still moaning “Oh yeah, sweetheart” over and over. And what comes to you right then is that struggle to be normal, which went on for so fucking long, saying no to your voice, falling down at the altar, believing in a delivering god—no, believing he will change you as long as you don’t ask him to change you and fighting your own self for so long because that’s what Jesus said, to deny yourself and pick up your cross. Still inside him but it feels like defeat.

“What’re you doin’, sweetheart? We’re right here? Where you goin’? Get back here. Get back hard, you son of a bitch. You don’t think I’m good enough, is that it? Huh? Huh? You nasty faggot. Fuck me, you piece of shit.”

Reeling from the sting of his slap you don’t notice the hands until they are around your throat crushing your Adam’s apple, cutting your breath off, chopping your scream in two. Never in the entire history of the whole fucking universe have eyes showed so much hate. That’s a lie. You’ve seen it on a dozen faces all at once, sometimes blurring into the same face, sometimes splitting into twelve again. Eyes that scream even when blank, hate so fucking real and fleshy that it had its own smell. These are the eyes that left scars on your back, the eyes that make you run for cover when men together simply shout. Eyes that shine when the room is dark are the same in Florida as they are in Kingston. You can feel the blood trapped in your face. Now is when these hands try to punch, “these” because they don’t feel like yours but he has pinned your knees harder into your chest and your arms can barely move. Jesus, this man is strong and he wants to kill you, that is what’s powering him and all you can do is land weak punches to the outside of his thighs, punches that turn into faggot slaps. You read somewhere that strangling a man to death takes an awful long time and this is awful. Shifting jerking twisting shouting nothing is working. And the son of a bitch is grinning. On the edge of a shit street in a shit town in a shit city in a shit state, you’ve paid for the whole week in advance, which means it will be three days before anybody discovers your corpse in a room nobody will bother to describe in the police report. Your cramped legs can’t push—look how hard he is and that fucking smile and his fingers are squeezing tighter like that alien that wraps its coil around your neck to fuck your mouth to leave a baby and you punch his thighs and shift and shift and shift until you finally free a left hand, which slaps his shoulders scratches his arms, digs into skin until under the nail is red and sticky, scratch his face, pull his hair, slap his fucking awful grin away. Pulling the bedsheets, clawing his nose, his stomping knees try to pin your hand. You have not been breathing for so long that your tongue tastes blue, so this is it, this is really it, maybe just surrender. But your left hand can’t stop won’t stop, but he is still fucking laughing still saying sweetheart fuck him fuck the world fuck my mother when she hears that her son died from apparent sexual misadventure and asks if they could inter me somewhere up there because she is more ashamed that this man fucked me than that he killed me and you know what you bitch I have always hated you from the day you sent me to primary school and made me stay in grade one when you knew I was supposed to be in grade two just because. But left hand is not having it, left hand is not playing dead or dying for real, left hand is desperate and on fire. He swings he slaps he taps he grabs for everything and drops it just as quick, the sheet, the pillow, the belt, the power cord of the bedside lamp. Left hand grabs bedside lamp and swings it right into the motherfucker’s smiling face. Knocks him clean off. Too many things to do at once, gather himself, think straight, block the next blow, laugh at me, fight back. But you are younger than him and quicker and this lamp base is the perfect grip so you swing and swing and slam and slam and hit and hit and stab and stab and he is still laughing, but he is gurgling and his left hand flops midway and the right hand flails around and neither is blocking his stupid head so you smash and smash and smash until inside of him splashes on you.

Between you showering off the blood, putting on clothes, and packing your suitcase, he doesn’t move. The motel photocopied your ID and maybe somebody in this city is named Thirwell Jones, but that person is not you. And heart pounding really is a thing, because it won’t stop, not even when you realize that the pump is powering you, from motel to cab to airport where you put yourself on standby for the first flight to Jamaica that will take you. This is not your place.

When his blood hit your face it was a second baptism.

The family doctor gives you Xanax and says consider taking something stronger because these shakes that hit you off guard can rock you to the bone. He doesn’t understand. You don’t want to be rid of the shakes, only regulate them so that you can feel them coming. And they are not shakes but shivers. Every morning for three weeks, you wake up already running from whatever is coming to get you: revenge, the police, a ghost, your mother who somehow heard what you thought about her. Every morning it comes over you, an ecstasy—there is no other word at having caused a turning point in your own body. What never comes is 1988, not even deliberately, not even through forcing yourself to think about the year. Scars on your back are on your fucking back and eyes look straight ahead. No mention of a body in a motel on American news. Maybe he was alive and maybe he also disappeared until he could find a car wreck to match his face, so that he could tell the wife. Look at you fooling you, says a voice that is unmistakably American and undoubtedly from your own head. That deh man dead. Deader than dead. A better man would not have felt empowered by this and by this you mean like an IV packed with nerve, balls, juice, and clarity was pumping itself into you.

Does anybody notice that the first sign when a battyman comes into his battymanhood is how he walks? Somewhere between a strut and a glide, a stride doubled up because now you step into every Jamaican space crotchfirst. In yuh fucking Levi’s Offenders. Fucking come for me if you bad.

Can’t beat all of you but I will drop one of you, so decide who wants to lose an eye or a finger or a tooth, who wants to gain a broken nose, or a ballpoint pen stabbed into your fucking neck because that is the price for killing me. T-shirt too black and too short and yes it says “Paradise Garage,” and fuck if you don’t have any idea what that means, only that a pretty face with biceps is holding a tambourine and this T-shirt is a whole sentence. Your Levi’s Offenders stuffed up to a whole new level of offense by subtracting underwear—holy moly, Chinaman.

Three months later you’ve stopped shaking without the Xanax. You’ve also walked from Half Way Tree to Trafalgar Road to Lady Musgrave Road in a pink T-shirt just to prove you could do it. Honestly, that nobody even cared was almost disappointing. Not just your left arm, but your other limbs have minds, too, and if you surrender to them they will take you where you never thought you would want to go. Like this place. It is 2:30 p.m. and nobody in Kingston is on their lunch break. You are at the law firm that celebrated its twentieth anniversary in church.

“Edmond Porteous?” you ask.

“Do you have an appointment?”

“New business. He was recommended.”

“I’m sure he was—”

“By Hector Matalon.”

“Matalon?”

“Yes.”

“Oh. I see. Let’s see if he is available, but you might have to come back. Mr. Porteous is very popular this week. Who should I say?”

“Rupert Holmes. Him not goin’ know me.”

“You don’t look like a Holmes.”

“Now you sound like me daddy.”

She bursts out laughing.

“Have a seat, Mr. Holmes. Just in case he is too tied up, can anybody else help?”

“No. Thanks, but no.”

After two minutes of assuring the receptionist that yes, you can wait, he comes out, a pile of papers masking his face. Eddy Porteous. You never thought he was handsome, or even sexy, not really, but still the most beautiful boy.

“Mr. Holmes, nice to meet you,” he says, taking your hand. “Rupert? Can I call you Rupert? This way.”

He takes you into his office right beside the corner, which sounds right because a corner office would have led to all sorts of assumptions. His firm is downtown, at the edge of the sea. His view is of ships coming into the harbor and planes about to land, ten miles away. A lawyer’s office, whatever that means. Big dark mahogany desk, no pictures, but they are probably stashed in a drawer. A library of leather-bound books and massive folders. The law. A black chair like a throne that looks like it would swallow him. He motions you to sit but you go to the window.

“Hope you don’t mind,” you say.

“Getting your steps in? Everybody on that nowadays,” he says with a smile. “Listen, I don’t know if you know that I only do civil stuff, and the boring stuff like taxes and will prep. The occasional lawsuit, but this is Jamdown, you know, that case goin’ take years.”

“Everything in my life take years.”

“Beg you pardon?”

“Still every bit, Eddy. You know what I want to know? At what point you start forgetting me. Because it’s a choice, right? At least it is for me.”

“Sorry, man, I know you?”

“No. Yes. In a sorta way. We go far back. When Shabba Ranks drop ‘Mr. Loverman,’ original version.”

“Shit, ’88, ’90? I don’t know. This don’t feel like a business convo.”

“Not a clue. Is weird how the brain work, eh? My father give me the most beating out of all his children yet I don’t remember a single occasion. Not one. But here I thought you had to go through trauma to forget it.”

“I mean, I feel it might be coming back but not goin’ lie. You drawing a blank still.”

“How often you drive on Lady Musgrave Road?”

“Every day, unfortunately. Legal briefs and traffic jams, that is what my life is.”

“No time for love?”

“Not sure that’s your business…Rupert, right.”

“Rupert this week.”

“You always this cryptic?”

“You didn’t know me for long, that might be it.”

“High school. I think I would remember you.”

“Guess I not so good-looking anymore. But you though. You still—”

“Hey, listen, I not—”

“It’s fine. ‘Dorothy has friends all over the place,’ that old fogy in the green jacket would say. I can just picture him saying it. Fucking velvet in the fucking heat.”

“All right, man, I don’t know what this is—”

“But something in your head saying, I must know him for sure. Trauma by association is a fucking thing. Me never know.”

“Maybe if you turn around and stop looking through the window, I could—”

“What happen to you that night.”

“What night?”

“The same year as ‘Mr. Loverman.’ God or the devil save you that night.”

You stay standing, still looking away. He is hovering, wondering.

“You still talk to him? He still wear that ragged green velvet jacket?”

“Green velvet…green velvet…Havelock Titus? You know him?”

“For fuck’s sake, Eddy. You have literally seen me drop my pants. You’ve seen me bleed. You almost saw me shit myself.”

“Wow. Ah…sorry, man, the liquor must did take over my head that night. Listen, I feel it. I know that I know you, or have met you, or maybe something else.”

“That’s not what you want to say. You want to say that you’re afraid that the way we know each other we can’t talk about. Don’t fret yourself. We never knew each other in the biblical sense. That beautiful black man at the church service is yours?”

First his face goes white. You see his reflection.

“Everything criss, man. Just did want to see your face.”

“You don’t want me to see yours.”

“Thought you saw enough. You was the only one, did you know? The only one who checked after me. See you later, handsome,” you say and turn. He grabs your shoulder.

“Hold on. You can’t just leave. I know that I know you. I know that I more than know you.”

“1988—”

“Stop saying that. It was nearly twenty years ago.”

“Mattachine Society. Ever hear ’bout it? I going to guess no. Founded in Los Angeles, United States, 1950, for boys like us. I don’t know if it was the first, but it was the first for boys like us. Or the first I ever hear ’bout.”

“You keep saying ‘boys like us.’ ”

“What the bloodclaat, man,” you whisper. “Mattachine Society.”

“Mattachine Society.”

“Mattachine.”

“Mattachine?”

“Matta…Chine.”

“Matta…Ch— I don’t catch this drift, brother, I don’t—”

You think he wants to remember and the words come out of you like they’ve been waiting there all this time.

“When in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes, / I all alone beweep my outcast state, / And trouble deaf heaven with my bootless cries, / And look upon—”

“Myself and curse my fate. Oh my G—”

“I’m Smitty. You must be Mona.”

But he says nothing. He just stares at you in disbelief and grabs your shoulder again, not to feel if you are real but because his knees are buckling under the weight of so much shock and sorrow.

Acknowledgments

More than anything else, The Disappearers is a return to a home I barely knew. The novel is total fiction. The novel actually happened. In all the stories I love, both sentences tend to be true, so I hope that is the case here.

Thanks first and foremost to the Jamaica LBGTQ+ community for letting me into their lives and sharing their histories, tragedies, and triumphs.

As always for support, guidance, second-guessing, generosity, fantastic dinners, outrageous laughs, and blind faith, thanks to: my miracle working agent Ellen Levine, my (now longtime) editor Jake Morrissey, my (even longer-time) assistant Jeffrey Bennett, my UK editor Simon Prosser for the extra eyes, and my family for the extra love.

Massive big-ups to Geoffrey Kloske, Jynne Dilling Martin, and everyone at Riverhead Books; Ingrid Riley, from back when we were living this fiction; Steven Barclay; Paul Morrison, Patrick Waldemar, Nathaniel Muir, Herman Pinnock, Leasho Johnson, artist and longtime inspiration for the cover; Larry Chang, and the life-changing sisters, brothers, and others at The Gayly News; the Gay Freedom Movement; J-FLAG; the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture; Sara James, Richard James, Andre James, Michelle James, Claude Fletcher, Odessa Chambers, Lisa Lucas, Saeed Jones, Teddy Goff, Christopher Jerrolds, Isaac Fitzgerald, Che Cowan, Leopoldo Gout, Brian Montopoli, Stephen Winter, the Boggs Family, the James family, the Dillon family, my chosen families, John Wray (whom I probably owe rent), Rachel Eliza Griffiths (soul sis), Salman Rushdie, Lena Waithe, Stephanie Mei-Ling, Mary Karr, and Max. You done know.

I suspect that while he was writing Baldwin, A Love Story, it had not occurred to my partner, Nicholas Boggs, that he was also laying out the blueprint for how to be an artist in this world while staying true to one’s own soul. Sharing your art is one of the many ways you love, so for all the ways you show me love, thank you.

My mother celebrates her ninetieth birthday this year, so she can read whatever she wants.

About the Author

Marlon James is the Booker Prize–winning and New York Times bestselling author of A Brief History of Seven Killings; the bestselling and National Book Award finalist Black Leopard, Red Wolf; as well as the bestselling Moon Witch, Spider King; The Book of Night Women; and John Crow’s Devil. In addition to the Booker Prize, James’s novels have won the Amer­ican Book Award, the Anisfield-Wolf Book Award, the Dayton Literary Peace Prize, the OCM Bocas Prize for Caribbean Literature, and the Los Ange­les Times Ray Bradbury Prize for Science Fiction, and have been finalists for the National Book Critics Circle Award and the NAACP Image Award. The recipient of a Guggenheim Fellow­ship and named in 2019 one of Time magazine’s one hundred most influential people in the world, James lives in New York City.
